FACTS ABOUT SCGAR.—Nowadays, especially in London, people have great fancy for Demarara sugar, which they innocently suppose comes from the country of that name. Most of it no doubt comes either from Denaarara or from some neighbouring part, but there is a variety of " Demerara " about which we have secrets to tell. This is called " Whitechapel Demarar' a " because in that delightful neighbourhood it takes its birth. We do not mean that it , is grown there, for it comes originally from the Continent, in the form of white " French crystals" made from beet- , root. But sugar refiners have found out the public mind, , and they know that people have a prejudice against beet- root, and like to think they are eating the produce of the i sweet juicy sugar cane. And so they turn the white— rather dirty white—beet crystals from the bags, and spread , them upon the door; and then they pour upon them some , of the molasses which are the drainings of West India hogs- , heads, and have therefore the smell of sugar made from the cane, and men go with their naked feet and trample the , syrup into the crystals by a kind of wriggling movement, until a spurious Demerara is produced. The men who do , this are called the "Tipperary Gang," and are supposed sometimes to wash their feet; but we know on good autho- rity that a large producer of sugar once, watching the motions of a gang, felt constrained to address one of his men thus: "My lad, don't you think you could get a bit of the crust off ?"—Design and Work. INVENTION OF SHODDY.—Several years ago the writer was staying at an hotel in London, when, some one remark- ing in the commercial room that he came from Yorkshire, the jesting talk turned on shoddy, and he was asked who in- vented it. He replied that it was attributed by one local report to a Benjamin Parr, of Batley, and by another to a Benjamin Law. "Eh, wilt is that you are saying about the invention of shoddy ?" broke in an elderly Jewish gen- tleman. "You're quite mistaken—neither Law nor Parr invented it; they Only adopted it. My father was the very first man who ever thought of or made it." "How was it, and when ?" was the general inquiry. "Well, I'll tell you about it," replied our Jewish friend, "exactly as my father used often to tell me. It arose thus: My father was an exten- sive dealer in second-band clothes in Whitechapel here, and when the Peninsular War broke out, after old Bonaparte had overrun Spain, owing to the stoppage of the supply of Spanish wool and the brisk demand for army goods for the contemplated expedition to Spain of Sir John Moore and the rest, Spanish wool, which was 'then used for making them, rose to a great price, and My father, who, as a 'clothes-duffer,' had been used to seeing the lot of woollen dust, or 'mill-puff,' as it was then called, brushed off the old clothes in preparing them afresh for market, got a new idea in his head. It occurred to him," he said, "that if he bought wool in London, opened the bales, and inserted amongst the fleeces 50 per cent, of old blankets or white flannels, torn up with currycombs into fibre again, it would be a paying speculation. He consequently flung aside his second-hand coats and trousers and covered his ' duffing- cushions ' with old blankets, and sent off a lot of 'doctored' bales, and realised full prices in Yorkshire. When my fa- ther first began to tear up the old blankets into shcddy he was able to buy them at 4th each, but he had not been at work over a month before they rose to the price of Is. He kept at this work till wool fell in value, and then turned to making flocks for stuffing saddles and inattrasses, to replace weol, which had previously been used for those purposes. That, gentlemen, was the origin of 'shoddy," concluded our informant, putting his cigar into his mouth again, and casting a glance of triumph towards us. This gentleman gave no absolute date as being that on which his father began his shoddy pulling, but as between 1803 and 1805-6 wool rose on the average some 32 per cent, in price it will be safe to place the genesis of his operations about the latter date. I have made considerable effort, and spent some time in researches, to acquire proof or otherwise of the above anecdote,as I did not at the time ask the narrator his name, and from various quarters, both in London and Yorkshire, have gained information corroborative of its general ac- curacy, and am led to believe that the narrator's name was a Mr. Davis, who then or afterwards carried on an extensive business as an outfitter and merchant tailor in Cheapside, under the style of Moses, Son, and Davis. The name shoddy itself is also Confirmatory, as it is of Persi-Arabic extrac- tion apparently, being a modification of " Shodjah," which signifies "a mass of tangled fibres," and other cognate ideas, and testifies to the Semitic origin of the inventor of the article.—Textile Manufacturer.

TOMMY WORMALD AND THE OUT-PATIENTB.--SOIMe years since, rich people of a mean sort would drive down to St. Bartholomew's and get gratuitous advice, as out-patients. Tommy was determined to stop this abuse, and he did it by a series of outrageous assaults on the self-love of the offenders. Noticing a lady, dressed in silk, who had driven up to the hospital in a brougham, Tommy raised his rich, thunderous, sarcastic voice, and, to the inexpre.,sihle glee of a roomful of young students, addressed the lady thus : " Madam, this charity is for the poor, destitute, miserable invalids of London. So you are a miserable invalid in a silk dress—a destitute invalid, in a rich silk di ess—a poor invalid, in a dress that a duchess might wear. Madam I refuse to pay attention to miserable, destitute invalids, who wear rich silk dresses. You had better order your carriage, madam." The lady did not come again—Cannel's "Old and New London," _ _

. .. CHASING A CDTTLE.—A RACE FOR LIFE.—On the 26th of April, 1875, a very large Calamary was met with on the north-west of Boffin Island, Conn, mara. The crew of a " curragh" (a boat made like a "coracle," with wooden ribs covered with tarred canvas) observed to seaward a large floating mass surrounded by gulls. They pulled out to it, believing it to be a wreck, but to their astonishment found that it was an enormous cattle-fish, lying perfectly still, as if basking on the surface of the water. Paddling up with caution, they lopped off one of its arms. The animal im- mediately set out to sea, rushing through the water at a tremendous pace. The men gave chase, and after a hard pull in their frail canvas craft, came up with it, five miles out in the open Atlantic, and severed another of its arms and the head. These portions labelled Arehileuthie dux, can now be seen in the Dublin Museum. The shorter arms measured each eight feet in length and fifteen inches round the base. The tentacular arms are said to have been thirty feet long.—Cassell's Natural History. RUSSIAN Konariss.—This, the favourite alcoholic drink of the nom, die tribes in Southtastern Russia, is made from mares' milk. The excellent effect it has on weak constitu- tions, and on persons brought down very low by disease and exposure, was known long ago to the nomads; but it is only during the last thirty years that the medical faculty has made al y use of it. Up to this day its effects are not closely studied, but it may be stated that it is a rich food, easily assimilated, and of very beneficial effect on the energy of the physiological processes in the human body. The pre- paration of koumiss is simple. Some old koumiss is poured into a vessel, and fresh milk is added. The whole is stirred violently for fifteen minutes, and then again for a few minutes every few hours. The next morning some more milk is added, and the same treatment is pursued during the day. In the evening the koumiss may be passed through a sieve (to hold back the casein) and filled into bottles. Some of it is, however, reserved to be used as fe, merit for a new leaven. In three days after bottling the koumiss may be used, but it may be readily kept another fortnight and even longer, growing stronger all the while.„ The bottles must be strong and the stoppers secured, otherwise the bottles will burst and the stoppers be driven out by the force of the carbonic acid which is developed. The temperature of the room in which koumiss is made ought not to be below 60 degrees Fahr.—"Dairy Farming," by Professor Sheldon, for May. t THE MERCHANT OF VENICE.-A friend states that he overheard the following conversation between bootblacks on Vine-street, about six weeks ago:—" Say, Skinny, where was you last night ?" " Me? I was up ter Renck's. Where was you ?" " I was down ter Pike's ter see 'The Merchant. of Venice.'" " Wot kind of a piece is it, Bill? Wot'e it about?" "Well, Skinny, it's first class, an' no inis- talze. Yer see, there's a cove in it named 13ossanyo, an' he's dead struck on er gal named Porsher, an' he wants to marry her, but he ain't got the scads to go housekeeping. So he goes to a friend of his'n named Antonio, wot keeps boats to let, and tries to borrow the sugar off'n him. Well, biz, d'ye see, hasn't been very brisk with Tony fer awhile hack, and he hasn't got the ready cash ' • but, as Bassanyo hez done him many a good turn, he sea he'll get it for 'im. Well, he ups and goes to an old pawnbroker named Sheelock, an: strikes him for the ducats. Well, d'ye see, this yer Shea- lock doesn't like Tony for a cent, 'cause he called him tuff names, and camped him a time or two onct down to the market-house. Howsumdever, he at last agrees to let Tony hey the money, provided he'd promise to give him a pound of flesh next his heart, d'ye see, if he can't make good when the dust is due. Tony says 'Swipes,' and the bargain's made. Well, Bassanyo and Porsher got spliced, an' go off on a bridal tower or suthin, and hey a happy old time all to themselves. Bimeby, the river freezes up or suthin, and the boat-hiring business gets awful dull, and when hia little note falls due, Tony hasn't got the wherewithal to liquidate. 'Come and see me,' sez Sheelock. 'Sorry for that, old man,' sez Tony' 'but yer had better come around this day a month. I'll be better heeled then.' Well, wot does the old duffer do but go off'n and get a warrant, and jerks Tony inter gaol. Well, when Bassanyo hears this he skirrnises around like fun, and by the day of the trial he has enuff of wealth to take up the note ten times over, but Sheelock won't hey it that way, and swearsthat he'll hey his pound of flesh or bust up the bull city government. Just as things look mighty rocky for Tony, in comes Porsher disguised like a lawyer. She makes a big talk, an' to hear her go on you'd think she was dead agin Tony. All of a suddent she wheeled around, an' sez she to Sheelock, says she, 'lt's all right for Ter pound of meat, old man, but nixey en ter blood" an' when she said that, Sheelock looked meaner nor pizen, as yon could hey knocked hina over with a club."—Cincinnati En- "dram

Asmostosty.—A teacher in a western county in Canada, while making his first visit to his "constituents," got into conversation with an ancient " Varmonnt " lady who had taken up her residence in the " backwoods." Of course the school and former teacher came in for criticism, and the old lady, in speaking of his predecessor, asked, "Weal, master, what do you think he larnt the scol lards ?" "Couldn't say, ma'am. Pray what did he teach ?" "Waal, he told 'ern that this 'air airth was reound, and went areonnd, and all that sort of thing. Now, master, what do you/think about sich stuff? Don't you think he was an ignorant feller ?" Unwilling to come under the category of the ignorami, the teacher evasively remarked, "It really did seem strange but still there are many learned men who teach these things." "Waal," said she, "if the airth is reound, and goes reound, what holds it up ?" "Oh, these learned men say it goes around the sun, and that the sun holds it up by virtue of attraction," he replied. The old lady owered her "-specs," and, by way of climax, responded, "Waal, if thee high larnt men sez the sun holds up the airth, I should like tiz know what holds the airth up when the sun goes down!"

HER MAJESIY'S PRIME MINISTERS, LORD PALMERSTON. When in 1852 Lord Aberdeen became Prime Minister, Lord Palmerston was made Home Secretary, and during the early period of the Crimean War we find him plodding on at the Horne Office as if there was no such thing as Foreign Politics, and as if smoke nuisances and sewer nuisances were the only great themes of Ministerial anxiety. He dilated upon manure, and informed the world that "dirt was only a good thing in the wrong place." He discussed the subject of cholera, and informed the English public that cleanliness was a more certain preventative than prayer. In this last piece of advice it was wittily said that the Foreign Secre- tary peeped out—he treated Providence as a Foreign Power. But when the Ministry-of-all-the-Talents broke down in 1855, the question at once arose, Who shall be Prime Minis- ter? Who shall take the helm and conduct the vessel of State through the storm, and bring her into her desired haven? Lord Derby was the first to be summoned into the presence of the Queen, and certainly he did all in his power to accomplish the task with which her Majesty had en- trusted him. He invited Lord Palmerston to join him, and it was intimated that if he consented Mr. Disraeli would waive all claim to the leadership of the House of Commons, in order that Palmerston should have the place. But Pal- merston did not see his way to join a Derby Administration, and without him Lord Derby could not go on. The Queen then sent for Lord John Russell, but his precipitate retreat from office on the 23rd of January had discredited him with most of his colleagues, and he soon found that he could not get a Government together. It was now the 4th of Feb., and the country was still without a Government, although at war with Russia. This state of things was producing the worst effects abroad. That very day Lord Cowley wrote from Paris to Lord Clarendon :—" I wish to heaven that a Government of some sail was formed. I cannot exaggerate the mischief that the state of things is causing to our repu- tation as a nation, or the disrepute into which it is bringing Constitutional Government." In this dilemma the Queen lost no time in addressing herself to Lord Palmerston, and asking him whether "he could undertake to form an Ad- ' ministration which would command the confidence of Par- liament and efficiently conduct public affairs in this momen- tous crisis." Lord Palmerston replied in the affirmative, and in a few days submitted to her Majesty the names of thoee who would compose his Cabinet. It most have been a proud day for him when, in answer to the long series of attacks upon him, he was elevated to the highest office in the State, as the only man able and ready to carry out that Policy of a war with Russia and an alliance with the French Emperor which had been the source of misunderstandings innumerable and recriminations without end. It showed, also, immense courage on his part that he was willing to undertake this arduous task with the assistance of a Cabinet which Lord Brougham is said to have characterised as "a staff of eleventh-rate men." We read in Luther's Table Talk that Maximilian one day burst into a great laugh. On being asked the cause— " Truly," he said, "I laughed to think that God should have trusted the spiritual government of the world to a drunken priest like Pope Julius, and the government of the Empire to a chamois hunter, like me." We have it in evi- dence that an idea of this kind used to flash through Lord Allthorp's honest brain. In his retirement at Broadlands Lord Palmerston may have indulged in a similar laugh. The last thing he seemed to aspire to was the Premiership. It was offered to him, and he could not well refuse it. On the 15th February, 1855, we find him writing in this fashion to his brother, Sir William Temple—" A month ago, if any man had asked me to say what was one of the most impro- bable events, I should have said my being Prime Minister. Aberdeen was then in office. Derby was head of one party —John Russell of the other; and yet in about ten days' time they all gave way like straws before the wind, and so here I am writing to you from Downing-street." Further on he adds, "I am backed by the general opinion of the whole country, and I have no reason to complain of the least want of cordiality or confidenee on the part of the Court." The first question which the re-constituted Ministry found itself compelled to deal with was that which had caused the resignation of Lord Aberdeen. Three of its , ablest and most distinguished members—Sir James Graham, Mr. Gladstone, and Mr. Sydney Herbert—had offered a strenuous opposition to the appointment of Mr. Roebuck's Committee, and their objection to it was still strong and de- cided. Lord Palmerston proposed the adoption of a middle course. He felt that a very large majority, both in the House and out of it, were bent on an investigation—that it would be useless to oppose it; but he hoped to save the honour of the Government by substituting another Com- mittee selected by the Government whose names he thought would inspire confidence in their decisions, for that which Mr. Roebuck had proposed. Mr. Roebuck accepted the altered list, but the three gentlemen who had originally de- I precated the inquiry were not satisfied with this arrange- ment, and gave in their resignations. Sir James Graham was succeeded be Sir Charles Wood, Mr. Gladstone by Siri C. Lewis, and Mr. Sydney Herbert by Lord John Russell. ' Thus, almost before the new Ministry was installed, it un- derwent a most important change. Lord Aberdeen and the Duke of Newcastle had now been followed into retirement' by the rest of the Peelites. The admission of Lord John Russell into the Cabinet, while proving that its chief was the most placable of an- tagonists, and that he could work with anybody who would work with him, interposing no difficulty on the ecore of past quarrels, proved to be a source of danger to the new Administration. Lord John Russell had been sent as the English Plenipotentiary to the Congress at Vienna, and had returned, the negotiations having failed for the time. "On the 24th of May, Mr. Disraeli brought forward a motion condemning the ambiguous language used by the Govern- ment in reference to the continuance of the war. In op- posing this motion, Lord J. Russell adopted a tone so war- like, he so strongly condemned the propeeals that had been made at Vienna, that all his hearers imagined that the negotiations there had been broken off with his approval; indeed, Mr. Roebuck afterwards declared that, having pre- viously intended to vote against the Government, he had been induced by this speech to support it." The warlike tone of Lord John Russell's speech led to a manifesto from Count Buol, the Austrian Plenipotentiary at the Vienna Conference, in which attention was called to the inconsis- tency of Lord John Russell's language in Parliament with that which he had held in his coafidential interviews with Count Buol at Vienna. On this document being made pub- lic, Mr. Milner Gibson lost no time in seizing the vantage ground which it gave to himself and his friends of the Peace Party. Accordingly, on the 6th of July, he asked for an explanation on the subject, and succeeded in eliciting from Lord Russell the admission that he had been of opinion that the terms proposed at the Conference, and to which Russia was willing to accede, were such as, in his opinion, ' would have afforded the basis of a satisfactory peace; but that, not being authorised to agree to them, he had rejected them against his own judgment, though he had subse- quently come over to the opinion entertained respecting them by the rest of his colleagues that they were inadmis- sable, and had expressed that opinion in his speech on Mr. Disraeli's motion. This explanation, however, was received with great dissatisfaction both by the House and by the country. It was clear Lord John had made a series of mis- takes, and the Prime Minister, writing to the Queen, and referring to the discussion on the explanation of his Foreign Secretary, said, " This evening in the House of Commons has not been an agreeable one." The temptation which "Lord John's embarrassing escapade," as the Prince Con- sort called it in a letter to Baron Stockmar, afforded for dealing a blow at the Ministry was irresistible, and on the 10th of July Sir Edward Bulwer Lytton gwe notice of the following motion:—" That the condi ct of Lord John Russell at the recent negotiations at Vienna has in the opinion of the House shaken the conduct of the country in those to whom its affairs are entrusted." After this it be- came apparent to Lord John that his continuance in office could only embarrass and endanger his colleagues, and on the 13th—the day appointed for the discussion of Sir Ed- ward Bulwer Lytton's motion—Lord John Russell himself announced to the House that he was no longer a Minister. The danger was averted, and public distrust was appeased by this honourable sacrifice on the part of the "guilty Member." We have observed that Lord Palmerston was the most placable of antagonists, and hence the appearance of Lord John Russell in his Cabinet, and the consequent result. We have further to observe that he never forsook a subordinate. In this respect his generosity sometimee outran his pru- dence, and he took upon himself the responsibility of other people's blunders, which not only impaired his own reputa- tion, but sometimes committed him to a doubtful policy. An illustration of this is found in his conduct in relation to China. In 1857 hostilities were commenced with the Celestial Empire, and a very strong feeling prevailed in this country that the Government had one rule for the weak and I another for the strong, and that the conduct of Sir J. Bow- ring, our plenipotentiary, for which the Government was responsible, had been characterised by overbearing inso- lence towards the Chinese authorities. This feeling had been expressed in the House of Lords by Lord Derby, who brought forward a motion condemning the conduct of the Government, but it had been rejected by a majority of 36. On the same evening Mr Cobden in the House of Commons moved—" That this House has heard with concern of the conflicts which have occurred between the British and the 11 Chinese authorities in the Canton river; and without ex- pressing an opinion as to the extent to which the Govern- ment of China may have afforded this country cause of complaint respecting the non-fulfilment of the Treaty of 1842, this House considers that the papers which have been laid upon the table fail to establish satisfactory grounds for the violent measures resorted to at Canton in the late affair of the 'Arrow;' and .that a Select Committee be :appointed to inquire into the state of our commercial relations with China." The debate which followed was one of singular ability. The policy adopted was denounced not only by Mr. Cobden, but by such men as Mr. Gladstone, Sir James Graham, Lord John Russell, and Mr. Disraeli. The bom- bardment of Canton was described by Mr. Whiteside as "an onslaught upon old men, women, and children, based upon a miserable, contemptible, and cowardly quibble:" Mr. Philli more characterised the war as "unjust in its origin, and nnblest in its continuance;" while the Govern- ment policy was denounced by Mr. Rouniell Palmer "as discreditable in itself, and utterly unlikely to exalt the reputation of this country amongst Western or Oriental nations." Lord Palmerston defended, with great spirit, the policy of his Government, asserting that the op- position to the Government policy Li China on the part of the Conservatives was a mere party move. Replying to this taunt, Mr. Disraeli said: —"Every wove in the House

div.head: I MISCELLANEOUS.
div.p: I MISCELLANEOUS.

The Suez Canal is again open for traffic. The news of the wreck of the steamer Tararua off Otago, with an appalling loss of life, is telegraphed from Mel- bourne. It is stated that 80 persons were drowned. On Tuesday night a serious accident occurred on the North Wales Narrow Guage .Railway, whereby one man
was killed and three seriously injured.' The statue to Sir Rowland Hill at Kidderminster was

placed on the pedestal on Tuesday. The inaugural cere- mony has been postponed beyond the time first proposed. At Lewe§ assizes, John Williams, charged with the murder of a fellow labourer in a fight, was convicted of manslaughter, _ .

and sentenced to 18 months' 'imprisonment. A destructive fire occurred on Tuesday at the Be.ehive Cotton Spinning Mill, Stockport, the property of Messrs. 'I. and J. Leigh. The building, a modern and substantial one, was entirely gutted. Edwin Briscoe, bittnaker, Walsall, cut the throat of his step-daughter, Mrs. Baker, and then committed suicide by cutting his own throat. Mrs. Baker was removed to the hospital, and is going on favourably. By a fire on Tuesday at the extensive confectionery works

of Messrs. Lindsay and Law, Dundee, damage to he ex- tent of £15,000, covered by insurance, was done, and over 100 workpeople were thrown out of employment. Mr. H. Crossley, local newspaperproprietor, has consented to contest Knaresborough in the Conservative interest. Mr. T. Collins (Independent Conservative) remains in the field, and Mr. Miles Gaskell (Liberal) is actively canvassing. At the Central Criminal Court, George Harris,late cashier and manager to Mr. Graves, publisher, was found guilty of stealing three cht:ques, valued at £2OO, £lO5, and £5OO, and sentenced to seven years' penal servitude. Christina Marshall, aged 14, residing at Strathaven, has, it is alleged, entered upon the eighth week of her fast. The doctors can find no ttace of internal disease, but she is gradually growing weaker. Mr. Price, district coroner, held n niuest on Monday on the body of Edith Maud Watson, aged 13 months, who was stabbed to death by her father, Aratur Watson, on Fri- day, at Old Trafford. A verdict, of " Witful murder " against Arthur Watson was returned. Mr. Fawcett intends, it is stated, to make an expqriment in the General Pest Office which will h. 3 v, etched with great interest and sympathy by the public. He has decided to give employment to a number of deaf-and-dumb persons in the uepartment devoted th the sorting of newspapers. Mr. Bradlangh, affilressing a town's meeting at Northamp- ton n Saturday, denied that his cause would have been strengthened had he refused to take the oath. Had he done so his seat might have been declared vacant. The meeting unanimously condemned the course taken in preventing Mr. Bradlaugh from taking his seat. A shocking murder was committed in Manchester on Saturday. A telegraph clerk named Watson, after a quar- rel with his wife, who had left him and who reft.sed to retum to him, stabbed his infant child six times in the breast with a chisel. Some doubts are expressal as to the sanity of the prisoner, who was brought up at the police court on Saturday, and remanded. The number of immigrants landed at New York recently has been exceptionally large. There were over 60,000 in January; over 8,000 in February; over 9,000 in March; and nearly 30,000 in April; making a total for the first four months of the year of about 105,000—nearly 25,000 more than than the number received in the corresponding period
of last year. It is stated that Mr. Chamberlain has proposed to take into consideration a proposal of Mr. Macdonald, M.P., that . .

a clause should be Inserted in the Bankruptcy gill, making it applicable to the debts of working men who, through ill- ness or other misfortune, are unable to meet their engage- ments. It is understood that several difficulties now stand in the way of this proposal now being incorporated in

the bill. On Monday evening a complimentary dinner was given at the Lord Nelson Hotel, Urmston, to Mr. J. D. Prior, formerly general secretary of the Amalgamated Society of Carpenters and Joiners, but who has recently been appointed inspector of factories and woakshops in Birmingham and district. Mr. Prior was presented with a gold watch suitably inscribed and a cheque for 15 guineas. In a sermon which be preached at Middleton the Bishop of Manchester said he could not help but remark that the principles of true religion were not as much in the minds of the people of this country as was the case some 50 years ago. Much of the unhappy condition of Ireland might be attributed to the fact that in that country there was a want of the principle of "1)0 unto your neighbour as you would wish to be done by." A SPLENDID BIRTHDAY GIFT TO A SCHOOL BOARD.—Mr. Thomas Shaw, of Allangate, Halifax, has made a present of .£l,OOO to the Halifax School Board for the foundation of scholarships of yearly tenuse, and open to competition with- out regard to sex or religion of the children attending the public elementary schools. The gift is made to ass.ociate the coming of age of the son of the donor, Mr. Wm. Rawdon Shaw, with educational work. The School Board has accepted the offer, and tendered Mr. Shaw a cordial vote of thanks for his handsome bequest. Some of the French exiled Fathers of the Society of Jesus were walking in scattered groups of two and three, a ghort time ago, along a road at St. Heliers, when a man, driving rapidly past, struck at each party with his riding whip, and wounded in the faice six of the Fathers who were too much taken by surprise an be able either to detain or identify the assailant. One of them was Father Winners, the Pope's theologian at the Vatican Council. The perpetratca is well known, it seems, in Jersey as a person of some standing and wealth. A youth named William Henry Turner was charged at Sheffield, on Monday, with a brutal assault upon Mrs. Davidson, wife of a labourer. Prisoner's brother was using obscene language on Saturday night, and Mrs. Davidson came to the door and rebuked him. The prisoner thereupon ran at her, "punched" her in the body several times, and knocked her down. She was near her confinement, and a doctor certified her to be in a most dangerous condition. The prismer was remanded. At Birtningham, on Tuesday, a young man named Adams was charged with committing a burglary on the premises of a licensed victualler named Martin. The landlord heard a noise in the bar early that morning, and going down stairs was confronted by the prisoner, who pelted him with glasses, spittoons, and other utensils, and finally leaped through a large plate-glass window, shattering the glass into frag- ments, in the street 1 e was captured by a policeman, and was found to have ransacked the money till. Prisoner was committed for trial at the sessions. The Queen showed in a very marked way, on Saturday, her partiality for the late Earl of Beaconsfield. Her Majesty, accompanied by the Princess Beatrice, paid a visit to Hughenden, and placed a splendid wreath on the late Earl's tomb. The Queen's intentions had keen kept a strict secret, and there was no demonstration of any sort during the journey. Arrangements were made by which the Queen took "the exact road followed by the late Lord Beaconsfield ! when returning from Windsor Castle, where the noble earl L had been the guest of Her Majesty, on the 10th December . last?'

--- Mr. Bradlaugh, before the Appeal Court on Monday, sub- mitted that, having averred be had made affirmation in lieu of the oath, it should have been left him to prove at the time that he was a person permitted by statute to affirm. Lord Justices Bramwell, Brett, and Cotton, without calling on Sir H. Giffard, Q.C., who appeared for the plaintiff, were unani- mously of opinion that the statement for the defence was bad, because it did not raise the issue of fact that defendant came within the exception of persons entitled to affirm, but stated that he had affirmed. They accordingly gave judg- ment against Mr. Bradlaugh with costs. EXTRAORDINARY DEATH AFTER MArcettamt.—An inquest was held on Saturday at Fornham, on the body of William Turner. It appeared that the deceased, who was a builder, of Wrecclesham, drove a few days to the village of Heriard, near Alton, in order to be married to a young woman in the service of the Rev. G. Jones, the vicar of the parish. The marriage duly took place, and the deceased proceeded to drive his wife to her new home. He bad got about three miles on his journey when be fell from the trap in a kind of fainting fit. His wife attended to him as beat she could until assistance arrived. He was ultimately placed in the trap in a state of semi-tmconsciousness, and the services of a man were engaged to drive to Farnham. Before, how- ever, this place was reached the deceased expired in the arms of his newly-married wife. The medical evidence showed that death resulted from natural causes, and a ver- dict in accordance therewith was returned. MR. BRIGHT ON THE SIIGAR BOI7NTIES.—A conference of the committee of the Birmingham Trades' Council was held on Monday, condemning the foreign sugar bounties. A reeolution was passed urging the House of Commons to adopt remedial measures for the suppression of the export bounty system. Mr. Bright wrote as follows :—" I cannot come down to your intended public meeting on the Sugar Bounties Question. Whilst regretting that the bounty system exists I am quite unable to act with you and your friends in favour of what are called countervailing duties, whether as regards sugar or shipping, or any other article of trade. If I was of your opinion I should ask you to excuse me from being with you, under the pressure of business during the session; and when I do not agree with you, my presence would scarcely add to the harmony of your meet- ing. I need not telt you how much I regret not to be able to act with you in this matter." Mr. Chamberlain wrote in a similar strain, saying the Board of Trade had already et- pressed its views. Mr. Muntz expressed entire agreement with the meeting, but excused himself from illness. LIBERAL OROANISATION.—A meeting of representatives of Liberal associations in London and the home counties was held in the City Liberal Club, on Tuesday, for the pur- pose of organisising the party in the metropolitan and home Counties. Mr. S. Morley, M.P. presided, and explained that the object of establishing a central association was not for the purpose of ordering or directing, but to assist where there might be any slackness in the work. Over 2,200 gentlemen were present, and after considerable discussion, resolutions were carried for establishing an association for promoting political education and Liberal organisation in the metro- politan and home counties, under the title of the London and Counties Liberal Union. It was explained by the chair- man that the woril " home " was left out, in order that the association might be at liberty to extend its sphere of use- fulness should circumstances render it desirable. Resolu- tions passing rules and appointing officers were also carried. ' A proposttion, too, approving the legislation of the last ses- sion, and a second, moved by Viscount Lyrnington, support- ing the Irish polio, of Her Majesty's Government, were acquiesced in unanimously. On the motion of Mr. W. H. James, M.P., Mr. S. Morley was appointed first president of the new union. Mr. James said there would be no attempt, 1 as some alarmists would say, to eneure dull uniformity in Liberal opinion.

-- SONNET ON THE DEATH OF DONNA CATHARINA DE ATJIAIDE. My gentle spirit thou who hast departed So early, of this life in discontent, Rest thou there ever, in Heaven's firmament, While I live here on earth all broken-hearted; In that Ethereal Seat, where thou didst rise, If memory of tins life so far consent, Forget not thou my ardent love unspent, Which thou dids.t read so perfect in mine eyes. And if, perchance, aught snot thy thee appears In my great cureless anguish for thy death, Oh': pray to God who closed so soon thy years, That He will also close my sorrowing breath, And swiftly call me hence thy form to see, As swiftly He deprived these eyes of thee. .—Translations of Canwens by J. J. .Aubertin.

FORTUNE FAVOURS THE BRAVE IN LOVE. Never did love his boldness hurtful find; Fortune hath ever favours for the bold; For cowardice, that shivers in the cold, Hangs like a stone on freedom of the mind. Who dares the Firmament sublime ascend. Meets there a star, whereby his course is told The good mere fancy in its range doth hold Illusive is, soon scattered by the wind. A path for fortune should be opened free : To none, without himself, will greatness fall; Chance moving only in first steps appears- To dare is valour, madness 'twill not be ; He to whom fortune shows thee loses all, If, coward like, he doth not scorn his fears.

BARN-YARD CRITICISM. As I once was out a-walking on my farm, I heard a talking, And very slyly tiptoeing, I hid behind a tree; For an animal convention claimed my curious attention, And I feared 111 were iaoticed it would break it up, you see. There were pig and fowl and donkey, and colts so tall and
And a goose of vast importance that was sitting in the chair; For they all had met together to discuss their faults, and whether There was any one among them they could easily repair. _

Rose a duck and said, "You waddle, my friends, you middle- waddle Whene'er you try to walk about. I say it for your good." "And apropos of that, dears," squealed a pig, " you re much too fat, dears, And your greediness in eating is a fact well understood." Said a colt, so cross and grumpy, "Your knees are big and lumpy." "Quack, quack I" pronounced the chairman; t. your voices are too rough." Cried a turkey, "Gobble, gobble ere you get into a squabble; Remember, self-importance in itself is fault enough." Then rose a lamb so fleecy. "I'm sure 'Us not as easy," He humbly said, "to cure the faults of others as our own. If we our evils seeking "—but, braying, quacking squeaking, His angry friends quick fled away, and left the lamb alone. I nodded very sadly, and woke up, oh, so gladly I And pondered the dream-lessons as I sat there on the grass, Confessing it is daring to assail with blame unsparing The faults that I am fearing, would be quickest in appearing, If we only took a peep into a moral looking-glass.

Very amiable and good natured are those people who can have their own way in everything. There is no charity in helping a man who will not help himself. When a poet tells you that the ocean kissed the shore, he does not refer to fishing smacks. The everlasting longing for something we have not ought to satisfy us that there great things in store for us. Theodore Hook once said to a man at whose table a pub- lisher got very drunk, " Why, you appear to have emptied your wine cellar into your bookseller !' On a child beim: told that he must be broken off a bad habit, he replied, "Papa, hadn't I better be mended ?" THE KNIFE CLEANER.—TWO fishwomen being in New- castle Market, saw a knife-cleaning machine. One of them turned the handle once or twice. "It gang vary clivvor," she remarked; "but the music is not see nice as a hordy-

gordy!" The following anecdote, I venture to think, points to the fact that an occasional sense of humour in the British yokel (whether accidental or otherwise) survives the age of Shaks- pere's "clowns." A vicar of a countq parish had occasion lately to remonstrate with a lowly member of his flock, who had regularly been "conspicuous by his absence" from the celebration of the Holy Communion, for his non-attendance. Hodge hazarded the excuse that he didn't consider himself sufficiently qualified to attend. "Why not ?" urged the vicar; "you have been confirmed." " Yes, sir," replied Hodge, "and vaccinated, too, but they neither of 'ens took !" A story is told of a good squire in the country, who, dur- ing a time of prolonged solitude, sought to wile away the weary hours by reading the "Vicar of Wakefield." He was a very slow reader at any time, and his I ule was to read ten pages each day, carefully placing a mark in the book at the point which he had reached. A roguish niece who was in the house watched him take up the book daily; and as he laid it down she shifted the mark back eight pages. When he had finished—for he did make progress at the rate of two pages a day—she asked him hw he liked the book. "It is very good, iieleed," he sal but there are a great many repetitions of it." What a happy faculty is that of self-possession! A friend dropped in to make a call on a wedded couple who were in the very crisis of a family jar. The evidences of the little un- plea3antnesa were too plain to be concealed, but both smiled a cast-iron smile, and the visitor politely observed, " You, madam, I perceive have a bad headache." "No," she re- sponded, trying to look angelic, "my dear little Fido has just swallowed a button-book. and I'm so alarmed." Then he turned to the husband, "And you, sir, are doubtless worried shoat sornt business affair." "No," he said, in a sepulchral voice, " Ficio has swallowed that button-hook before, and I'm -fraid it won't kill him." Cattivm—There is a picturesque story going about to the effect that Mr. Carlyle was a terrible domestic tyrant. !sir. Yates says that at breakfast time the Scotch philosopher would come down grumbling, and, glancing at the well- spreal board, declare the food to be unfit for a dog. Mrs. Carlvle thereupon would order the servant to take the de- noised viandS bdelt to the kitchen. Presently, when the philosopher was begiurg, to grow desperately hungry, his ipouse would order the same dishes to be brought back, which het husband immediately proceeded to devour with infinite relish and without any more ado. No wonder that the sage considered his wife a greater woman than either George Sand or George Eliot.— Toronto Mae. It was on board of a troopship outward bound. In the ladies' cabin were four wash-hand basins, one of which was much larger than the others. There were three ladies in the cabin whose husbands were about equal in rank. Women always think they have a right to presume on the rank of their husbands when taking choice of berths, (Itc., and there was a great discussion as to who was entitled to the use of the large basin. It was referred to the paymaster of the ship, who could settle nothing, and eventually to the cap- tain. He gave a decision worthy of Solon. After asking them if they would abide his verdict, and not to give any more trouble in the matter, which they readily agreed to do, he said he thought it was only fair that the oldest lady should have the largest basin. The basin was never used

during the whole voyage out. PIGMY ELEPRANTS.—It is commonly supposed that all elephants are huge creatures, and though, as a rule, they are an enormons size, there is one species which is very small. This kind is found in the Malay peninsula, and some specimens have been procured which are only from twenty-eight to thirty-six inches in height, with a thick coat of bristly hair or wool. Two of these pigmy elephants were recently exhibited in New York. They are described as playful an inoffensive, holding out their tiny trunks for strangers to touch—a practice of which they were particu- larly fond. They used to keep up a swaying movement, sometimes from side to side' sometimes backwards and for- wards. One of them would occasionally take hold of a visitor's hand,gently curl his trunk around it, carry it care- fully to his mouth, and then " trumpet " with great glee.— Little Folks Magazine. GOODY TWO SHOES.—Who wrote the letters f,r " Junius?" and is Gauden the author of the " Eikon Basilike," or was it composed by King Charles, of sacred memory? are questions which have occupied the attention of the world of letters since the first appearance of those famous productions. Volumes have been written on the subject, and authors of all sorts have contributed to the controversy. Wh ;6rot,: "Goody Two Shoes ?" and when was the delightful little nursery classic published? seems not unlikely to become a matter of polemics. It might be thought beneath the dig- nity of sober men of letters to discuss the authorship of such a work ; but the tales of the 'nursery must of necessity interest all who through them were first introduced into the fairy realm of romance. Although "Goody Two Shoes" and the rest of them have, in some degree, been in our day superseded by works more suitable to the precocity of modern childhood, they are yet of bibliographical Interest. That the number of editions of "Goody Two Shoes' issued in England and America is beyond computation, or even surmise, is itself enough to excite interest as to the author- ship of a romance which has secured 99 world-wide a circu- lation, and maintained its position for so long a time. It is not surprising, therefore, that the A qiencetim has opened its columns for the discussion of the nutter. It used to be taken for granted that Oliver Goldsmith wrote it. It is known that it originally issued from the house of Newberg, at the corner of St. Paul's-churchyard --and it is also known that the author of the "Deserted " was employed by Newbery, and wrote for him many books and booklets, tio which his name was not attached. A decade ago a claim was made, in the teeth of tradition, in favour of another of of Newbery's literary hacks—Giles Jones—and the delight- ful romance is to him attributed in the catalogue of the British Musuem. A correspondent of the Atheneum, who appears to have duly qualified himself for the task by a thorough examination of the publications issued by New- bery, and which he assures us are "as scarce as blackberries in mid-winter," now cornea forward with a view to restore to Goldsmith the honours of authorship. A certain distinct literary flavour struck him as being common to a group of little volumes all published about the same period. This would, of course, only prove that the series was written by the same hand. But it is alas shown that this distinct literary flavour is the distinct literary flavour recognisable it the professed works of Goldsmith. The poet, we know, when a sizar in Trinity College, Dublin, used to write songs for street songsters.—Globe. As the debate proceeded the interest therein deepened. It was evident that the Government was in peril, and the peril was the more considerable through the loss of many supporters which the Government had sus- tained through its indifference and opposition to the ques- tion of Reform. The division was therefore likely to be a very close one, and it was anticipated with that feeling of intense earnestness and trepidation which is only excited when the fate of a government is in the balance. When the House divided the numbers were:—
For Mr. Cobden's resolution 263 Against

• Majority against the Government l6 On the very day on which this division took place news ar- rived that the war between England and Persia had .been terminated by a peace the terms of which were satisfactory to both of the belligerents. On the day following, Lord Granville in the House of Lords and Lord Palmerston in the House of Commons announced the decision at which the Government had arrived in consequence of the adverse vote that had been given. They stated that the Government had determined not to resign, but to dissolve, and explained that if the state of public business had admitted an imme- diate dissolution Parliament would have been dissolved at once. However, the estimates were not voted, the taxes , were not arranged, the Mutiny Bill was not passed, and would expire before the Parliament could reassemble. When these and other necessary measures had been carried then the Dissolution should at once take place. In about 14 days the necessary business of Parliament had been so far com- pleted that the Government was able to carry its resolution into effect. Accoidingly on Saturday, March 21st, 1857, the two Houses were prorogued with the ordinary formali- ties by commission with a message of more than usual brevity.

div.head: DEATH OF MR. EDWARD MALL
div.p: DEATH OF MR. EDWARD MALL

Mr. Edward Miall, late M.P. for Braderd, died quietly in his sleep on Friday evening, after an illness of two weeks. Mr. Miall WaS born in Poi tainouth in 1809, and was educated at the Protestant Dissenters' College at Wymondley, Herts. His last public appearance was at the Liberation Society's conference in June, 1880, but he was then too weak to ad- dress the a,ssembly. Mr. Miall, after spending several years as pastor of a Congregational church at Ware, and after- wards at Leicester, established the Nonconformist newspaper in 1841, and two years later his labours resulted in the formation of the British Anti-State Church Association, now -tyled the Liberation Sc s ety. He unsuccessfully contest_d Southwark and Halifax, but was first retarned for Rochdale in 1852. He proposed a motion on the subject of the Irish Church,but was def eated. At the request of the Derby Ministry he became a member of the Duke of Newcastle's Commission on Education. He was defeated in 1857, together with Bright, Cobden, and other opponents of the China war.. At the general election of 1868 he was defeated at Bradford by Mr. Ripley, but on that gentleman being unseated in 1869 Mr. Miall was returned by a large majority, and sat until 1874, when he retired from public life. He twice brought forward motions in favour of disestablishment, Mr. Glad- stone on the last occasion opposing him. Mr. Miall has twice received substantial marks of the appreciation in which his public services were held both as a public writer and as the foremost champion in Parliament of the principle of religious equality. On the first occasion, at the Free- mason's tavern, he was presented with 5,000 guineas, and on the second, in 1873, at the Crystal Palace, with 10,000 guineas, that amount being put in trust on behalf of himself and family. Two years ago, en the occasion of his 70th birthday, Mr. Miall was presented with a congratulatory address by a deputation headed by Mr. Bright and Mr. Richard. His works include "Views of the Voluntary Principle," 1845 ; "Ethics of Nonconformity," 1848; "The British Churches in relation to the British People," 1849; "Tithe Deeds of the Church of England," 1861; " Politics of Christianity," 1863 ; "An Editor off the Line," 1865. These are mostly contributions to the Nonconformist, but "Bases of Belief," 1858, has long been a text book in many Dissenting colleges. We are informed that until a couple of weeks ago Mr. Miall contributed an article weekly to the Illustrated London News.

div.head: TRADE NOTES.
div.p: TRADE NOTES.

The peddlers in the employ of Messrs. Russell Brothers, Cinderfonl Valley, Forest of Dean, have struck against a proposed reduction of 61. per ton. The mill hands em- ployed by the same firm are also resisting a reduction of 5 per cent., and a stoppage is apprehended. The Oldham journeymen painters have resolved to go out upon strike for an advance of one half-penny per hour. The employers say that trade will not allow of the advance. The operative painters in the Teeside district have resolved to apply for the half-penny advance in wages. On Tuesday morning the work of damping down two large blast furnaces at Elsecar, near Barnsley, belonging to Mr. George Dawes was almost complete. The whole of the four furnaces at Elsecar, which have been in blast for several years, are now idle, the other two having been blown out several weeks ago. Close upon 100 hands have been thrown idle. Uuremunerative trade is reported to be the cause.

An important oonference of ironworkers representing the Midland counties was held on Monday at Wednesbury for the purpose of considering an insurance scheme in lieu of the Employers Liability Act. It was stated that the iron- masters were willing to contribute 25 per cent to the fund, and to pay for medical assistance for disablement. The delegates were of opinion that the employers should con- tribute an equal sum to employes, and the conference was adjourned to enable the operatives to consider the offer made by the employers.

div.head: IRON AND COAL TRADES.
div.p: IRON AND COAL TRADES.

A wages dispute has arisen at Kidderminster which threatens to bring about the removal of one branch of the carpet trade—the staple industry of the place—from the locality. It seems that the tapestry weavers have for a long time been paid higher prices than those paid in other centres of the trade ; and the masters recently framed a list which, while reducing the earnings of the hands, still enabled a weaver working full time to earn £2 a week. The artizans, however, refuse to accept these terms ; and the employers have signified their intention to remove the looms from the town unless an accommodation is arrived at. The operatives have decliaed to submit the matter to arbitration.

BARROW•IN-FURNESS--NO change of moment has taken place in connection with the hematite pig-iron trade during the week. Business has been rather more brisk perhaps, but several makers hesitate about accepting many orders in face of the low prices which are now the rule. It is neces- sary to practice the greatest economy in working in order to ensure a profit with iron selling at from 565. to 608. per ton at works. Stocks of iron are very large at some works, but now that shipments are being made with more freedom to the Continent and America the amount of iron in hand has been considerably reduced. Steel is in good request; but makers being well supplied with orders are not pressing for new business. Shipbuilders are very busy. Iron ore and coal steady. Tine IRON AND COAL TRADES.— Lascasurn.n.—ln the coal trade business is naturally slackening off with the warmer weather, and in some districts stocks are accumula- ing, whilst stoppages for one or two days a week are not at all uncommon at many of the collieries. The better class of round coal especially are in lessened demand for house-fire purposes, and although in the Manchester district the list rates quoted by the leading firms are without alteration from last month there is an easier tone generally in prices, and re- ductions of about 6d. per ton have been made this month at many of the collieries in the West Lancashire districts. In some few cases 9s. 6d. per ton is still being obtained for best coal at the pit mouth, but for good house coal the average price is about Ss. 6d. to 99., and for seconds 6s. 9d. to 7s. 6d. per ton. Common round coals for iron making and steam purposes continue in very poor demand, and are being pressed upon the market at extremely low figures, avenging about ss. 3d. to ss. 9d per ton at the pit. So far, however, as en- gine classes of fuel are concerned the tendency is to stiffen, and although there has not yet been any general upward mevement in values, notices of an advance of sd. per ton have been sent out from some collieries this month. Good burgy at the pit mouth ranges from 4s. 6d. to 58. 3d. and good slack from 4s. to 45. 9d. per toe, with inferior sorts offering at 6d. to Is. per ton under these figures. The ship- ping demand for coal continues very limited, and extremely low prices are taken to secure cargoes. The iron trade of this district continues without improvement. During the week, business has again been extremely dull, with prices still tending downwards. There is, however, such a general absence of any disposition to buy that coto Iners and dealt rs pay little or no regard to any present fluctuations of the market, and although iron is offered for long forward delivery at very low figures this does not lead to any business of im- portance. Lancashire makers of pig iron have during the last few days secure I some moderately good orders at prices equal to about 445. to 455. per ton, less 2 per cent, for forge and foundry quilities delivered into the Manchester district and as fair deliveries are still being made from works on account of old contracts local makers are less anxious sellers than many of the makers in outside districts. For out- side brands offering in this market prices are nominally with- out alteration, but Lincolnshire and Derbyshire d irons are beim,: pushed in this district by needy holders at extremely low figures. In the manufactured iron trade there is not quite so much weakness as in pig iron, and, as some of the principal local makers are still fairly busy with old orders, they are tolerably firm in their prices. New orders, however, are coming in very Slowly, and for good specificatiors there are sellers at very 1v A -(u figures, averaging from £5 12s. 6d. to £5 15s. for bars delivered into the Manchester district. Trade generally is also very quiet amongst machinists and engineers, although a few firms are tolerably busy where they have specialities in hand. skin

IMPERIAL PARLIAMENT.
HOUSE OF COMMONS-MONDAY.

THE PARLIAMENTARY OATH.—MV. MACIVER wanted to know whether•the form of affirmation did not contain a statement of allegiance to the Throne which could not be made by an atheist and a Republican.—The SPEAKER, amid laughter and cheers, answered that Mr. Maclver was asking him to construe an Act of Parliament, on which he must leave him to form his own opinion.—Mr. CHARLES LEWIS gave notice that when the Attorney-General moved for leave to introduce the Oaths Bill, he would move an amendment, declaring that in so much as the proposed Act is brought forward to admit a professed atheist to the House of Com- mons, the House declined to be a party to it. THE PROPOSED MONUMENT TO LORD BEACONSFIELD.— Mr. LABOUCHERE gave notice that on the motion to provide funds for erecting a statue in Westminster Abbey, in memory of the late Lord Beaconsfield, he would move the previous question, an announcement received with cheers I from below the gangway on the Ministerial side. THE GOVERNMENT TRANSVAAL POLICY—Ad reply to Sir Michael Hicks-Beach, Mr. GLADSTONE said that since he had last been asked to afford facilities for the discussion of a motion with respect to the Transvaal, circumstances had considerably altered. It had been admitted by the Boers that the capitulation of Potchefstroom was brought about, by an act of treachery on the part of the commander of the besieging forces. Communications on the subject were in progress, and all he could promise was that he would under- take the responsibility of infiorming the right hon. baronet of the first opportunity consonant with public convenience for discussing the matter. THE STATE or IRELAND—In reply to a series of ques- tions with respect to Mr. Dillon's speech at the Land League meeting on Tuesday last, Mr. FORSTER said the attention of the Government had been closely directed to it, and that was the only answer ho could make at present. THE PARLIAMENTARY OATHS BILL.—Mr. GLADSTONE moved the postponement of the orders subsequent to the second reading of the Irish Land 8.11, in order that the Attorney-General might move for leave to introduce the Oaths Bill, and an animated discussion followed.—Lord ReNnotrot CHURCHILL, who was received with laughter and ironical cheers from the Ministerial benches, opposed the motion, primarily on the ground that it interfered with the progress of the Land Bill, though he said the Oaths Bill, had one thing in common with the Land Bill, that it was a con- I cession to violence and mob law. The Bill was introduced from apprehension that Mr. Bradlaugh would come down and turn the House of Commons into a bear-garden, and under the protection of the Prime Minister, would have another romp with the Serjeant-at-Arms. He hoped there would be many members who would follow him in resisting an effort to place in the House of Commons the representa- tive of brazen infidelity and rampant disloyalty.—Mr. NEW- BEGAT& attempted to continue the discussion of the Bill, when he was called to order by the Speaker.—Mr. OtasLow thought the proposed .neasure was utterly subversive of the Constitution of the country. From his well-known " religious proclivities " he thought the Bill must be distasteful to the Premier, and expressed his belief that the Premier was com- pelled to take this course by his colleagues in the Cabinet -- the two members for Birmingham. Amid much laughter from the Ministerialists, he solemnly warned the Prime Minister that if he listened to the right hon. gentlemen his Government would not last long.—Sir STAFFORD NORTHCOTE counselled that no opposition should be made to the introduction of the Bill, but observed that the dignity of the House was concerned in not letting it appear that it was in hot haste to complete the legislation. It was too early to resume the discussion on the morrow, and he thought a proper interval should elapse before the Bill came on again—Mr. GLADSTONE pointed out that so tar from her Majesty's Government being responsible for the difficulty in which the House now found itself, it was entirely due to the action of the majority of which the Governmen% had formed no part. The Premier was too much in earnest about the Irish Land Bill to do anything that might seriously inter- fere with its progress. Therefore, much as he should regret such an unusual course, lie would submit if necessary to the arrangement that the Attorney-General should make hisl atatoment on introducing the Bill, and that the debate should thereupon be adjourned. But he trusted that the House would permit the Bill to be brought in in the usual way, the second reading being deferred to some subsequent date.— nsmeir. ,nng: ebgttsshthr;oo:i,Citdehh,ni Mr. CHARLES LEwrs intimated that whatever right hon. gentleman on the front Opposition bench might do he and, adjournmentsaptcAi urilvviniasdihnsetethtfeeromsDni measure, e aaoevonnai of tile utehr ,s; he trusted, some others would not follow them into the lobby These 111o:wee: tsnhseeear eetehywmieo whatever was interrupted measure yenaawts seuimrshr reeenwti peeaotxesfbespdypapl uiTobr. int,ceyoeeef explained divi- sion ee- otes against 43, and ultimately the adjournment of the debate. Mr. SHAW-LEFEVRE, in an able reply, pointed out that Mr. Smith had conceded the main principle of the bill, from which all the other proposals naturally sprang.—The debate was continued by Mr. O'Shaugemessy, Professor Thorold Rogers, Mr. Balfour. Mr. P. J. Smyth, and other members.—Lord JOHN MANNFRS moved the adjournment of I:esi—nllniuiiceitnvnyeTgi jremfd, gbisEenti:eai,aifistinrleeoradnim ARRESTe amendment d moe R the debate, and Mr. PARNELL, rising amid cheers from the Irish party, endeavoured to seize the occasion to offer some remarks on the arrest of Mr. John Dillon, news of which had reached the House within the half-hour. Before he had ad- vanced through many sentences the SPEAKER interposed, and pointed out that on the motion for the adjournment he might speak only on the subject of the Bill. The ques- tion that the debate be adjourned being put was challenged by the Irish members, and on a division was cart ied by 263 votes against 34. THE PARLIAMENTARY OATHS BILL.—The SPEAKER then called on the Attorney-General to proceed with his motion for the introduction of the Oaths Bill.—Mr. PAR- NELL, rising again, moved the adjournment of the House.— The SPEAKER ruled this out of older, lie having already called on the Attorney-General.—Mr. A. O'CONNOR raised a fresh point of order requiring that notices of motion pre- ceding that relating to the Oaths Bill should be taken first. —The SPEAKER pointed ont that he was simply following the order of the House, and after some insistence on the part of Mr. Parnell, the Attorney-General proceeded to explain the provisions of the Oaths Bill. The simple proposition of the Bill is to make it optional with members presenting themselves at the table to take the oath or make affirmation. Anticipating the objection that persons like Mr. Bradlaugh might elect to take the oath, the Attorney-Gencral pointed out that the House would retain the privilege which it exer- cised on Tuesday of refusing to permit a member to take the oath.—On the motion of Lord RANDohrit CHURCHILL, the debate was adjourned ; and the remaining orders disposed of, the House adjourned. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—TUESDAY. THE IRISH MAGISTRACY.—Mr. FORSTER, in reply to Mr. Corbet, said he had no means as Secretary to the Lord- Lieutenant of ascertaining what might be the religion of Irish magistrates. Ile might state that so far as the present / Government were concerned—and he had no reason to say ! it was not the same with other Governments—religion ' formed no element in the appointment of justices of the peace in Ireland. (" Oh, oh," and laughter.) • IRisit PRISONERS AND THEIR NEWSPAPERS.—Mr. HEALY asked the Chief Secretary whether it was true that political prisoners in Kilmainham and elsewhere were prevented from ' receiving certain newspapers, including the Newcastle Chronicle, Echo, Graphic, Illustrate,' London News, and the frishmon ?—Mr. FORSTER replied that persons im- prisoned under the Act were allowed to see the Dublin daily papers and the journals of their own locality, and he thought that all reasonable requirements were met by this arrangement.—Mr. Healy presSed the Chief Secretary for a more precise answer, and ultimately elicited from him that if the papers named had been sent they had been stopped. THE FOOT-AND-MOUTH DISEASE. Mr. MUNDELLA in- formed Mr. Arnold that the subject of relaxing the ordersof the Privy Council relating to sheep imported from the United States had been carefully considered, and the diffi- culties in the way of doing it with safety were found to be inthirmountable. The right hon. gentleman subsequently stated that an outbreak of foot. and-ment h dieease had been reported from Newcastle, and that the Privy Council had declaredthreepwlyliionlge of the borough an infected area. Law OF DISTRESS.—Mr. BLasrignairassurr moved that it is desirable to abolish the powers of levying distress for the rent of agricultural holdings in England, Wales, and Le- land. Caoss be- lieved that a small tarmer would have a better chance of , getting on and of being trusted by his landlord with the
