lAlderman HOLMES seconded the resolution, and hoped the Council would unanimously adopt it. He dared say a good many of the gentlemen present were interested in a vai iety of charitable properties, and as he thought the bodies with whom he was associated would look upon that Bill with a great amount of disfavour, he thought the gentlemen pre- sent would do the same. Councillor MILNER asked if the Town Clerk endorsed that description of the Bill, because it was such an extra- ordinary description that be did not believe it. Councillor BURGESS said that was the third time the Council had had to exprees their opinion upon the Bill which they had not seen, and he thought it would be better for them to see the Bill. The MAYOR said the town clerk of London would not send a circular to the various Corporations stating certain things unless they were true. Councillor BURGESS wondered be had not sent the Bill. Alderman DAVIES Said what the Council had to do was to set their faces against any localisation or centralisa- tion or what he would call maelstromisation. Hethoug,ht they should set their faces against the Bill if it was in accor- dance with what was stated, and he did not think for a moment that an official of the standing of the town clerk of London would issue a circular which on the face of it was a lie. The Council could not do wrong in endeavouring to set their faces against anything which gave absolute power to destroy local interests and charities, and the way in which they were distributed. Alderman KEAN said it seemed the Charity Commissioners had power to act independently of the Government. There I was no appeal except to the Attorney-General. The Com- missioners would appropriate the charities just as they thought best, without at all considering whether the action they took would bring destitution to anyone, and be thought they could not do better than set themselves against the Bill. Councillor CROSFIELD said be agreed with the remaks of Alierman Davies, and would resist to the very utmost every attempt at centralisation. He thought the more this country was governed by local bodies the better. He had very little faith in London and the way in! which it managed its own affairs, and he could not himself believe that the House of Commons would be such a set of idiots—(laughter)—as to consider such a Bill as that which had been referred to. (Laughter.) Councillor PLATT said the last time the Council was asked to express an opinion upon a Bill, they had a copy of the Bill before them, and several members had seen it, but he did not think they would be doing right in expressing an opinion upon this Bill,without knowing more about it than the e.s parte statement they had heard. He should protest against centralisation as strongly as anyone, but considered they were not in possession of facts to justify them passing an opinion on the Bill. Alderman HARRISON remarked that ode thing was quite clear, on the face of the Bill—that its object was to take out of the hands of local trustees the funds of these charities, and to concentrate them in London. That was the main object of the Bill, and whether they saw the Bill or not, if they passed such a resolution as the Mayor had suggested, lie did not see how they could possibly do wrong. Councillor BROADBENT said they were called upon to ex- press disapproval of a Bill, of which they had no means of judging. There was no doubt whatever, that what this country was suffering from just now, was the fact that large sums of money, which had been left by charitable people in times gone by had ceased to be of advantage, and were doing harm rather than good; and it was very desirable indeed that, where charitable bequests of this kind were found from change of circumstances,to be doing no good, there should 'ae some power to divert them, and to bestow them in such a way that they should do good. He thought it very likely indeed that there were two sides to this question—(hear, hear)—and that when they had the means of reading the Bill and hearing it discussed in the House of Lords, they would find that there was something to be said even in opposition to the rown-Clerk of London. (Hear, hear.) He thought the best and most dignified course would be to wait until they heard more about the Bill. Alderman Vt'EnsTER stated that there was a good deal of difference as to what was doing good. Although they might think some of these charities were not doing good, they might be doing good for ought they knew, and if they were intntoeatnt ttahfloe tl r mpr aou tms t,t eee rreesdt tadoliwvt eahryetms t hadthe money. mhaotnpower to appeal to Parlia- ya.s doneß u t in ne other rnpoat parts think f the country. They bad to look after their own charities. He did not think there was one charity in the neighbourhood administered in such a way as to require the interference of any central authority. This was no more than another attempt at centralisation, which was to swallow up every- thing, and land them in London. It was impossible that the Commissioners could know what was required here, or could tell what was the most desirable way of spending any funds they had. The letter showed that the effect of the Bill was to take the management of charities out of the hands of trustees arbitrarily, and place them in the hands of authorities in London, and he thought that alone entitled the Council to oppose the Bill. Councillor JEANS did not know whether it would benefit them much if they petitioned or other- wise, as most of the petitions got into the waste paper basket. But he thought they ought not to go. as a matter of course, either in favour or against a bill of which they knew nothing. Some of the provisions of ihe Bill might be good, and he did not think they should at the re- quest of any other party send a petition simply because they were asked to do so. He thought they should see the Bill as to whether there was anything particularly objectionable in regard to anythingconcerning their own affairs. But what- ever the Bill might contain, as a matter of principle they ought not to petition against it not knowieg what it con- tained. (Hear, hear.)

A Idernian Div'Es ;aid he thought they had recently had an illustration of the overbearing of the Charity Commis- sioners in regard to the recommendation of the Council as to the Grammar School. He looked upon the Bill with sus- picion because it was brought in by the Lord Chancellor, as the authorities were constantly devising bills of this character for the purpose of making centralisation their per- fect aim and object. Councillor PERCIVAL supported the resolution. He did not believe in centralisation, but believed that most of the charitable institutions in the town were very well con- ducted. The resolution was passed without dissent. WATCH COMMITTEE. A meeting of the Watch Committee was held on, the 31st March, when the Visiting Committee reported that they had visited the Bridewell and premises, and found it was neces- sary the following work should be done :.—Sitting-room and dining-room to be whitened, sessions house, entranee ball, and two bedrooms to be whitened and papered. It was re- commended that tenders be obtained for the work. At a meeting held on the 21st April, the Visiting Committee re- ported that they had visited the Bridewell and found every- thing in good order. On the proposition of the MAYOR, seconded by the Ex- Mayon, the minutes were confirmed.

div.head: HOUSE OF COMMONS. --WEDNESDAY.
div.p: HOUSE OF COMMONS. --WEDNESDAY.

Tim ARREST OF MR. DILLON.—The SPEAKER stated that he had received a communication from the Lord-Lieu- tenant informing him of the arrest of Mr. Dillon. The read- jog of the letter was received with groans by the few Irish members present —Mr. T. P. O'CosNoß descanted on the arbitrary and extreme use of the Lord- Lieutenant's power, and Mr. BIGGAR sugges'ed to Mr. Forster the propriety of his withdrawing from a position for which he was notoriously unfit. Mr. Biggar further intimated that he and his friends would be "under the necessity, of speaking very plainly" with res- pect to Mr. Forster when Mr. McCarthy's motion came en for discussion. Subsequently Mr. Healy gave notice that on the motion to nominate the committee on the Conservancy Bill, he would move to add the name of Mr. Dillon. THE DOTEREL DISASTER.—Mr. TREVELYANmadP a state- ment on the subject of the blowing up of Her Majesty's ship Doterel ; but no authentic explantion of the disaster had then come to hand, and the exact loss of life was not ascertained. The ship was manned by eight officers and 135 men.

SUNDAY CLOSING IN WALES.—Mr. ROBERTS (Flint Dis- trict) moved the second reading of the Sale of Intoxicating Liquors on Sunday (Wales) Bill. He explained that the purpose of the bill was to close public houses in Wales on Sundays. Petitions had been presented in favour of the bill by a quarter of a million of people, or rather more than one-third of the entire population of Wales. Of the 30 Welsh members, he was happy to say 28 were Liberals, and were unmistakably in favour of the bill. Of the Conserva- tive members, one-half—(laughter)—were also in favour of the bill. In these circumstances, he appealed to the Government to help the members for Wales to pass this law in the present session. It was a question which was near and dear to the people of Wales, who were desirous to preserve the peace and order of the Sabbath day, which he was glad to say was held in much reverence in Wales.— Mr. WARTON opposed the Bill, denouncing it as a proposal for cheating the tourist. The reason for the existence of Wales, he observed, was its beFitif ul scenery, which attracted tourists, whose convenience ought not to be interfered with. He held that Wales and the Welsh should show themselves more conscious of the dignity accruing from their union with England, and should not seek after separate legislation in this fashion.—The Bill met a very general approval in the House, what opposition was manifested coming from the Conservative side, and from gentlemen like Mr. Onslow, whose opinions on all that relates to the interests of licensed victuallers are well known—Mr. GLADSTONE gave a thorough support to the Bill. He strongly urged the House to give a kindly attention to a wish which was almost unanimously entertained in Wales. The proposal was one which should receive the ready assent of the House when it was proved to represent the feelings of one of the great sections of the country; and this was the principle which had been followed in the case of Ireland and Scotland. The Prime Minister suggested that it bad not been sufficiently the habit of Par- liament to consult Welsh opinion en many subjects. Wales had a great deal to complain of, and in the mode in which the patronage of the Welsh Church Establishment was administered the treatment of the Principality was almost barbarous.—Upon a division, the second reading was agreed to by 163 votes to 17. The result was received with loud cheers, and the Bill was read a second time. BANK NOTES —Mr. ANDERSON moved the second reading of the Banking Laws Amendment Bill, but withdrew it after a discussion. THE PREVENTION OF FLOODS.—Mr. COURTNEY having proposed the nomination of the select committee on the Rivers Conservancy and Floods Prevention Bill, Mr. Non- WOOD found fault with the constitution of the committee. and Mr. A. Bnowlex moved, and Mr. HENEAGE seconded, the adjournment of the debate.—Mr. CALLAN supported the adjournment, with the view of placing one or two Irish mem- bers upon the committee, and after a short conversation the motion for adjournment was assented to.

div.head: HOUSE OF LORDS.-THIIRSDAY.
div.p: HOUSE OF LORDS.-THIIRSDAY.

- - The House of Lords re-assembled to-day after the recess. THE PREMIER AND THE TRANSVAAL.—Lord CARNARVON gave notice that he should call attention to the Premier's letter to Mr. Tomkinson, the Liberal candidate for West Cheshire, in which the words "blood guiltiness" were used with reference to the Transvaal war. THE LATE LORD BEACONSFIELD.—EarI GRANVILLE, whilst postponing till Monday night an elaborate reference to the late Lord Beaconsfield, in a few graceful sentences expressed his appreciation of the loss which the House had sustained.—The Duke of RICHMOND added a warm tribute to the memory of his former leader. THE AFGHAN WAR—Votes of thanks to the officers and men engaged in the Afghan war were moved by Earl GRAN- VILLE and adopted, after the skill of the generals and the fortitude and good conduct of the men had been warmly acknowledged on all sides of the House.

HOUSE OF COMMONS.—TIiURSDAY. JUVENILE OFFENDERSa—Sir W. HARCOURT, replying to 3 question, said he was anxious to introduce a measure with reference to the treatment of juvenile offenders. The point to which the question referred—namely, the imprisonment of juvenile offenders before being sent to a reformatory school—was one of which there was a good deal of diversity of opinion. Of those whose opinions he had collected, 39 were in favour of imprisonment and 135 were against it. He confessed his opinion inclined to that of the laajority. PRISONERS UNDER THE PROTECTION OF PERSON AND PROPERTY ACT.—A question submitted by Mr. T. D. Sulli- van as to whether newspaper proprietors imprisoned under the Coercion Act would be allowed“o supervise copy prepared for insertion in their journals elicited from the Chief Secretary the statement that editors in prison could write any but political articles, but that it was for articles in a newspaper that at leastone of the prisoners was detained. THE ARREST OF Mn. DILLoN.—Mr. Sexton sought to ob- tain from Mr. Forster a statement of the passages in the re- cent speech of Mr. Dillon which were in the opinion of the Chief Secretary objectionable, but the right hon. gentleman declined to give the information, as it would anticipate a discusssion of which notice bad been given. THE DOTEREL DISASTER. Mr. TREVELYAN announced that the story of the disaster to the Doterel, as told by the , survivors, might be expected about the Ist of June. He added that there was 4 tons 7 cwt. of gunpowder in the fore magazine of the ill-fated vessel, which was quite enough, he said, to account for the accident. THE ARREST or SOCIALISTS INT AUSTRIA.—Mr. J. COWEN called attention to the police searches and arrests in Vienna for papers and evidence connected with Social plots, and the HOME SECRETARY stated that the arrests in question were in no way connected with the arrest of Herr Most in this country, or any information derived from tho English Government or police. THE BEACONSFIELD MoNtrumay.—Mr. GLADSTONE an- nonaced his intention of moving an Address to be presented to the Queen praying that Her Majesty may give directions that a monument may be erected in the Collegiate Church of St. Peter, Westminster, in memory of the Earl of Beacons- fieldovith an engraved inscription of the high sense enter- tained by the House of his rare and splendid gifts and of his devoted labours in great offices of State, and to make sure to Her Majesty that the House will make good the expenses attending the same. MR. PARNELL AND TIIE HAND BILL.—Mr. PARNELL gave notice of a lengthy amendment, which he will move on the second reading of the Irish Land Bill. THE AFGHAN ,WAR.—VOTES OF THANES —A vote of thanks for the military operations in Afghanistan was moved by the Marquis of HARTINGTON, who stated that Her Majesty had offered the honour of a baronetcy to Sir F. Haines, Sir D. Stewart, and Sir F. Roberts, which honour had been accepted by Sir D. Stewart and Sir F. Roberts; but Sir F. Haines, for personal reasons, had not for the present intimated his acceptance. Lord Hattington also stated that the Government of India has conferred on Generals Stewart and Roberts pensions of £l,OOO a year each.—The motion was seconded by Sir S. NORTHCOTE.—An amendment having been moved by Mr. Healey, Mr. GLAD- STONE deprecated a division on the subject, but the bon. member for Wexford refused to withdraw, and upon a divi- sion his amendment was defeated by 304 to 20, and the motion was agreed to. NEW WRIT.—A new writ was issued for Knaresborough. THE Inisn LAND BILL.—The debate on the motion for the second reading of this bill was resumed by Sir H. Bruce who adversely criticised the measure. The debate was con- tinued by Mr. O'Connor Power, Lord Fitzmaurice, Lord J. Manners, and on the motion of Mr. ERRINOTON, it was again adjourned.

div.head: WARRINGTON TOWN COUNCIL.
div.p: WARRINGTON TOWN COUNCIL.
TIIE MAINTENANCE OF INCORRIGIBLE BOYS.

A special treating of the Town Council was h'eld at the , Town Hall on Tuesday to take into consideration the making of a contribution towards the maintenance in a certified in- dustrial school of three boys, ordered to be sent to such school. There were present the Mayor (Alderman Pickmere), Aldermen Kean, Webster, Davies, Holmes, Harrison, Thewlis, Councillors Wallington, Percival, Litton, Broad- bent, Ridgway, Burgess, Taylor, Fairclough, Milner, Platt, Dixon, Whittle, Barker, Jeans, and Brown ; Messrs. J. L. Whittle (deputy town clerk ), C. Chorley (borough treasurer), T. Longdin (borough surveyor), and J. H. Gornall (medi- cal officer). Alderman WEBSTER said the Council was asked to make a contribution towards the maintenance, in a certified indus- trial school, of three boys, named Patrick Higgins (12), Mark Norman (9), and Walter Whitley (11), ordered by the magistrates on the 21st March to be sent to such school. These were the second lot of cases that had arisen in which such an order had been made in the borough. The cases arose under section 12 of the Education Act, 1876. Where AB attendance order was not complied with without any reasonable excuse, the court might on complaint made by the local authority upon a second or subsequent case of non- compliance with an order, order the child to be sent to a certified day school, or if it appeared to the court that there was no such school suitable for the child, then to a certified industrial school. By section 4of the Act of 1879, the Council had power, on the recommendation of the commit- tee, to contribate towards the maintenance of children in an industrial school in the same manner as if they were a School Board, and the expenses of such contribution should be paid in like manner as the other expenses of the School Attendance Committee under the Act of 1876. Section 27 of the Act of 1870 provided that a School Board should have the same power of contributing money in the case of an industrial school as was given to a prison authority. By section 12 of the Industrial School Act, 1866, the latter section provided that a prison authority might from time to time contribute suck sums of money as they thought fit towards the support of inmates of a certified industrial school, but required that 14 days previous notice of the intention to take into con- aideration the making of such contribution be given by advertisement, and that where the prison authority was the council of the borough (as was the case here) the order for the contribution be made as a special meeting of the Coun- cil. The necessary advertisement had been given. Each of the cases were brought several times before the committee, and were also before the magistrates on several occasions. Patrick Higgins had been before the magistrates six times, Norman five, and Whitley once; and on the 21st March last they were ordered by the magistrates to be sent to a certi- fied industrial school. Arrangements had been made with managers of certified industrial schools for the reception of these children, for which they would require 6s. per week at one school, and ss. 6d. at the other. The Treasury con- tributed the sum of 2s. per week towards their maintenance in the school if the case fell nnder sub-section 1 of the eleventh section of the Act of 1876, and 3s. Bd. if belonging to class mentioned in sub-section 2. All the cases now before the Council were under section 2, and therefore the Treasury contrithuted 3s. 6d. per week in each case. The Council would therefore have to contribute the difference between the Treasury grant with the amount payable by the parent, and the amount required by the school was as follows: Patrick Higgins, 3s. 6d. Treasury grant, parents' contribu- tion not settled, 2s. contribution of Council; Mark Norman, 3s. 6d. Treasury grant, parents' contribution not settled, 28. 6d. contribution of Council; Walter .Whitley, 3a. 6d. PreasuiT grant, parents' contribution Is. 6d., Is. contribution of Council. The boys would be detained in the iniustrial schools until they had respectively attained the age of 16 years. Alderman Webster concluded by proposing that the above-mentioned contributions should be made by the Council, and the propositions were seconded and carried. Alderman DAVIES asked whether the borough of Warring- ton was a prison authority under the meaning of the Act of Parliament. Alderman WEBSTER It is. Alderman DAVIES asked if the Town Clerk was quite satisfied on that point. The DEPUTY Tows CLERIC: I may say he is satisfied that it is so. _ . .

Alderman DAVIES very much questioned whether they had an absolute prison authority in Warrington. They had the power to commit prisoners to gaol, but they had no prison wherein to keep them, but had to send them to Kirkdale, where they Lame under county jurisdiction. Alderman HARRISON: It appears that if we are not a prison authority within the meaning of the Act, then wear. not in a position to do this. Alderman DAVIES did not say that. Alderman HARRISON: You are aware we have One it before Alderman Devises remarked that if similar resolutions had been passed before, that was better than any answer that could be given him. Councillor PLATT asked if the Corporation had received any contribution from the Imperial Authorities in repent to the boys who had been already sent to the schools. Alderman WEBSTER said he believed nothing had been received as yet. The time had not yet arrived for a contri- bution to be made. He did not think there was the slightest doubt that the Council were a prison authority within the meaning of the Act, because the Town'Clerk had been very particular about the matter.

EXTRAOTIDLNARY DEATH RATE. The REGISTRAR submitted his report for the month of April, from which it appeared that the births bad been 19 as against 23 in the corresponding period of last year. The deaths numbered 27, being at the rate of 5018 per thousand as compared with a death rate of 12 02 in the corresponding month of last year. Twelve deaths had been the direct re- sult of scarlet fever. Seven deaths were those of children under one year, seven under five years, and six between five and fifteen.years. .

It was resolved the Clerk be empowered to obtain copies of the education codes, regula- tions and other documents issued by the Education Depart- ment, and that he take proceedings under the Education Act, 1879, to obtain the consent of the Council to the recommen- dation of the committee for the contribution towards the Maintenance in a certified industrial school of three boys, named Higgins, Norman, and Whitley, ordered by the magistrates to be sent to such school. MUSECIII, LIBRARY AND ARTS COMMITTEE.—THE LATE MR. JOHN SHARP. Thd minutes of the above committee cmprised the report of the Curator' which stated that for the month of March the visitors to the Museum were 2,680, a decrease of 570 com- pared with March, 1880; volumes issued to subscribers 3,101. an increase of .50;5 volumes issued to readers 990, an increase of 55. It was decided that the thanks of the com- mittee be sent to the following donors :—Mr. J. Porter, Dr. Kendrick, the Mayor of Preston, Mr. H. B. White,the Local Books Fund, the Agent General for New South Wales, Mr. Beamont and the Cobden Club. It was resolved that the members of the committee, having heard of the sudden death of Mr. John Sharp, who bad rendered mostvaluable service to the town by cataloguing and arranging the seals and coins in the Museum, desired to express their regret at his loss, and to record theirappreciation of the services so kindly rendered ty him, and that a copy of this resolution be for- warded to Mrs. Sharp, with an expression of the sincere condolence of the committee with her in her loss. It was recommended that the tender of Mr. J. Mounfield for shelves and partitions in the lecture room be accepted. Alderman WEBSTER moved the adoption of the minutes, and said he thought the increased comfort at the library had had something to do with the great increase of readers. No chubt the Courcil would sympathise with the committee in their desire to convey to Mrs. Sharp their appreciation of the services of her son. (Hear, hear.) By nis death the committee had lost a most valuable assistant.

Councillor BoumEtrr seconded the passing of the minutes, and said it was pleasing to know that the public reading room was so much used by the people of Warring- ton. He thought the time would come before long when it would be found necessary to enlarge it. They all joined in their regret at the loss they had sustained by the death of Mr. John Sharp. He had rendered the committee valuable service, and he was respected by all who knew him; and it was only his delicate state of health that had prevented him being much more widely known and admired. The minutes were agreed to. THE CONDITION OP SANKEY-STREET.

`• The minutes of the Town Rail, Park, and Baths Commit- tee contained the report of the Baths keeper that the income from the Bsthe for the past month was £22 7s. Bd., as I against £6 38 Bd. in the corresponding period of last year. It was recommended that the following addition he made in the prices to be charged for the use of the Baths to members of the same family :-Ist, season ticket, 155., ad- ditional tickets for members of the same family under 18 years, 10s.; and that the buildings used by the Sanitary Committee as pail :stores be converted into loose boxes, to cost about £2O.

The MAYOR moved, and Councillor RIDGWAY !seconded the passing of the minutes. Councillor Dram asked if the committee bad taken into consideration the removal of the wall in front of the Town Hall, in order that the street opposite the post office might be widened. The number of people in Sankey-street, especially on a Sunday night, was so great as to render it almost impassable. Councillor PEncrwa. said that if the suggestion of the last speaker were carried but, there would be no telling where the expose would end.

The MAYOR said the question of the removal of the stone wall and embankment had been frequently before the com- mittee, but under present circumstances they thought that they should study a little economy. (Hear, hear.) They hoped when better times came they would be able to make a great improvement there. The minutes were confirmed.

div.head: MARKETS commtrrEE.
div.p: MARKETS commtrrEE.
The minutes of this committee contained orders for the payment of /..54 8s 103, and the income from all sources for tha past four weeks was Ptated to be £194 lOs 9d.
On the motion of Councillor Lirrow, seconded by Coun- cillor TAYLOR, the minutes were passed.
THE SANITARY COMMITTEE-ADULTERATED MILK. -

The Sanitary Committee had received the quarterly report of the public analyst, from which it appeared that nine samples of milk had been analysed, seven of which were pure, one was adulterated with 20 per cent, and the other with six per cent, of water. Three samples of water had also been analysed, all of which were impure. Mr. W. Owen, architect, attended the committee on behalf of Mr. Jeans, in pursuance of the notice served upon him relating to his houses at Latchford, and, having undertaken, on Mr. Jeans' behalf, to secure the walls from outside damp, either by cement or slating; to drain and make good the cellar floors, and otherwise remedy the damp existing, and make the houses in a habitable condition, it was resolved that the Council be recommended to adjourn the subject for three months to enable this work to be done. The commit- tee also recommended that the sum of £5 5s per annum be paid to Mr. J. C. Sutton, clerk, to the Guardians, for the weekly returns of cases of pauper sickness supplied by him to the medical officer of health. Councillor MILNER moved, and Councillor CHOSFIELD seconded, the confirmation of the minutes.

Alderman WEBSTER, referring to the analysis of samples of milk, asked whether, in the case where the milk was adulterated with water to the extent of 20 per cent., any steps had been taken to prosecute the vendor. Mr. MILNER said the vendor was brought before the committee and fined. (Hear, hear.) Alderman HARRISON: Had the committee any power to do that? I think it ought to have been brought before a higher tribunal. _
bouncillor CROSFIELD said they would have done so had they thought it necessary, but the committee in their judg- ment—weak as it was—(laughter)—considered it best to deal with it themselves.

Alderman Davins: No doubt the committee thought there was no higher tribunal. (Laughter.) CounePior MILNER said it was very undesirable to send cases when a conviction was not certain, and there were certain technicalities in the case under discussion which pre- vented the committee sending it forward. The MAYOR supposed it would have been sent before the magistrates hart it been a glaring case of adulteration. CouncillorMmtag : It was a glaring case. He offered to give a full explanation of the matter, but the Mayor said , they could trust the Sanitary Committee, and the minutes were passed unanimously.

GAS COMMITTEE. Accounts for two weeks ending April Ist, amounting to £Bl5 17s. 6d., and also accounts on gas extension' account for the same dates, amounting to £729 19s. 6d., were •re- commended for payment. The committee recom- mended that the tenders of Mr. John Chinley, to supply an 8-horse power high pressure engine, with four pumps, gearing, and cast iron tank for the new works, according to the specifications for the sum of £398; of Messrs Butterworth and Brooks, for the supply of flags at 3s. sd. per square yard, and setts at Hs. 4d. per ton ; and of Messrs. Collin and Son, to supply a pair of sheer legs, for the sum of £B, be accepted. On the motion of Alderman liontas, seconded by Coun- cillor Mllzran, the minutes were passed.

THE GRAMMAR SCHOOL SCHOLARSRIPS. At a meeting of the General Purposes Committee, held on the 25th April, it was resolved that the following resolu- tion passed by the Governors of the Warrington Grammar School at a meeting held on Monday, the 11th April; 1881, be entered on the minutes, viz. :—" That four free scholar- ships be given in the Grammar School itself after the Mid- summer examination and before the Midsummer vacation, two to boys who were under 17 years of age and two to boys who were under 14, on the 30th June, 1881, any boy under 14 to vacate his scholarship in two years; and that four free scholarships be given after the Government examina- tions and before the Christmas vacation, to boys from Public Elementary Schools who were net above 12 years of age on the 30th September, 1881; and that the clerk be in- structed to communicate this resolution to the papers and to the Town Clerk of Warrington." The MAYOR moved, and Alderman Ilawasox seconded the adoption of the resolation.

was thought advisable not to limit the time. A boy twelve Nears of age could stay in the school three, four, or five years, and continue his studies as long as possible, so that if he were an intelligent boy he would have an opportunity of shining in some profession and probably of going to the university. (Hear, hear.) Therefore if they drew a hard and fast line he lost probably the benefit of the education. The resolution was confirmed.

ILLYORAL VISIT TO THE CHURCH. The Mason announced that he should attend church on Sunday and he should be glad if any member of the Coun- cil would accomnany him. (Hear, bear.) They would meet at the Town Hall at 10 o'clock.•

THE ORDER OF BUSINESS. Alderman HARRISON moved "That the Town Clerk shall in the summons convening any monthly or quarterly meet- ing of the Council insert the business to be transacted in the following order:— let, the minutes bf the last meeting; 2nd, Mayor's communications; 3,d. the proceedings, resolutions, and reports of the several committees; 4th, motions. That each business shall be taken and transacted strictly in the order in which it is entered in the Council summons, unlese the Council shall otherwise direct; and that every item of the Finance Committee's minutes having reference to the payment of money be read over to the Council before tbeyare confirmed." In support of his motion Alderman Harrison re- marked that for nearly everything they did at the Council meetings they had standing orders, but they did not seem to think it necessary to have a standing order controlling the printed form of the Council business, lie gave bast-awes where much inconvenience bad been caused by a departure from the order of business as printed, and specially referred to the motion brought forward by Councillor Burgess on the 4th January, which he considered was in its proper order. That was, it was taken after the reading and confirmation of the minutes of the Council. On the let March Mr. Councillor Platt had also a motion before the Council, and that actually took precedence of the reading and confirmation of the minutes, thus giving rise to the observation from Mr. Coun- cillor Burgess in his reply when be said that the "variety was not charming." He did not think it would be charm- ing, and it was not advisable that it should be repeated. They would remember what took place that evening. Mr. Councillor Platt's motion no doubt from his point of view was a very important one, and, as an abstract proposition, one which he (the speaker) had longed to support, and he certainly shonld have done so had it not smelts, strongly of partizanship. (Laughter and "Oh, oh.") The motion consumed nearly the whole of the evening, although it was rejected by the Council as being one which they thought they should rot entertain. He bad no fault whatever to find with the way in which Mr. Councillor Platt introduced I his motion. He did it in a very pleasing manner, and indeed with such a manifestation of quiet virtue as nearly to seduce him (Mr. Harrison) to support it. (Laughter.) But he took up the whole of the evening, and by the time the motion was finished gentlemen were very impatient to get away, so much so that they had great difficulty to get a quorum to enable them to finish the business. He spoke of the relief his motion, if passed, would be to the Mayor and Town Clerk, by releasing them from the difficult task of staying no to any member, who wished the minutes of a certain committee read out of their order. Councillor PERcivAt. seconded the motion, and a long discussion ensued, from which it appeared the general body of the Council were in favour of leaving the orderof business in the hands of the Mayor, in whom they had implicit con- fidence, and at the suggestion of Alderman Holmes, Alder- man Harrison withdrew his motion, it being understood that something should be done to follow out the suggestions con- tained in his resolution.
MISCELLANEOUS. The minutes of the Finance and Cemetery Committees, which contained nothing of public interest, were confirmed. This concluded the business and the Council adjourned.

div.head: PRESCOr LOCAL BOARD
div.p: PRESCOr LOCAL BOARD

----- The first monthly meeting of this Board for the ensuing year, was held at :the clerk's offices, Derby-street, Prestot, on Wednesday. There were present Messrs. C. Spencely, H. Fogg, J. Wycherley, E. Beesley, T. S. Preston, T. Prescott J. Mawdsley, and A. T. Galloway; with Mr. Cross (clerk), and Mr. Goldsworth (surveyor.)

ELECTION OF CHAIRMAN AND COMM./TEES. Mr. PRE,corr said he had great pleasuse in moving that Mr. C. t'penceley be re-elected chairman for the ensuing year. He thought they might go further and fare worse. Mr. J. MAWDSLEY seconded, and the motion was unani- mously agreed to.

Mr. SPENCELY, on taking the chair, returned thanks. It was an office which involved a certain amount of trouble, but is was trouble which he readily gave so long as it was for the interests of the ratepayers; and he had been ably supported by the members of the Board in the discharge of his duties, trusted the business would be conducted as quietly and satisfactorily as it had been in the past year.l The following gentlemen were then appointed as members of the committees 'receding their nlimes :—General Purposes Committee, Messrd. Galloway, Bees ey, Preston and Mawds- ley ; Finance Committee, Messrs. Wycherley, Fogg, Prescott, and Twist.

NEW RATE. On the motion of Mr. narscurr, seconded by Mr. WYCHERLEY, it was unanimously resolved that a general district rate of Is. lld, in the pound be laid for the half- year ending September 29th, next.

GENERAL PURPOSES COMMITTEE. A meeting of this committee was held on the 2nd inst., when the CLERK reported that be had received from the St. Helens and district Tramways Company (Limited), their agreement under seal relating to the future extension of their lino to the railway station.—The Assisresrr- SURVEYOR reported that the Prescot Waterworks inspector had received instructions from the Liverpool Corporation to lay the requisite water mains in Hill-street. —The MEDICAL OFFICER attended, and reported the prevalence of scarlet fever among children under five years of age, and fully ex- plained his views to the commit,ee, with reference to the steps necessary to be taken. He also recommended that regulations which he had drawn up should be printed and circulated. AS to the schools, he did not think it was advisable to close them; bat the families where sickness prevailed, should be isolated in their own homes and a strict course taken that no child suffering should be allowed to enter tbe schools. He also reported that the ashpit and privies at'the church schools in Hooghton-street had been complained of, and be had met the Rev. L. W. Sampson, the vicar, and he gave orders for the requisite alterations to be made. He (the Enedical officer) considered the schools should have more ventilation.—The Sußvitvoß stated that the Prescot Gas Company had agreed to pay the Board 6d. per yard for relaying the flags and for damage done by the company in relaying their mains in St. Helens-road. The CLERK was instructed to write to the Rev. Mr. Samp- eon, calling his attention to the deficient ventilation. The committee's minutes were signed. THE REPAIRING OF THE FOOTPATHS. The Surtvarou submitted plans for the improvement of the footpaths adjoining the King's Arms Hotel. Mr. Golds- worth remarked that as the footpaths were being repaired in the New Brighton, he called Mr. William Evans' attention to the Atte of the footpaths adjoining the King's Arms Hotel, and told him that if he would find new materials it was very ' probable the Board would find the labdnr. The cost of new materials would be about £29, and the value of the old materials X 9, so that the cost to Mr. Evans would be about £2O. The cost of labour would be about £5. Mr. EVRDS had written saying be was agreeable to that. It would be a considerable improvement. The CHAIRILLN: Is that the course we have generally adopted? _
The SURVEYOR: Iti. The Board agreed to find the labour, and the work will be carried out at once.

div.head: FINANCE.
div.p: FINANCE.

From the minutes of the Finance Committee it appeared that the balance in the bank was £lO4 Gs. 11d. The sur- veyor's expenditure for the month amounted to £39 7s. 10d. Amounts amounting to £123 On. 7d. were ordered to be paid, and cheques were signed to that Smount.

div.head: ITOLE_IX THE STREET.
div.p: A ITOLE_IX THE STREET.

Mr. Mawnsunr called attention to at hole in a level crossing near the Market Hall, which was very dangerous both to foot passeagers and to vehicles. Several ratepayers had complained to him about it. He was rather surprised to hear the Surveyor speak so highly of the Assistant Surveyor at a previous meeting, and say there was nothing wrong in the streets. Mr. WYCHERLEY moved that the road be repaired. - Mr. BEESLEY seconded. Mr. PRESTON thought it highly negligent on the part of the Assistant Surveyor in not attending to the matter, as he must Lave perceived the hole passing and re-passingls he did along the Market-place. The Cmunstax said they must remember the streets in the town required a great dekl of repair. They could not dh all the repairs at once; they were going round improving the streets as well as they could. If the ratepayers would agree to a rate of about Ms. in the £ they might be able to put the town in a proper state of repair. Because there were holes in the street, it did not follow that the Assistant Surveyor had neglected his duty- (Hear, hear.) The motion was then carried.

THE REMOVAL OF /*MAT SOIL. Mr. PRESTON cOmplaitupd that on the 25th of April the refuse from 'a midden in the town was not removed off the public street until about a quarter to ten o'clock. Mr. DICKINSON, the nuisance inspector, explained that the refuse was thrown out but that the carter Wag not able to take it away quick enough, and consequently it had either to be on the street or be thrown back into the midden again. He bad complained to the c.irterand the owner about such negligence on more than one occasion. It was pointed out that the refuse was carted away volun- tarily, and therefore the Board bed very little power over either the owner or the carter. It was moved and seconded that the inspector's explanation be considered satisfactory. It was also moved, as an amendment, that the inspector's answer be not considered sufficiently explanatory of the neglect of duty, but on being put to the meeting the original motion was carried.

At a recent prosecution, under the Canal Boats' Act, by Mr. Farrington, the inspector to the Runcorn Rural Sanitary Authority, it was stated that many boat-people managed to evade both that measure and the Education Act by 1 sending their children forward when starting from a terminus and taking them on board afterwards. Mr. Farrington is an o'fficer with no small degree of energy, and I hope that he 'will be able to fully circumvent all beat people who may feel inclined to attempt to evade the responsibility of giving their children a good, sound education. What chance will an uneducated young man stand of getting a position of the slightest importance in the world Ina few years 2 I should imagine his opportunity to be exceedingly small. It is much to be regretted that some of the working people ef this country appear te be so stupid in a matter affecting the future welfare of their childon, and cause such needless trouble to the officers whose duty it is to see that they go to school. In the land o' cakes, the inhabitants of which are generally; credited with possessing even a little more than the average amount .of shrewdness in any- thing affecting their own interests, there is very Tittle of this watchfulness needed, as the Scat knows that if be crosses the Tweed with the idea of making his fortune,he must have his head well stored with knowledge, or hemight as well stay where he is. There w..,s a great rush to heat the Lord Billion of Liver- pool preach, on the occasion of the opening (if %Halton View church, Whines. The discourse was of a very practical and evangelical-nature, but I should be guilty of gress flattery if I said* that his Lordship possessed "the ,tongue of the elocpient orator." _ . _ .

• Judging from the statement made by Mr.'W. H. Linaker, solicitor,kbefore the Runcorn magistrates the other day, on I the appointment of overseers, they still mange things, to a great ettent, in the good old-fashioned way in 'the township of Aston-by-Sutton. Theinfluence of the progressive thought ef the century does notseem to trouble -some of the people Oere," for at the meeting at which the memination of over- seers took place, there were only three people' present, if Mr.ltinaker s statement be correct. !['his reminds one 61 the three tailors of Tooley-street, of Southwark, whom Can- ning says addressed?. petition describing their grievances, wirtob began with the words" We, the people of England." Wis pleasing to see that the magistrates decided to utterly ignore the nominations made by Ore meeting referred to,and appointed twe other gentlemen, upon the recommendation • of Mr. Linaker.

' I hear that Mr: Maccabe cleareid about £3O by is last iFisit to Runcorn. Strange to say,..this entertainer, who has -been before the 'public for so many years with an entertain- ment the leading features of Which are pretty similar to what they were twenty years ago, is nearly as popular as ever. On this occasion, though Mr. MaccAtie's will litera- ture made very much of the piece ,entitled " Vanquished Villany, or Virtue Victorious,"•the piece was not" trotted out," as an Prinerican would say, at all, so that the audience were not permitted the pleasure of seeing Rudolph, the hero of the 'midnight assignation, "borne to the deepest dungeon in" Sir Rowland's Castle !" Possibly it maybe produced imcase the veteran entertainer finds rit needful to break his 'heart strings once more by bidding;larewell—a long, last larewell—to his Runcorn friends.

It will b.; seen from an advertisement in your columns, that the R-,:ncorn Gas Co., have, no doubt with a desire to be "up vt:th the times," decided to reduce 'the price of gas sixpence 7er 1,000 feet, and your reader!, will-be pleased to hear that the reduction is retrospective from theffirst of April last. The prices given are said to compare 'favourably with those of towns in the surrounding district. There is another point which deserves attention, viz, that theriquality of the Runcorn gas is 30 candles illuminating power, which is higher than that of any 'surrounding lownorith the excep- tion of Liverpool. am glad to seethat 'the-directors are so wel: disposed to meet the public lathe matter of price. A very entertaining bit of scandal hes been 'varying the monotony of a parish otot 1,000 miles away during the last few weeks. A faithful son of "Mother • Church" had become the happy father of twins, and in course of time the day arrived when the new members of his family were to he christened. It appears, however,dbat owing to a press- ing engagement elsewhere, the vicar was unable to be pre- sent, and the rites of the church had 'therefore. to be con- ducted by his curate. The curate-wasn baelleler—not •an uncommon thing—but, unfortunately,,he was'ako possessed of a strong sense of the humourous. The consequence' was that no sooner were the two wee 'babies arrayed in their long baptismal robes placed in his arms Ilturthe ness of the situation quite overcame him, and be gave way to an uncontrollable burst of laughter, in which, I regret to say, not a few of the spectators !joined, and it was only Milt considerable difficulty that he was able- to keep his risible organs in order-during the continuancetof the service. The father of thebsbes, howeveryfailed to appreciate the joke, and therefore wrote to the vicar demanding an explanation of the curate's hilarous conduct. The-vicar bast in replyinz' expressed deep reg-set Jos what transpired, and stated that tris curate is subject to severe attacks of hysteria, and that what appeared to be unseemly levity was caused altogether by excitement.

Our eccentric and talented friend,,Mr. Traeey Turnerel li, of Beaconsfield wreath renown, coed not poscibly be ex- pected to allow such an opportunity-der airing his gen'us AS that offered by the death.of Lorcißeaconsfielol., to pass by. He has sought to forget the cruel sneers of an unsympa- thetic world by wooing the Muses. 'How he ha aucceeded, my readers can imagine when they read the following lines, with which he concludes his-effusions upon the death of the late Tory chieftain:—

- "But the ruin so soon'to come, The long-threatenell blow ! 'rho triumphing foe . Who will lay us so low! lle was spared these bitter hours. Better So die than to see England the,urreck•Ese is doomed to be." Who does not feel deep commiseration for poor raxey'e sad condition? To him the future has been revealedofar upon his shoulders has fallen thomantle of the great Zadkiel, and ate% alas, whilst his chief has fallen asleep, poor TS2CV must await the dire results whidh his imaginative von sees looming in the future. There is one man who is able to resist the infic.ence of sleep, "tired natures sweet restorer." Of couroe,,be is an merican. He buaete that'he can wolk for four months Without feeling drowsy. His peculiarity in this direction , was discovered in his infancy, when his constant wakefulness so alarmed his parents that they had to retort to opiates to Isoothe the brain of the noisy youngster. But an, opiate t,which would have sent his father into, a trance was com- placently swallowed by the eccentric,: juvenile without any ; other effect than to make him snore wide -awake 1 than ever. But perhaps it woOld not be amiss to lot him explain his feelings in his own way. 'llesays :—" When I I go long periods without sleep the only peculiar sensation I ' experience is that everything I look at seems distant and I larger than it really is. A short man. coming towartl me , , would apparently be very tall. 'Biding in the cold snakes I me drowsy, if anything does. Imenmmer time I can umlong periods, and feel up-top all the time. 'Last summer I did not , sleep for four months, and I worked every day." What a , splendid fellow for a railway employe! If the Yankees ' could ficd a dozen or two of his sort and seed them ever here they would be invaluable to .our railway companies, i who are rather fond of getting their men to do without sleep ' for lengthy periods. A very discouraging and therefore unplewant rumour reaches on, and it shows to what a sad condition the stiple ' !trade of the St. Helens district has been reduced to. I hear ' i that one of the largest, and one of the xsually busiest, Srnae i ,iu St. Helens engaged in the chemical trade, has been under ! the necessity of giving notice to a large number of their 1 ,workpeople to quit, as there Is not sufficient work to keep i athemcoemmptwg employed In every branch of industry the principaia re that "there is nothing doing," and that if I there is not a, turn of the commercial tide ere long business I will come to a dead lock. The wit-look is not inviting. This incident reminds me of a story I beard the other day of a tradesman, greatly in want of money, who started out on a mission of collecting debts due to himself. The man he aecoretuurnntesd. to his amount owing was not inconsiderable, but made up of a good In the evening, after a day's dunning," • place of business, his collec- dont totalising the magnificent sum of one shilling! Runcorn. o ncornf the late E . A CHILD SCALDED TO DEATH LT ItHNCOBIL—An inquest was held on Monday4by Mr. Ridgway, county coro- ner at the Railway Hotel, Runcorn, on the body of a child aged one year and eight months, the son of a man named Johnson, who died owing to it pulling a bowl of hot soup off the table, and thus scalding itself severey about the cheet. FROX LIVERPOOL TO YORE'VE'ROLD.—A Liverpool contemporary states :—" In beautifel weather, and amid the hearty cheers of a great crowd. which had assembled to wit- ness& eight familiar enough to our forefathers, but known to us now only from books, 'Hudson's coach' left the Adelphi Hotel at eight on Tuesday morning on its first journey to York. It'had its full complement ofepassengers—eeventeen —and one of these was a representative of the fair sex. ril) e coach ieselfwas probably as different ie. its appointments and appearanee from the vehieles of by-gone days as the condi- tions under-which it travels, and the circumstances of its start, were different. It is a-strongly-built, compact, and handsome ecoach, wearing 'necessarily a modernised and present-day' aspect. Yoked bit were four splendid4ook- ing horses, with trappings worthy .of themselves and the coach, and the reins were held by an expert driver, whose •get-wa Was in keeping with the rest of the turn-out. The -passengers occupied the whole of the outside seats on the coach, and naturally bore a cheerful and complacent air in anticipation of a pleasant journey—an expectation justified by the beautiful spring sun an i balmy air with which they started as accompaniments. At eighteaclock to a second the horn was sounded, and ,the coach, which had taken up a position immediately in front of the Adelphi Hotel entrance, (hove off .along Lime-street, amid the hearty huzzahs of a crowd numbering some thousands of people, the majority of whom probably had only the faintest idea of the old- fashioned travelling of which Dickens and others have made picturesque sketches." The coach arrived in Warriogton about ten .o'c!ock on Tuesday morning. A stoppage was made at the Lion Hotel, where homes were changed, and afterwards the coach proceeded on its journey, its departure being witnessed by a large crowd of interested spectators. The coach.will leave Liverpool every Tuesday, Thursday, and Saturday at eight o'clock in the morning en-reefs for York via Manchester, Hudienslidd, and Leeds, returning from York every Monday, Wednesday, and Friday, at the same hour. S.°- DEATH OP A girtdoOUß BOATMAN AT Benteanan. —On Wednesday; Mr. Hdge,,coroner, held an inquest at the Leigh Workhouse, on the remains of Thomas Nichols, 24 years,of age, belonging to Runcorn, who died on Mon- day morning•from the result of injuries sustained on Satur- day night,by falling over a wall. He had been drinking in the Bull's Head public-house at 'Bedford, and left there to fight a manmamed Thomas Whittle.—Mr. Buckley watched the proceedings on Whittle'e behalf:4ol;o lialliwell, land- lord of the public-house, deposed tri,finding deceased in his house, without coat, and tballenging Whittle to fight. He ordered them oat, and saw nothing of them afterwards.— Thomas Johnson, canal boatman, said deceased worked with him. He heard him quarrel with Whittle about boats and horses. When on the bridge, after leaving the inn, he saw them "capering about" and trying to hit each other. De- ceased was carried into witnesies house, and, believing that he was simply drunk and cit=ed, he -was left lying on the floor, and was feund in that condition next morning. A doctor was called, who said he had sustained a spinal injury. Both men were drunk.—By Mr. Buckley : Whittle was five or Sex yards from the deceased when be fell over the wall. Deceased 'was wranglesome when in chink. He had known him all his life—Mice-Silas, married woman, deposed to seeing the deceased walk to the wall and, fall over.—Dr. 'Paradise, medical officer of theiWorkhouse, said he had made a post-mortem examination, and the cause of death would be the dislocation of the spinal column. De- ceased was an exceptionally healthy man.—The Coroner, in summing op, said if deceased was threatened with a blow by Whittle, and if in retreating he tumbled over the wall which caused his death, Whittle in thatcase would be technically guilty of manslaughter. This appeared to be the case, but ; he would not advise them to return such a verdict, but te I leave it to the magistrates, if they thcught tn send the case for trial.—The Jury returned a verdict to the effect that , deceased died from injuries received through falling over a wall. Rearocatet SCHOOL BOLHD.—Thia Board held their monthly meeting on Wednesday, at the officec in Bridge- water-street. The Rev. Canon Barclay presided, and there wore also present Messrs. Norman, Pritchard, and Lea.—Mr. Vgby, clerk to the Board,referree to an objection raised by Mr. Ashton, the Runcorn magistrates' clerk, at the last Ron- oOte Petty Ssmione, to the order for presecution of parents' brought before the Bench not being signed by two members of the Board (reported in another part of our columns). The speaker gave his views of the election of the Educat:on Act as relating to the matter, and argued that the coarse he pursued was a qtelte correct one, inasmuch as section 82 of the Act of 1870 provided that orders, precepts, and other documents requiring anthentication by .1 School .Board might be signed by the elerk.--Che Cekairman asked-if the clerkceneidered it was worth while fighting the matter.— The Clerk : I contend that we are acting strictly w.ithin our rights in giving tbismrder, and that the magistrates' clerk has no right to object to it.—Mr. 'Norman was of opinion that Mr. Rigby wasquite right in the view. he took of the matter.—The Chairman (humotrously) : It is a questeon between the two clerks—the clerk to the magistrates and our own'; and if they choose to fight it out—The Clerk: lam not afraid of fighting it out with Mr. .Ashton, be- cause he is an amiable, good fellow, and open to reason.— It was decided to leave the matter in the hands of the clerk.—Mr. Bowyers, school attendance officeral presented his usual monthly return, which was as follows : Returns from the public elementary schools for April, 1881: Certified Government accommodation, 2,289; total number OS the rolls. 2,783; total average attendance, 1.944 ;,average attendance for April, 1880, 1,858; average attendance for the year 1874, 1:252; accommodation in excess of average attendance, 344. The number on the rolls in excess of accommodation was 474. These figares showed an increase in the average attendance as compared with the correspond- ing period of last year, of 87-8, and an increase, as oom• pared with 1874 (the year preceding the formation of the Board), of 8921. The total number in attendance at private adventure schools, under 9d per week, was 52. During the peel month I have summoned before the magistrates 27 parents for contravention of the bye-laws. Four parents were summoned under the Canal Boats Act, who are in the habit of taking their children with them on board their- boats to evade sending them to school. Their boa % are registered as belonging to Run and subject accordingly to the bye-laws na the Board. Three were convicted, and he usual fine of GI and di 81 'ate imposed. The other case, corn, has not yet been dealt with, the police leaving been unable lisa granted, and the rental nue of 8d and 4s ad Mae to serve the summons. In 22 other cases convictions were in- flicted in each case.

The committee appointed to estimate the cost of extra- ordinary traffic at Appleton, caused by Messrs. Turner and sorycontractors, reported that they had been over the roads with the surveyor where the new sewer had been put In, and they were unanimously of opinion that the contractors had damaged the road to a vely considerable extent, and they recommended the Board to claim £l6 from them, as extra cost, to that which had already been incurred, owing to the cartage of sewerage pipes and sand over the roads by Messrs. Turner and Son. It would cost a considerable sum to put the road§, which the contractors had interfered with, into good repair, and they estimated that 50 tons of stone would be required. The report then went on to give particulars of the damage done to the road, andconcluded by saying that the 'committee were informed during their inspection, that there had been numerous cases of the roads giving way under , ordinary traffic, owing to the tunnelling which had been ' resorted to in putting in the sewer. The CLERK said the claim against Messrs. Turner and Son would. be £47 17s. 6d., made up of £l6 expenses in- curred, 50 tons of stone required at 103. 91 per ton, £26 1 17s. 6d., and £5 for laying the stone. Mr. PERCIVAL moved the adoption of the report, and that that portion of it which related to the present conditionof the work be sent to the engineer, and inform him to see that the matter was put right, or there wonld be a still further claim made on the contractor. Mr. LOWE seconded the motion, which was carried.

He also stated that the auditor required the surveyor to obtain orders for raanuel labour, and on account of this not having been done he had surcharged the surveyor • £9l 7s. 7d. THE BOARD ECONOMISE.—THE LABOURERS' WAGES. Mr. BENTLEY said the Board were paying large wages for men that were doing very little, and there were many rate- payers outside the Board who were finding fault with it. He would like to know the wages of the head men in each town- ship, and wheder they were competent to pull up and lay down a pavement. They had men travelling six or seven miles to put down pavements, and he thought the men em- ployed in each township should he capable of putting any road In good repair, without having to pay other men to do it whilst they were idling their time away. The CnenzataN thought Mr. Bennett's remark had a good deal of weight about them as their labour men at times -.walked aboutdoing nothing. Mr. PERCIVAL said they had many labourers who were not worth 12s. Farm labourers did not get such wages, and vet they were at work earlier in a morning, and worked later: in the evening. He considered all the Board's labourers over- paid. The SURVEYOR gave the wages of the foremen in each township accompanied with comments upon the efficiency of his men. He said he had only-two or three men capable of undertaking the whole of the work of making good roads. The CHAIRMAN remarked that he understood Mr. Bennett to mean that the headmen in each district should be able to properly repair roads without having to bring men from other districts: If the surveyor had not men able to so he must find such men and change them.

. Mr. BnwnErr : That is what mean. A clesultry discussion followed in which the majority of memberscresent expressed thetneelves satisfied that they had a large number of men who, considering the work they were capable of doing, were overpaid, and that these ought at once to have their wages reduced. The CLERK formulated the following resolutions, which were moved by Mr. Bmairrr, and seconded by Mr. LOWE —That, when any contract work has to be done on any highway it shall be let to the head workman in each district cin which the work is to be done, and another man shall not brought from any other district to do such work; that so far as possible all pavement shalt be taken up and replaced bv the head workmen or extra men employed by Mm, and that stones be broken at per ton or cubic yard. The SURVEYOR said the work was done cheaper at present than it could be done by the method proposed, and he doubted if men capable of doing the work in that manner could be got for each district. Mr.Nsin slid he understood that the head workman had only to do the work at a day wage. The CtiIIkIRIVAN said that if he was capable they did not mind letting it to him on contract. Some further conversation took place, and eventually the resolutions were passed. This terminated the business.

div.head: SATION BILL.
div.p: SATION BILL.

The select committee of the House of Commons to whici! ! this bill was referred at at Westminster, on Thursday. The bill is promoted by owners of property in the neighbourhood of Nantwich and Winsfoid, its object being to recover corn peneation for damage done by the subsidence of land in con- sequence of the pumping of brine. Sir Sydney Waterloo oc- cupied the chair, and the other members were the hon. E. L. Stanley, Viscount Emlyn, Mr. Storey-Maskelyne, Sir Henry Tyler, Colonel St. John Barne, and Mr. Blennerhasset. The counsel for the promoters were Mr. Pope. QC. Mr. Michael Q.C., and R. S. Wright; and for the owners of salt works Mr. Fember, Q.C., and Mr. Balfour Brown; and for the river Weaver navigation Sir Edmund Beckett, Q.C., and Mr. fig- gin, Q.C.; while the ratepayers and owners were represented by Mr. Salisbury—The Chairman, at the outset, announced that he had, through the Home Office received a petition against the bill from the working men of the salt districts engaged in the trade. Mr. Pope, Q C , in opening the case, said the bill was a simple matter, though it involved questions of some interest are.] novelty. The object of the bill was to provide a fund out of which compensation might be adjudged by a board to 'be constituted under the provisions ot the bill in respect of damage to property arising from the subsidence caused from the pumping of brine from below the surface, which pump- ing of brine was used in the manufacture of salt. The scope cf the bill was something as follows :—The brine which pro- duced 32 cwt. of white salt represented 1 cubic yard of rock salt dissolved, or the manufacture of 1,800.000 tons of white salt meant the abstraction in the shape of brine of 232 acres, Cr 1,120,000 cubic yards per annum of rock salt from below the superinctunbent stratification. The scheme of the bill was that the consumers of brine or the salt proprietors should contribute to this fund in proportion to the amounted brine which they actually consumed, and, therefore, practi - cally, in proportion to the amount of contribution to the in- jury complained of. It VCIE proposed to limit the amount of the contribution to the fund to 3d. per ton upon the salt produced, but it was hoped that the sum would not be so large. The fund would be administered by a board consisting of the various interests—the property owners, the ratepayers, and the salt proprietors—and nothing would be paid for compen- sation which did not pass under the cognizance of the board. The principle of raising by a general system of taxation under a fund for such a purpose was novel, and therefore, that was a matter which the committee would have to consider. The general law was well-known ; ordinarily speaking, if a miner withdrew from the surface by his mining operations support to which the surface was entitled, he must make good the damage which he caused. The solid stratification was removed by pick and shovel, and everybody knew who was working at the spot let down. The peculiarity of the present case was, that inasmuch as this was not the removal of the solid stratification of rock gall', which in a st-te of nature would support the surface, by pick and shovel, but meant the use of a solvent—to wit, water which was pumped at some distance from the spat which subsided, it became impossible to identify by which pump, or stroke of the pumps, or by which particular individual, the injury was caused. The question therefore arose whether, under such circumstances, compensation ought to be awarded at all, and, if provided, by what means. The pro- moters submitted that it should not be left to the parties to resort to endless litigation, but by a fund, contributed to by all the parties, and distributed among the claimants by a board equitably and fairly constituted. He was d'lfie to point to no exact precedent for this scheme, but he could call the attention of the committee to claims for legislation en ex- actly the same lines,and involving identical principles. The learned gentleman went on to allude to the North Stafford- shire drainage works, Where Parliament enabled a board to tax an entire district In proportion to the advantage derived by the various persons from the drainage works. In the c e presentea as casee the tra Popexntio wouldhen tnw wenton no z proportiontisotmo edetails them s h f d m of the quanties of salt produced from the mines, and he had no hesitation in saying that if they could identify the in- tdividual causing the mischief, the general law would be sufficient; but they could only tell that it was the result of the general trade of the district, and they submitted that. they: were justified in asking for exceptional legislation. . .
The Chairman asked whether -compensation had ever been granted Mr. Pope said he knew of none. _

Mr. Balfour Brown remarked that the rents paid had been held to cover compensation. Mr. Pope, resuming, .said that efforts were made to induce te late Government to make the question a subject of zeneral legislation ; but they could not see their way to adopt the proposal. as the injury complained of only affected one pArticular district, and it was at their suggestion that the present bill had been introduced. The learned counsel then proceeded to deal with the various petitions against the bill. Mr. Stanley asked who were the promoters of the bill?

Mr. Pope replied that they comprised about 200 of the principal landowners and ratepayers of the district. The first witness tilled was Mr. Joseph Dickinson. principal inspector of mines to the Home Office. He stated that in 1873 he, in accordance with instructions received, examined and made a report upon the salt works of Cheshire, including Northwich, Winsford, Middlewiah, and Sandbach. After detailing the geological nature of the-salt districts, the witness stated that since he made his repert the subsidences had been going on extensively in Nortbwich and Winsford. In the latter place there was only one rock salt or dry mine. He had not the slightest doubt that the subsidence was caused by the pump- ing of brine. It could only have been caused to a very small extent by rock salt mining. The result of sinking a shaft and pumping was to draw away the underlying strata of the whole district. Ile did not believe that any of the subsidence was due to quicksand or to lirne springs as had been suggested. The Chairman: What increased extent of subsidence has occurred during the last twenty years in the districts under consideration, in consequence of the pumping, compared with what might have occurred if there had been no pump- ing but only the natural flow of the brine springs? The witness said that almost the whole of the damage which had taken place was due to the pumping. There would have been scarcely any perceptible damage but for the pumping of brine. In cross-examination by Mr. Pember, Q.c., witness said that the Combermere Lake was found in the sixteenth cen- tury, and was, be believed, due to the pumping of brine at Nantwich, the works at that town being then in full opera- tion. Combermere Lake was about six miles from Nant- wich, and a considerable elevation above it. There was no doubt that the subsidence was going on at a greater ratethan in former times, for by the ordinance map forty years ago there was scarcely a patch of water of any extent in the dis- trict, whereas now there were numerous lakes of considerable size. The increased agitation of the under current of water, caused by the pumping washed the rock salt and took up the brine to an extent that it would not be taken up by the ordi- nary natural now. By Mr. Higgin, Q.C. : He thought that the proposed sys- tem of taxation on salt would be a very proper way of giving compensation for damage caused by the pumping, and that the landowners who obtained royalties for the use of the brine pits and pumps ought not to be exempted from the provisions of the bill. The committee adjourned.
The committee re-assembled in No. 13 committee room at Westminster, yesterday, under the presidency of Sir Sydney Waterlow.

Mr. Dickenson, Her Majesty's did inspector of mines,i who was examined on Thursday for the promoters, was now cross-examined by Mr. Michael, who represents certain pro- perty owners, principally salt proprietors, who oppose the Bill. Mr. Dickenson stated that in consequence of the pro- perty being built on sand, the subsidence at Northwich was exceedingly small, and might be dismissed from considera- tion. In reply to questions by members of the committee, he stated that at Northwich and Winsford the rock salt had been pressed to lie below the sea level, and that at no part of either these districts did the uppremost bed of salt come up to the sea level. The wasting that had been going on in these districts belew sea level had been almost entirely due to the pumping operations. The only place he knew of at which rock salt had been proved to be above sea level was Lowton, but there the thickness of the rock salt was such that if the whole of it was dissolved and gone the land being at such a high elevation would not fall below that of the sea. In further examination Mr. Dickenson said that he had recently made an investigation into the sub.idences c nisei by a landslip at Dunkirk in his official capacity, and partly with a view to tendering evi- dence upon the Bill. The solicitor of the Bill (Mr. Cook) had requested him to visit the spot, and see what had taken place, as he would be examined as a witness. He (Mr. Dickinson) then communicated the request to the Home Office, and was then recommended to go. He had not read the Bill. His principal object was to offer evidence on the question of compensation. He was in favour of extending the scope of the Bill by throwing the expense and compen- sation on those who benefitted from the cause of the damage. Mr. Thomas Wald, manager of the salt works of Messrs. Ashton and Sous, Nantwich, stated that he was largely acquainted with the salt mining districts, and did not think the proposed tax of 3d. per ton upon the salt raised would at all affect the price of salt. In Northwich 1.200 acres of land had subsided. Witness produced an ordnance map dated 1717, which showed that land forming green fields was now under water.—The examination of the witness was proceeding when the Committee adjourned for the day.

STRAEDE AND SUDDEN DEATH OF • Graz. AT Si,. HELENS. —A girl, 14 years of age, named Mary Elizabeth Keenan, who regided with her parents at 60, College-street, died vbry suddenly under the following circumstances on Monday night. • Deceased has been troubled with fainting fits since her birth, and was seized with one about three weeks ago. On the day of her death she looked very ill, but had her meals as usual and went out to play at twenty minutes past eight in the evening. Whilst amusing herself with two girls at the :mint door, she said to one of them "I'll knock at Mrs. Cur- ran's doer with my head and pretend to be dead when Mrs. Curran comes out." She knocked her head against the (loci ind was soon after fen home insensible where site died In about an hour in the presence of her parents.

THE BANKRUPTCY BILL.—Mr. CHAMBERLAIN Said that in committee he would be willing to consider proposals for extending the provisions of the Bankruptcy Bill to estates now in liquidation. THE BEACONSFIELD MEMORIAL.'-Mr. MACDONALD asked if a copy of the inscription to be placed on Lord Beacons.. field's statue would be laid on the table.—Mr. RYLANDS asked whether, considering the importance of the Irish Land Bill, the motion for the erection of the memorial could not be postponed until after the second reading of the Irish Land Bill.—Lord HARTINGTON said Mr. Gladstone being slightly unwell he could only say the inscription would be in accor- dance with the terms of the motion. It was impossible he could in the absence of his right hon. friend answer the question of the member for Burnley. No doubt the Premier had fully considered the time when the memorial was to be proposed, and he would not therefore be disposed to consider a proposal for its posTonement.—Mr.MACDONALD wishedto know whether the inscription would embrace words referring to the political services of the deceased.—No answer was given to this. THE DOTEREL DISASTER.—Mr. SMITH asked if there was any truth in the loss of the Doterel being attributed to a torpedo lost some time 'ago by H.M.S. Shah?—Mr. TRE- VELYAN said the unloaded torpedo was lost by the Shah, but it had been picked up and brought home by H.M.S. Ocean. THE RUSSIAN EMBASSY AT CABUL.—Lord lIARTINGTON said he had received no information to confirm the report published that another Russian Embassy kad left for Ca bul . THE CONDITION OF IRISH LABOUREES.—On the motion to go into C mornittee of Su tply, Mr. CALLAN called atten- tion to the condition of the Irish agricultural labourer. He urged the pressing necessity that existed for affording facilities for the erection of cottages and the providing of suitable garden plots, and moved that in the opinion of the House it was expedient and necessary that measures should be taken in the present session of Parliament to improve the condition of the agricultural labourer's habitations of Ire- land.—Mr. DALY seconded the resolution, and said Go- vernment ought to give immediate attention to the subject. —Mr. A. MOORE and Mr. O'Snottvax supported.—Mr. FORSTER admitted the condition of the Irish labourer was very bad, and frankly said all that could be done should be done. He also admitted that they ought not to permit the Land Bill to pass without allowing amendments to be , mule that were germane to it. He regrett d the temporary absence of the Prime Minister, but in his absence he could not pledge the Government to any particular line of action. They would look at the bill in order to see if anything could be done, if not the Government would give their attention to the subject. He would, if the words " during the present session of Parliament" were omitted, support the resolution,—Mr. PARNELL did not see why something should not be done with the Land Bill to improve the condition of the Irish labourer. He suggested that the Land Commissioners should purchase land and sell small allot- ments to labourers. This, with improved cottages, would make them independent of both farmers and landlords.—Mr. JOHN BRIGHT thought it would be a mistake to encourage the Irish labourer to live on the produce of his allotment rather than wars, as by such a step they would be build- ing up a system worse than that which now existed. He thought the only way of permanently improving the condi- tion of Irish labourers was to stimulate the industry of the country. He wished to see, if possible, clauses in- troduced into the Land Bill to improve the condition of the labourer. If any plan was suggested by hon. gentlemen opposite which would not rob anybody, and was really practical, Government, he felt sure, would he glad to adopt it. Mr. O'DONNELL took objection to the observations made by Mr. Bright.
