WARRINGTON -UNION SCHOOL ATTRNDANCH COMMTT- TER.—The first meeting of the newly constituted committee was held at the Workhouse on Wednesday, when there were present the Rev. G. F. Roberts, Rev. J. Yenge, Messrs. R. Garnett, W. Derbyshire, I'. Hall, S. Sutton (assistant clerk), and B. Hobson (attendance officer).—The Rev G. F. Roberts was appointed chairman, and Mr. W. Derbyshire, vice- chairman.—Mr. Hobson reported that most of the schools in his district kept up their attendance, and several of the schools showed a slight increase • in the average attendance. Hollinfare school had averaged 97 during the past quarter, which was the highest quarter's average it had ever had. He experienced some difficulty with respect to the parents of children and small farmers, who were now buoy setting their potatoes. The fourth standard exemption debarred children of 10 to 13 years of age being employed half time in dropping potatoes, if they had not passed the fourth standard. At Grappenhall the children had nearly all recovered from the mumps, but at Thelwall schoool, last week there were 36 marled sick, who had the same ailment. At Padgate school there were four children still absent on account of fever. Some parents were afraid of their children being taken from them and sent to the Infectious Diseases Hospital at Warrington, and they kept the fact as quiet as possible. The rest of the district was, he believed, free from epidemic disease. The averages for the six weeksending April 29th, were :—Orford school, 155 ; decrease. 2. Penketb, 125; decrease, 2. Winwick, N; in- crease, 1. Grappenhall, 87; increase 2. Hollinfare, 100 ; increase 6. Martinscroft, 80; increase, 3. Padgate, 89- Increase, 4. Thedwall, 75; increase, 1. Sankey, 87 ; increase, 3.

DEATH OF MR. HERMON, M.P. FOR PRESTON. Mr. Hermon, M.P., senior member for Preston, died in Loudon at 5-30 yesterday morning. The hon. gentleman was seized with an apopletic fit in one of the rooms adjoin- ing the House on Th ursday night, and was at once removed to his private residence. He never rallied. The deceased gentleman was the son of Mr. Richard Hermon, and his mother was the youngest daughter of Mr. George Udny, formerly member of the Supreme Council of India. For many years he was connected with the firm of Messrs. Hoe- rocks, Miller, and Co., manufacturers, Preston, whose Man- chester offices are at 55, Piccadilly. From being a servant in the London warehouse he rose to the position of a part- ner, and, on the death of Mr. Thomas Miller, in 1865, became head of the firm. He continued his active cm nee- don with the firm till about 18 months ago, when he retired. Mr. Hermon was first elected for Preston in 1868. On that occasion the result of the polling was :—Mr. Hermon (C), 5,803; Sir T. G. F. liesketh, 5,700; Mr. J. F. Lees (L), 4,741; Lord E. Howard (L), 4,668. On the death of Sir?. G. F. Hesketh, Sir John biker, Q.C., Attorney-gentwa in the late Administration, was returned as the collaagde of Mr. Hermon. At the general election in 1874 afs Mention was again at the head of the poll with 6,512 voßs; Sir J. Holker obtained 5,211, and Mr. Thomas Mottershead, Liberal and labour candidate, 3,756. At the election, last year, the voting was—Mr. Hermon, 8,239; Sir John Holker, 5,641; and Mr. G. W. Bahr (Liberal), 5,555. As an employer of labour Mr. Hermon was exceedingly popular, and was highly esteemed in the borough.—A correspondent at Preston tele- graphs :—On Monday last Mr. Hermon was in Preston, and no complaint was then heard of. His death is causing pro- found consternation among all parties here. He was greatly esteemed in the town, to which he was a great benefactor. THE TRUSTEES OF THE BRITISH MUSEUM. At the meeting of the Trustees of the British Museum, yesterday afternoon, in the Premier's official residence, Downing-street, the Prince of Wales, Lord Houghton, and the lean of Christchurch were elected to fill the vacan- cies in the Board caused by the death of the Earl of Beaconsfield, Sir Philip Egerton and another. The official notification of the election will' not, however. be published until those elected have sign Med their acceptance of the trusteeship.

ATTEMPT TO BLOW UP CHESTER BARRACKS. Shortly. before eleven o'clock, on Thursday night, an ex- plosion took place at the rear of the Chester Militia Bar- racks, which are situated neat Chester Castle, and on land belonging to the county, although within the city walls. On the matter being investigated, it was found that a black satchel, filled with some explosive substance (supposed to be dynamite), had been hung against the wall of the build- ing. and exploded by means of a fuse. Owing to unskilf al- ness the damage was but trifling. Further particulars re- specting the attempt on Chester Castle state that the hole was dug on the west side of the barracks before the bag was deposited, but the hole was not deep enough to undermine the wall, and no damage was done. The combustible was deposited directly against the guardroom. Two men have been arrested on suspicion.

div.p: RANKS.

The Tories of Wolverhampton have just lost one of the "shining lights"—no less a one than the Rev. J. E. Glad- stone, a cousin of the Right Hon. W. E. Gladstone. The rev, gentleman has always been regarded in South Stafford- shire as a strong Tory and Anti-Ritualist, an-I his severance from the local Tory Association has come about this way. After the death of Lord Beaconsfield, the ex-Premier's fol- lowers convened a public meeting, at which the speech of the evening was made by a Roman Catholic clergyman named Canon Davies. Mr. Gladstone's cousin took umbrage at this, saying that the Conservative Association were pandering to the Irish and to the Roman Catholics, and he would leave It, and go in for Mr. H. H. Fowler, the Liberal member for the borough, if he would vote "Protestant." The Con- servatives are trying hard to get the rev. gentleman to alter his mind.

PRESENTATION TO A ST. HELENS POLICEMAN. At the St. Helens Police Court yesterday morning, Mr. William Pilkington, the presiding magistrate, presented to P.C. Frank Fielding the Royal Humane Society's testi- monial, for having, on the.9th March, 1891, jumped into the canal at St. Helens to the rescue of Kate Donelan, who was in imminent danger of drowning, and whose life he gallantly saved. Superintendent Johnson in forward- ing the particulars at the time to the Chief Con- stable, said that the officer swam across the canal to the other side, where the WM= was clinging to a coping ' stone. The woman said she lived at Widnes. She was taken to the police office where her clothes were dried. Mr. Johnston also observed that P.C. Fielding was a very smart fellow and constable, and had been 2nd class since July last, and hoped that the Chief-constable would promote him to the rank of Ist. This was dune. A large nu.nber of officers assembled in court at the request of the Chief-con- stable, and the magistrate in a few chosen words, presented the testimonial to P.C. Fielding, who returned thanks in a short neat speech. Superintendent Johnston also congratu- lated the officer. THE CHESHIRE LINES COMMITTEE RAILWAY

div.p: WARRINGTON POLICE CASES. _-- Sercrripta.—By Aldermen Burgess and Chandlev. A L'CRIOUS CASE OF DESERTION.—WiIIiam McCuo was charged with being a deserter from the 4th Royal Lam esiiire Militia, and also with riding from Blackburn to Wan ;egton on the 25th April, without ticket.—Sergeant-Major Tepham said prisoner had absented himself from the trainir'ee in 1873 math 1881.—Prisoner said that in 1873, before the com- mencement of the training, he wept to see Colonel Gn,dfrev to try and buy himself off, as he wanted to go to America. eolonel Godfrey would not release him, and he deserted. He wrote to the Colour-Sergeant last Saturday, asking if he would be required to attend the training, and be was answered in the affirmative. He did not think he should be tried for desertion, as he bad already served a teem of imprisonment for that offence, having been tried at Wigan in January 1880. He said a letter had been sent to the authoritiee, informing them of the fact.—Sergeant Topham handed in a letter, which stated that the prisoner on the date named by him, was brought before the justices at Wigan on three charges. First with stealing six hens, second with stealing two geese, and third with being a deserter from the 4th Lancashire Militia. The second charge was with- drawn, and on the first charge he was convicted and sentenced to six months' imprisonment. On that of deser- tion he was set free, in consequence of his term of service having expired previous to hie apprebension.—Alderman Ghandley did not think they could go into the case a second time.--Sergeant Topham said prisoner's term of service could not have expired, as he bad yet four years to serve.— With reference to the charge of rlding without a ticket, prisoner said he had tried to get a warrant at Blackburn, but could not, and he thoti!,ht his summons would be sufficient.—Mr. Ashworth, station master, Bank Quay, said, what the prisoner said was perfectly correct. If a man could present a summons, the military authorities would pay the company the railway fare, but, owing to prisoner being a deserter, they repudiated the responsibility. Were those summons not accepted by them, they would have to detain 20 men every week.—The prisoner was remanded, to allow inquiries to be ma dc respecting his statement. Dlownia.—Before His Worship the Mayor (Alderman Pickmere), the ex-Mayor (Councillor Fairclough), and Alderman Webster. THE SOLDIER AND HIS CLOTHES.—WiIIiam McCormick was charged with having deserted from Her Majesty's Bth Regiment on the 16th April.—Prisoner pleaded guilty. He stated that he was intoxiwted a few days before the date named, and a man robbed him of his clothes and sold them. Re was absent from his regiment five days in consequence . Re was ordered to be handed over to the military escort in waiting. THE CURIOUS CASE OF DESERTION.—Wm. McCue was brought up on remand chargen with being a deserter from the 4th Lancishire Militia; and also with riding on the London and North-Western Railway without ticket.—A letter had been received from the Chief Constable of Wigan stating that the prisoner was not dealt with for desertion when before the justices in January, MO.—Prisoner was fined 40s. including costs, or, in default, a month's imprison-

meat. THEFT FROM A Dyramauci-noersu.—Margaret Quin, re- siding at 127, Bowcock-street, was charged with stealing a pair of women's boots, value 55., from the dwelling-house of Mrs. Corcoran, 17, Thomas-street.—Prisoner pleaded guilty.—Prosecutrix said she did not wish to press the case. Prisoner, herself, and a few others were drinking together at her house on Saturday night. About 9 o'clock she went out leaving prisoner and another woman in the house. When she returned the boots were missing, but, as prisoner would not own to having taken them, she informed the police. She would not have done so but she had "some drink in her." Witness said she and prisoner were in the habit of taking articles in that way from each other's houses.—Prisoner was fined ss. and £1 costs, or a week's imprisonment. STREET OBSTRUCTION. Mary Daly was charged with obstructing Horsemarket-street, on Tuesday night, by sit- ting on the window sill of Messrs. Woods, grocers.—Mr. Hunt said there were many complaints about the footpath being obstructed in that particular place, and it was a great annoyance to passers-by.—Defendant was cautioned and ordered to pay the costs, 3s. 6d. BREACHES OF THE ELEMENTARY EDI:CATION ACT.— John Duan, Michael Melia, James Briddon, Wm. Tranter, and Thomas White were summoned for not sending their children regularly to school, and they were each fined ss. ILLEGALLY SUPPLYING INTOXICATING LIQUOR. John Hardman, grocer, Battersby-lane, and holder of a license to sell beer and porter to be consumed off the premises, was °barged with supplying a vessel of beer to be consumed, on Battersby-road, and T. Braisegirdle was charged with aiding and abetting—The Mayor did not sit during the hearing of this case.—From the statement of the Chief Constable, it appeared that Braisegirdle is a slater working near Hard- man's premises. On Friday morning, the 22nd April, Sergt. Berry observed Braisegirdle standing in the middle of the street, opposite Hardman's shop, drinking from a jug. He saw Braisegirdle take the jug into Hardman's shop and he followed, and found that the jug had contained beer.—ln reply to the Bench, Mr. Hunt said it was contrary to the law for defendant to allow liquor to be drunk on the pre- mises or to supply vessels so that it might be consumed on ground adjoining.— &Herm in Webster said they would deal leniently with the case, as it was the first time, and only inflict a fine of ss. and costs on each defendant. TWESDA.Y.—Before Alderman Webster, Councillor Fair- clougti, and Major Cartwright A BATCH OF FEMALE VAGRANTS.—Annie Flialaghan, Jone Flynn, Maria Shields, and Ellen Lavelle were charged with being vagrants, having been found sleeping in a closet in Dial-court, about one o'clock that morning.—Sergeant Berry, who proved the case, said the police had had much trouble with the prisoners. They " were the worst girls in Warrington." In answer to Major Cartwright, witness said Lavelle was 17 years of age, and the rest is. Fustian cut- ting ought to be their professiou.—Major Cartwright remarked that girls of the same description as the prisoners were an intolerable nuisance in Orford, and if there could be a little more police superyision it would be as well.—Mr. Hunt said that Orford was out of their jurisdiction, but there were two beats there that were never left in winter or sum- mer.—Prisoners were committed to Walton gaol for a month, with hard labour. THE TATOOED MILITIAMAN.—George Cahill was charged. on remand with fraudulently enlisting into the 2nd Royal Lancashire Militia.—Prisoner was before the Bench on Wednesday, but as the fraudulent enlistment had really been committed at Wexford, in Ireland, the magistrates' clerk said the Bench had no jurisdiction, and the case was ad- journed so that enquiries might be made. Mr. Hunt addressed a communication to the police authorities at Wex- ford, and a reply had been received (rem the inspector of constabulary in which it was stated that the charge they had against him was of a trivial nature and they would not prefer it, as the expense of fetchiog him from England would be so great.—Major Cartwright (laughing): He is not worth having, seemingly.—The Bench, acting on the advice ef Mr. White, discharged the prisoner. Tunusnar.—Before Captain Litton. A SOLD/ER BSWARDED.—James Travis was charged with deserting from the 22nd regiment of foot, stationed at Chester, on the 2ud May last.—Private Wm. Griffiths was walking in the streets at Warrington on the previous day, when he met the prisoner. He at once detected that prisoner was wearing military trousers, and he arrested him an suspicion. Prisoner gave his name as Joseph Wild, but afterwards admitted that he vas a deserter, and that his name was James Travis.—Prisoner was remanded to Walton goal to await an escort. The soldier who had made the capture applied for tee usual rewerd,and he was allowed the highest sum possible, Ll. James Helsby was charged with being a deserter from the Bth regiment stationed at Warrington. He voluntarily surrendered himself at the Barracks a week ago. He was ordered to be hincled over to the military authorities at the Warrington barracks. FRlDAY.—Before Major Cartwright (chairman), Aldermen Pickmere (mayor), Webster, Holmes, and Burgess, and Messrs. John White and Ziba Armitage. ATTICS ON THE POLICE: A WORTHLESS SOLDIER.— James Gallagher, a soldier, was charged with being drunk and riotous on the previous night, and also with assaulting P.S. Berry.—At about a quarter to twelve prisoner was observed by PS. Berry, to be annoying a woman in Bridge- street. The c,flicr requested him to desist and go to the Barracks, but he refused and became very abusive. The officer, therefore, with the aid of P.C.Trickett, took him into custody, but he was so violent that it wok them 20 minutes to convey him to the police station, having to drag him a portion of the distance. Whilst in Bridge-street, prisoner kicked P.S. Berry on the back.—Colour-Sergeant Alexander said the prisoner belonged to the I company at the barracks. He had only come out of prison on Wednesday, and indeed be had spent most of his time since he enlisted, in prison or the guardroom. He had not performed a day's duty since he enlisted seven months' ago. The authorities would be glad to get rid of him.—ln aaswer to Major Cartwright wisoner stated that he was an Irishman and a labourer by trade.—Major Cartwright said they must make an example of the prisoner, as they could not have their officers insulted by such fellows, when they were on duty.—For being drunk prisoner was fined 400. and costs, or in default, a months' imprisonment, and for the assault he was committed to gaol for three months' with hard labour. THE KEEFING OF LODGERS.—Bridget Mitchell, an old woman, was charged with keeping an unlicensed lodging house. Inspector Church said he visited defendant's house, on the 25th ult., and found there were six persons living in] the house, four lodgers and two of a family. The house was only adapted for four persons, but it was in clean condition. Defendant said she kept the lodgers to make a living and she would not again offend. She was lined Is. including costs. CHARGE AGAINST A LODGING HOPSE KEUPSll.—PatriCk Farrell, a common lodging house keeper, was charged with keeping more lodgers than he was entitled to by his license. On Thursday morning the 29th ult., at half past four, Ser- geant Spinks. and P. C. Chantler, visited defendant's house which is in Tanner'S yard, off Bank-street. The house was only registered for 41 persons, and en the morning in ques- tion there were 42 persons, being (lily one in excess, but in one room there were 15 persona whereas there only ought to have been ten. There were five beds in the room and three men in each bed.—Major 'Cartwright: You are liable to a penalty of £s—Defendant: Well, take myself and all to- gether. (Laughter.) It appeared that defendant had kept a lodging house for a period of 35 years, and there had been no complaints as to the manner in which the house had been conducted. He was therefore fined ss. and Cogs, 12s. BREAM OF THE PEACE —Winifred Shaw, a married woman, was summoned for committing breach of the peace on the lot instant, by beating and assaulting Sarah Marsh —Defendant was bound over to keep the peace for three months. NEWTON IMPROVEMENT COMMISSIONERS. The monthly meeting of these Commissioners, held in the Board-room at the Town Hall, Newton-le-Willows, on Mon- day, was presided over by Mr. W. F. Gooch, and there were also present Messrs.Winstanley, Emmett, Birley, Fairclough, J. E. I,Vorsley (law clerk), and R. Brierley (surveyor). THE COMMISSIONERS AND THE ALKALI BILL. The LAW-CLERK, replying to Mr. Birley in reference to the Alkali Bill, said according to instructions given hint he first of all wrote to the Local Government Board, and they requested him to send them the objections which the Com- missioners had to the Bill. He therefore had a copy of the printed Bill procured, in which he interleaved the objections the Commissioners had to the clauses and sent it to the Local Government Board. On Saturday week he went up to London, having made appointments with the members of Parliament, and on Monday he had an interview with the Local Government Board upon the subject, and they ap- proved of the alterations and suggestions. He also went to see Sir Richard Cross, Colonel Blackbume, Mr. Rylands, and Mr. McMinnies. He also saw the secretary to the I Municipal Corporations Association, a society that Mr. Brook was in communication with, as to what they were going to do. Sir Richard Cross, after seeing the objections which the Commissioners made, thought them very fair, and asked him if he could prepare the alteration which the Commissioners suggested in such a form as that it might be in- serted in the Bill as an amendment. On Tuesday, he had other copies of the Bill, which Mr. McMinnies got him from the House, interleaved with the clause as altered, inserted, and sent them to the House of Commons for each member he had seen. The alterations were very favourably received indeed; the members seemed to think they were very proper and very fair; and he thought that they might be very likely carried out. Sir Richard Cross promised that he would see Mr. Dodson, president of the Local Government Board, upon the matter, and if he would do so, he (the Law-Clerk) thought it was very likely indeed it would be done.

PROVISION FOR INFECTIOPS CASES. The LAW CLERK produced the agreement between the Mayor, Aldermen, and Burgesses of the borough of Warring- ton with the Commissioners for the reception of patients at the Infectious Diseases Hospital, which agreement was sealed, by the Warrington authority. HIGHWAYS PUBLIC WORKS &C. COMMITTEE. The meeting of the Highways, Public Works and Sanitary Committee, WAS held on the 25th ult. Upon the question of sewering Crow Lane, between the Oak Tree Inn, and junc- tion with Gas-street coming up, Mr. Brierley was instructed to prepare a statement of public works not yet carried out, and for which loans have been obtained. Plans for house, stables, etc., for Mr. Samuel Hewitt in Park-road and Mercer- street, and for a house and surgery in Cross Lane for Mr, J. N. Patterson, were submitted and approved. The minutes were passed on the motion of the CHAIRMAN, seconded by Mr. Emmgrr.

div.p: TILE COMMISSIONERS' ACCOUNTS.

The minutes of the Finance Committee stated that at the meeting on the 25th April, Mr. Brierley read letters from clerks to the Improvement Commissioners of Stourbridge, Spalding, Llandudno, Leek, Rhyle, and Middleton, express- ing their opinion that the new form of accounts issued by the Local Government Board, applied only to expenses in- curred under the Public Health Act, 1875, and not to their local acts. It was ordered that Mr. Brierley and the Law Clerk wait upon the secretary of the Local Government Board and state the objections to keeping the Commissioners' accounts under the new order and if necessary apply for their assent to depart from such regulations under Act 1 of such order. A communication was received from the secretary of the Association of Muni- cipal Corporations inviting the Commissioners to become annual subscribers of one guinea for which a monthly cir- cular containing parliamentary, law, and other matters affect- ing all urban authorities are published; and the committee recommended the Board to subscribe thereto. Accounts amounting to £337 Os. Pd. were examined and cheques signed for payment. The minutes were agreed to on the proposition of the CHAIRMAN, seconded by Mr. BIRLEY.

SCHOOL ATTENDANCE DURING THE QUAIITER. A meeting of the School Attendance Committee was held on the 25th April, when Mr. Ball, attendance officer, read his report, which stated that for the quarter ending March, 1881, the number of children on the books was 2,133; the average attendance, 1,473; absentees, 660; as compared wit's 2,066, 1,531, and 536 respectively in the March quarter of last year. The increase in the absentees was accounted for by the prevalence of scarlet fever, and the prohibition of children attending schools from infected houses, and also the severity of the weather. The CLERK (Mr. Brierly), reported that he had written to Mr. George Walton, Crow-lane, as instructed by the com- mittee at the last meeting, in reference to the non-attendance of his children at school on the day of inspection,and that Mr. Walton had not replied thereto. It was ordered that the matter stand over for the opinion of the law clerk. Mr. Eno!Err moved, and Mr. BIRLEY seconded the adop- tion of the minutes which was carried. The LAW CLELE, referring to Mr. Walton's case, said the regulations for making the bye-laws under the Education Act had been complied with by the Commissioners, and un- less there was some reasonable excuse he did not see that there was anything to prevent the Commissioners taking
_ proceedings. _ It was decided, on the motion of Mr. Birley, seconded by Mr. Winstanley, that proceedings be taken against Mr. Walton.

GAS COMMITTEE. The minutes of this committee, which contained nothing of public interest, were passed. TUE MAISITESTANCE or INFECTIOUS PATIENTS. The Law CLERK stated that he had prepared a caso for Opinion of the Local Government Board in the matter of Pickering's children, and he received a letter from the Local Government Board, which stated :—"As regards the ques- tion upon which the Impr.ovement Commissioners are desirous of obtaining the opinion of the Local Government Board, I am directed to state that the Board consider that, as a general rule, when any person attacked with fever or other contagious or infectious disease (whether the case occurs within the district of the urban sanitary or within that of the rural sanitary authority) is withotit means of obtaining such necessaries (including medical attendance and nursing) as he may require, it devolves upon the Guardians of the Union, or their officers, to afford the requisite relief. If, however, the removal of a patient to a hospital is only necessary for purpeses of isolation, and the patient is not destitute either wholly or to the extent re- ferred to, the Board are of opinion that it devolves upon the sanitary authority, and not upon the Guardians, to deal with the case." The next day he wrote acknowledging the receipt of the letter and stating that it was that view of the case which had from the first been taken by the Commis- sioners, and upon which they had been and would continue to be prepared to act. After a. brief conversation the matter dropped. This was all the business.

ST. PETER'S CHURCH ADJOURNED VESTRT.—The vestry meeting adjourned from Easter Tuesday, was held in the Town Hall, on Tuesday, the Vicar in the chair. The atten- dance was small. The Chairman explained that in accpr- dance with the notice placed at the church door the reason the adjournment of the discussion on the insecure state of the church had been made, was to give time to obtain the practical opinion of Mr. John Pierpoint, of Warrington.—Dr. J. I,Vatkins said that the Wardens lost no time in communi- cating with Mr. Pierpoint, who had promptly attended to the wishes expressed at the meeting.—Mr. Pierpoint's report which was read, dealt with the various defects of the edifice. The present belfry was certainly dangerous considering that the beds and joints were all loose,and the west front was in 3 very unsatisfactory state ; the church, however, could be made quite secure by removing the present weight., belfry, and substituting one of a lighter construction in wood and stone, the walls to the string-line would have to be thickened, and an arch introduced with other improve- ments as indic deal on the plans submitted. Questions were put to Mr. Pierpoint, by Messrs. It was better to expend £3OO and have the work thoroughly done than to fritter away £lOO iii unsubstantial work.—Mr. Fairclough thought churchmen ought not to have any doubts on a matter of £3OO to place their church in a creditable state. He believed a special tinance committee could get the money. and he proposed the election of one.—Mr. Pardey seconded the proposition, t l e and hop.ael that the vicar, curate, churchwardens, and sides- men would act on that committee.—The motion was carried unanimously.—The following gentlemen appointedwseerveer.algen m n o the committee :—The vicar, curate, wardens, salesmen, and Messrs. under the chairmanship of Mr. J. E. Pardey. There was a large gathering. After the dinner the Chairman expressed his pleasure in again meeting the leading tenantry of the locality, whom he hqped would have a prosperous year. The "Health of the Qu.en and Royal family" was proposed from the chair and loyally honoured. The following toasts were also proposed, responded to, and heartily honoured :—" The army, navy and reserve forces," "The Bishop and clergy of the diocese," "The health of Mr. and Mrs. Legh and success to the House of Lyme," "The tenant farmers," "The town and trade of Newton." The various toasts were judiciously interspersed with songs, which quite sustained the character of this pleasant gathering in the fee of Makerfield. ' 1.0.G.T. HOPE OF EARLESTOWN LODGB.—The quarterly meeting of this lodge was held on Monday, when there was a fair attendance of members. The report of the Worthy Secretary stated that the total membership was about 70; the average attendance, 36. There had been good work done during the quarter, several public meetings had been held, and a number of leaflets and tracts distributed. The pro- gramme for the past quarter had been very successful in every way; and it was intended to arrange for another this quarter. The Improvement Society in connection with the lodge, had held several sessions, with very good attendances, and would be of much benefit to the members of the lodge. The report contained several very good suggestions for the benefit of the lodge, which were laid over till next session. The report of Bro. John Taylor, W.F.S., showed the finances to be in a fair condition, leaving a balance in the hands of the treasurer. The report of Bro. E. Newman, superinten- dent of the juvenile temple, stated that the temple was pro- gressing very satisfactorily. The number of juveniles was about 50, a slight increase on last quarter; and in response to various invitations which had Leen given, six of the adult members had joined the temple during the quarter, as honorary members, in order to assist in this important part of temperk.nce work. The honorary members now number 10. The reports were all adopted with thanks to the officers; after which the officers for the ensuing quarter were duly installed by Bro. John Warburton, lodge deputy, assisted by Bro. Henry Warburton as G.W.M., as follows :—W.C.T., Bro. George Warburton, jun. ; W.V.T., Bro. Thomas Mayor, of Newton; W.S., Bro. E. Newman; W.F.S., Bro. J. Taylor W.T., Bro. E. Marshall, dm. Arrangements are to be made for fraternal visits with Golborne, Ashton, Leigh, and Wigan Lodges during the quarter. On Wednes- day evening last, the usual fortnightly meeting of the Improvement Society was held in the lodge-room, a fair attendance of the members being present. A paper was read by Mr. George Clarke, subject—Spirituous Liquors, their manufacture and composition. A good discussion followed, all the members present taking part. Tir LTntLeLUß.—Anti-vaccination was the subject of debate at the Liberal Club, on Wednesday evening, in- troduced by Mr. B. Harrisorr. After an interesting and animated discussion it was adjourned for a week.

LITERATURE. CASSELL'S FAMILY' MAGAZINE :—The variety of matter presented in this Magazine continues to be one of its best features. A couple of well written serial stories Asiving the foundation of fiction to the number are advanced a stage, and the interest of the reader proportionately increased. But the miscellaneous articles, it is, rather, which give value to this periodical, and these include a wide range of subjects, and prove very instructive reading. One of these on "Tile incongruities of Art in Dress" shews up many of our little weaknesses in regard to costume and personal decoration, and may be advantageously read by either sex. The fol- lowing is an extract from this essay:—" Nothing so forcibly strikes the innately sesthetic eye as the painful incogruities that are displayed by those who aspire to manifest artistic tendencies in their habiliments, nor the promiscuous way in which one and all rush into so-called art in dress, where 1 those of purer taste would hesitate to commit themselves; for nothing is more satisfactory than an old costume rigidly adhered to and carried out, nor so distressing as a potpourri combination of different periods in the dress of one person. It is to be deplored that the false canons of taste produced by the bad sesthetical and intellectual education of some who write as authorities on the art of dress and decoration, should fatally cause false habits of judgment in those who put their trust in them; for, starting from erroneous and im- perfect information, they but teach the exaggerations and inconsistencies which vulgarise true art and beauty, thus misleading the public they think to instruct. The real artist cannot tolerate what. is untrue, whether in form, com- . . . . •

plexion, or costume; and where form is fictitious, com- plexion false, and costume incorrect as a copy of a certain period, the artist's eye and sense of truth instantly detect the meretriciousness of the whole effect, and are propor- tionately shocked. Painted eyes that look like no natural eyes ever did; rouged and painted cheeks, utterly unlike the peachy hue of real health, and totally destructive to that great beauty of young faces—a blush; lips which resemble only those of a doll in their excessive redness; and skin of that peculiar bluish-pink tint never seen on healthy mortal face, except in those of slow circulation after long exposure to a bitter nor'-easter—all these give a shock not easily forgotten to those of refined cesthetic feel- ing. There is no disgrace in having a bad complexion, except when the result of intemperance; by medical aid it is often remediable if not curable." Under the head of "The Gatherer" a number of recent discoveries and inventions in science are described. Useful hints in horticulture in reference to each current month are also given. This magazine is one of a few of its class which includes a musical contribution in each number. These, in the form of songs with pianoforte accompaniment, are often well written and scholarly compositions. The one contained in the nu.nber under notice makes, if we mistake not, a new departure in so far as a violin obligato is superposed en the voice part. The music, however, scarcely reaches the usual standard of excellence.

Tug QUIVER for this month contains the commencement of a new serial story, "A Sailor's Daughter," and judging from the opening chapters here given we regard it as an in- teresting, well written tale. This excellent magazine also contains several ably written articles, and a choice selection of matter suitable for Sunday and general reading. Our readers can judge of the style from the following extract from "The Family Council," by Edward Garrett:—" I know that what one must call 'hard lives' are the most in- teresting to read about," said Mrs. Nieto ; "but then, I think, I have heard a phrase to the effect that 'Blessed is the man or the nation that has no history.'" "You might as well say. Blessed is the savage above the philosopher,' ay, and Thrice blessed is the pig beyond the poet,' said Aunt Mary. "Why, Emma, the best part in life is not our voluntary sacrifices, often as cheap as they are showy. It is rather our cheerfulness and zeal in our involuntary obedience to the great wheel of circumstance—the visible hand of God. Therefore he for whom it revolves- most swiftly and sternly has the true post of honour. Horace Bushnell declared that 'Necessity is a good mother,' and that he desired no other to be the nurse of his children. Ah, Emma! just now you owned that flattery is kept for amateur art, and se the loudest praises are generally given to amateur virtue. But it is the art or the virtue which is set to prac- tical uses, and called out by stress of hard facts, which win the true prizes at last." She went on: "I never like to hear one form which approbation of any good work= often assumes. You constantly hear it said, He or she under- takes such a task out of pure love. They do not need money.' Well and good, so far; but they might do the work quite as well—possibly better-ieif they did need money. The necessity for earning money might have been part of God's call to that particular work. People are not made mercenary by requiring to earn money, but by doing for I money what they would not do for love, or by doing that which earns most money, instead of that which they can do best, and which is best to be done. To have to earn our bread is a clear call to work, and to earn it is one clear good accomplished by work; and no work can be the les& worthy , for starting from such sound ground." BERTON'S GREAT Bona OP Nanny (London : Ware,' Lock & Co.)—The May part of this work contains selectiors of English poetry and biographical sketches of the poets during the fourth period from 1649 to 1689, including Bishop Jeremy Taylor, Richard Baxter, Abraham Cowley, I Henry Vaughan, John Milton, and Andrew Marvell, the friend of Milton—the abdiel of a dark and corrupt age_: John Dryden, Wm. Wycherley, &c. Referring to the life of Milton, the author say:—" Cromwell at length died, and SO zealous and sanguine was Milton to the very last that one of his latest political productions was A ready and easy way to establish a free Commonwealth.' It was in vain, however , to contend by pamphlets, with the national inclination, and Charles 11. returned ; in triumph Miltun was dischatged from his office, and lay for some time concealed in the house of a friend. The House of Commons deaired that his Majesty would issue a proclamation to call in Milton's de- fence, of the people and iconoclasts, together with a book of Goodwyn's. The books were accordingly burnt by the common hangman, but the author's were returned as haying absconded, nor in the act of indemnity did the name of Mil- ton appear among those of the excepted persons. He now in reduced circumstances, and under the discountenance of power, removed to a private habitation near his former resi- dence. His powerful mind, now centered in itself, and undisturbed by contention and temporary topics, opened to those great ideas which were continually filling it, and the result was Paradise Lost.' Much discussion has taken place concerning the original conception of this grand performance, but whatever hint may have suggested the rude outline, it is certain that all the creative powers of a strong imagination, and all the accumulated stores of a life devoted to learning, were expended in its completion. Though he appears, at an early age, to have thought of some subject in the heroic times of English history, as peculiarly calculated for English verse, yet his lelielous turn, and assiduous study of the Hebrew scriptures, produced a final preference of a story derived from the .acred writings, and giving scope to the introduction of his theological system. It would be superfluous at this time to weigh the merits of Milton's great work, which stands so much beyond competition; but it may be affirmed, that whatever his other poems can exhibit of beauty in some parts, or of grandeur in others, may all be referred to 'Paradise Lost,' as the most perfect model of both." "Milton not exhausted hy this great effort, followed it in 1670 by 'Paradise Regained,' written upon a suggestion of the Quaker Elwoods, and apparently regarded as the theolo- gical completior of the Paradise Lost.' Although, in point if invention, its inferiority is plainly apparent, yet modern criticism has pronounced that there are p +wages in it by nc means unworthy of the genius of Milton, allowance beim nade for the small compass of the subject, and his purpose in writing it. Together with it appeared his tragedy to • Sampson Agnoistes,' composed upon the model of antiquity and never intended for the stage.

CONFIRMATION SERVICE AT WAR- RINGTON PARISH CHURCH. There was a good atteudance at the confirmation service held in the Warrington Parish Church, on Saturday after- noon, by the Lord Bishop of Liverpool. Besides his lord- ship, the other clergy presew. were the Revs. W. Quekett (rector),S. Wilkinson, E. C : Carleton, M. Schonberg, W. H. Williams, E. St. A. Duke, •T. Louch. The first part of the service was read by the rec,or' and afterwards Bishop Ryle ascended the pulpit, and addressing the candidates, I said he was going to ask a very serious and solemn question —whether they really had come there to confirm and take upon themselves what was promised for them when they were baptised and admitted as infants into Christ's church. They were to understand he did not came so much to confirm them as they came to confirm themselves in their own persons what was promised for them. They had come there not merely for the purpose of walking up to the rail and having his hands laid upon them without understanding what they did. The laying on of his hands, if they did not understand i it, would do them no more good than the laying on of any other person's hand. They would all, he supposed, have i been brought into the church of Christ by baptism when ' they were but little children. When they did not under- stand what was done for them, when they were too young to understand, their fathers and mothers very rightly and pro-1 perly brought them to have their names put down in thel church of Christ, and to be admitted by the sacrament of baptism, in order that when they came of age to understand I these things:they should take upon themselves what was then ,1 promised for them. The parents acted wisely and rightly in so doing. No one, he supposed, would object to a child's name being put down in a will leaving a large fin tune to that child when the child became of age. So, in the same ' way, their names were put down in the list of peptised per- sons. They were baptised upon the belief that they would be I brought up as Christians; and when they became young men and young women, and were no longer children, they should take upon themselves what their godfathers and god- mothers had promised. Now the time had come they were no longer boys and girls; they were growing up to man- I hood and womanhood. The time had come when they should Lake upon themselves what was promised, and con- fess and declare before their ministers, before the congregation, and before their friends that they wished, intended, and desired by God's help to live as Christians from henceforth. After adverting to what the candidates' godfathers and godmothers promised tor them, his Lordship asked them to understand clearly what they were about and to think seriously what they did. He hoped no yourg man or young woman came just because their parson told them, but that they felt and really thought seriously what a solemn thing it was. The right rev, gentle- man urged the candidates not to tell a lie to God by going up and confessing themselves Christians if they did not wish and intend to be Christians; remarked that that day was the turning point in their lives; and concluded by ask- ing them to pray earnestly for God's blessing upon what they were going to do. Silent prayer was engaged in for a few minutes, and the ordinance of confirmation was pro- ceeded with. The number of confirmees was as follows : Parish Church, 85; Holy Trinity Church, 37; St. Paul's, 13; St. Barnabas', 26; St. Peter's, 14; and Padgate Church, 1; total, 176. His Lordship, at the conclusion, again ascended the pulpit, and remarked that the day of confirmation was a very solemn day. A bishop saw many young women and young men whom he never might see again. They were just launched out into life, like ships launched for the first time to go to sea. How many years might pass before they and he met again, who could tell? God grant that when they did meet they might all be found upon the right hand side of Jesus Christ in the day when He judged the world ! He had been well satisfied with the demeanour and manner of all of them when they went up to the communion rail. He was glad to say be saw no sign of levity ; he saw no foolishness ; he saw no laughing or smiles. He trusted that many to whom he spoke bad come there to be confirmed that day in a serious spirit and really feeling what they did. The Bishop went on to give the confirmees a few words of caution, encouragement, and advice. He cautioned them to beware of the weakness of their own hearts, to beware of the world, and the spirit of the world in which they lived, and to beware of that great tempter the devil; encouraged them to make God their friend; and advised them not to forget to pray, never to neglect reading the Bible regularly, and never to forget to keep holy the Sabbath or to partake of the sacrament. The service was then concluded.
MYSTERIOUS DEATH AT ST. HELENS.
An inquest was held on Wednesday at the Phcenix Inn before Mr. Drifßeld, on the body of Thomas Melly, a young man, who has been missing since the 16th ult., and was found in the canal on Sunday.

Wm. Mally, of Knowsley, brother at deceased, said de- ceased was a labourer at Messrs. Pilkington's works. He heard that he was missing, and could not ascertain any- thing of him until he was found in the canal on Sun- day. James Ridgway, keeper of the Derby Arms, said .he had known deceased many years. On Thursday preceding the 18th thedeceased had some drink in his house. During the evening a quarrel took place between him and a man named John Hart, and deceased was put out of the house three times. On being put out the third time, a woman came to him and endeavoured to persuade him to go home. He said, "I will not go home ; I will stop outside until I see Jack Hart to have my revenge, for he struck me." He then went away down Liverpool-road, and he saw no more of him. John Relly, of 17, Liverpool-street, said deceased ledged with him. He saw deceased on Saturday night (16th) in Liverpool-road, and he thought he was then quite sober. He had never seen him since alive. He knew Hart, but he had never known him to quarrel with deceased, and had never known him to harm anyone. As he did not come home on Saturday night he went to the Town Hall and other places, but could gain no account of him. He then wrote to his brother at Knowsley, who replied that he knew nothing of him. In August last he was taken very ill, and since that time had been in very low spirits, and on one occasioa he wished he was dead. He always drank very heavily, but he never would say what was the cause of ,his depression. He had never threatened to drown himself. He did not know of any tronble that affected deceased. He had a mother and brothers in Ireland, but he never would anscrer any letters addressed to him, which came from his mother or brothers. Deceased was all right when sober, but when intoxicated he was very offensive. A Juryman observed that decaased had gone near to the canal to fight, and had been thrown in by some one. The Coroner: To fight whom? A Juryman: That is the question, sir. P.C. Groarke said deeeased had his clothes on when found, and he had his braces bound round him.
- A Juryman thought the man Hart ought to have been at he inquest. - - •• •

The Coroner: It is a pity the police have not seen Hart and heard what he had got to say. It is simply a wanton exception. There is no evidence that he has drowned him- self, or that he accidentally fell in. In the state he was he might have fallen in accidentally. There was a mystery about him. A man is missed ard found drowned a fortnight afterwards. He had been in the habit of getting too much drink, and was known to be a very hard drinker. They had no evidence that Hart was mixed up in the affair in the slightest degree, but the police ought to have seen Hart, and brought him as a witness if he knew anything at about the deceased. P.C. Groarke : I neves heard a word about Hart until to-day. The Coroner: But I have done already. It ought to have been known at your office. It can be learnt in a minute from any of theqe gentlemen. A verdict of " Found drowned" was returned.

OPENING OF THE PRESCOT CON- SERVATIVE CLUB. On Saturday afternoon, the newly-formed Conservative club for Prescot was formally opened. The desirability of forming a club in the town was mooted some few months ago, and subsequently a meeting was held at the Royal Hotel, when it was unanimously resolved that a club should be formed, and a committee was appointed to carry the resolution into effect. It was feared at the time that some difficulty would be experienced in obtaining suitable premises, but this obstacle was kindly removed by Mr. W. L. Evans, J.P., who placed at the disposal of the committee a large and commodious house, pleasantly situated in Derby- street, one of the principal thoroughfares in the town. To adapt the building to the purposes of a club, the internal portion has undergone complete renovation, various altera- tions having been carried out at a cost of about £lOO. Among other apartments there are reading and smoking rooms on the ground floor, billiard, bagatelle, game, and bath rooms, lavatory, &c., on the second floor, and on the third floor there is a large meeting room capable of accom- modating a hundred persons. The billiard-room is capacious and well lighted, and the table, which was supplied by Bayliff, of Whitechapel, Liverpool, is of an excellent and substantial character. The seats in the room formerly belonged to the Prescot Masonic Hall, and were given by Mr. Evans. Attached to the premises at the back is a large piece of land, one portion of which has already been pre- pared for lawn-tennis, and it is proposed at some future time to have an American bowling alley, quoiting ground, tirc. The furnishing and fitting-up of the various rooms have cost £166 18s. 7d., towards which sum donations have been received and promised, amounting to £154 145., leaving a deficiency of £l2 4s. 7d. On the roll there are 174 mem- bers, whose subscriptions amount to £B3; the management expenses only amount to £2 12s. 11d., halving a balance of £BO 7s. Id, so that, after deducting the deficiency in the formation account, there would still be a balance in favour of the club of £6B 2s. 6d. Of the 174 members, 126 are subscribers at ss. each, 44 at one guinea each, and four at 10s. and 10s. 6d. each. For the present, at least, no intoxi- cating liquors will be sold or consumed on the premises, but otherwise the catering will be such as to satisfy the tastes of the members. An endeavour was made td get the President, Sir R. A. Cross, M.P., to open the club, but as this could not be conveniently done it was decided to ask the Conservative chairman of the Huyton polling district, Mr. Edward Ban- ner, J.P., of Roby, to formally open the club, and accord- ingly that gentleman attended on Saturday. He was met by a large number of members, amongst whom were Mr. W. L. Evans (chairman of the club), Dr. E. F. Hall, Dr. Morris, Messrs. G. J. Paris, James Berry, E. Dyson, T. Dennett, G. Eaton, Joseph Preston, C. S. Worthington, W. Worthington, R. Evans, P. Lightfoot (secretary), W. Lloyd (treasurer', J. D. Banks, T. Prescott, T. Evans, W. Everts, E. Range, H. Cross, F. Green, J. T. Hall, C. B. Johnson, A. F. Evans, J. Johnson Brown, dm. Mr. BANNER., after expressing his pleasure at being pre- sent on so interesting an occasion, observed that Conserva- tives were always prepared to fight in the good cause. He congratulated them most sincerely and heartily on the for- tnation of a club in Prescot; it would be an item, not a very large one perhaps, but still it would be an item among the general clubs of the country in bringing and keeping to- gether that great party which maintained and upheld the constitution of England. (Hear, hear, and applause.) That constitution, they might all admit, was at present in a rather precarious state. They were beaten, most terribly beaten, twelve months ago, but it was then foretold that a party was coming into power of such an incongruous character, that it would be impossible for them long to hold together. (Hear, hear.) They did not think, however, that the breakage would begin so soon as it did. Even in that twelvemonth they had seen a Ministry which began by the most abject apologies for what they bad said before getting into office; they had seen them truckling to the Irish party for their votes by refusing to renew the Peace Preservation Act; and the result of that had been that they had to bring in the Disturbance Bill, which was thrown out, not by the Conservatives, but by their own party, who would not have it. (Applause.) What else had the Ministry done? They had caused the flag of England to be dragged through the dirt, and they had de- graded us as a nation, and dragged us down from a first-rate power to a third-rate power. They were even looked down upon by the poor Africans, because we had withdrawn our protection from them. (Hear, hear.) The Government had said in the Queen's speech that they would uphold the dignity of England in the Transvaal; but what did they do? They began well by sending out troops, but because they had a few small reverses they instantly caved in. Was that the spirit of Englishmen? (No, no.) Was that what they would have expected if their late lamented chief, Lord Beaconsfield, had been in power? (No, and applause.) We should have been in a different position. He found even amongst his own Liberal friends that they looked upon the conduct of the Government with the deepest possible regret. (Hear, hear) The Government had gone on to bring in a bill which had turned away from them one of the best and highest members of the Cabinet—the Duke of Argyll. (Hear, hear.) Only on the previous night the Government could not find time to debate the Transvaal question, but they could make especial time to bring in a bill for legalis- ing infidelity. ("Shame.") He apprehended there were many among the Liberal party who had such strong religi- ous feelings that that detestable bill would be found diffi- cult, if not impossible, to pass. (Hear, hear.) They were told that if that bill was forced on, very important members of the Government would secede. (Applause.) No one could conceive that such a man as Lord Selborne, one of the most religious and conscien- tious men in existenoe, would assist in passing a measure of that nature. There was no doubt if the Govern- ment went on as it was going on they must expect a break-up before long, and therefore it behoved Conservatives to be ready, ready in good time, to fight for that constitution which they all loved. (Applause.) After calling their at- tention to the importance of looking after their votes and getting the'r friends to look after their votes in the registra- tion courts, Mr. Banner proceeded to say that they had for that division of the county members of whom they might he justly and very properly proud, and they would fight for them again as they had done before. (Hear, hear). He congratulated and complimented the committee on the very excellent institution they had provided, audit anyone would propose and second him he would like to become a member himself. Mr. Banner concluded by declaring, on behalf of the members, the club open, and he wished it every pros- perity. (Hear, hear, and loud applause.) Mr. W. L. EVAN, J.P., proposed a vote of thanks to Mr. Banner for his kindness in coming to open the club, and for his good wishes for its welfare. Mr. Evans then read a statement as to the financial position of the society, which be said was starting under very fair auspices. Dr. HILL seconded the proposition, and observed that Mr. Banner had proved by his words that he had the interest of the Conservative cause at hart. The motto the people of Prescot generally adopted was "Defence, not defiance." There was no doubt the Conservatives of England were act- ing on the defensive at the present time, but the titne would come when they would speak out and let the world know that they were not the detestable cowards they were represented to he, but that they were prepared to up- hold the honour of England. (Hear, hear.) The proposition was then put to the meeting and carried amid loud applause. Mr. Beaman, in acknowledging, said he had great pleasure in being amongst them, .and the statement Mr. Evans had read exhibited one thing which gave him far greater pleasure, and that was that there were in the club 128 members, at ss. each. He thought those members were of infinitely more value in the club, because it was to the workingmen they must look for the main support of the party. (Hear, hear, and applause). The proceedings then terminated.

div.head: PRESCOT BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
div.p: PRESCOT BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

The usual fortnightly meeting of this Board was held at Whiston Workhouse, on Thursday, Mr. S. Marsh presiding. There were also present the Revs. T. Chambers and J. Bar- nacle, Messrs. Meadows, Fidler, Tyrer, Jackson, Paris, Hall, Birchall, Dobell, Swift, Syder, Leigh, Gerrard, Matthews, Leatherbarrow' Gilbodv, Eatock, Buckley, Sadler, and . Fisher, with Mr. S. H. Hartley (clerk). WORKHOUSE MASTER'S REPORT. The Workhouse Master (Mr. Bicknell) reported that the number of inmates in the house on the last day of the week was 478; last day of preceding week, 477 ; corresponding week last year, 547. The number of vagrants relieved during , the week was 134-85 men, 30 women, and 16 children. There had been nine deaths in the workhouse during the past fortnight. The number of children at Kirkdale was 156. There were eight cases of typhoid fever in the work- house. The Master also reported that the musical instru- ments were delivered at Kirkdale schools on the 29th ult. The governor had since reported that they needed a little attention and cleaning, not having been used for some time. The maker of the instruments had offered to do what was necessary to put them in good order for £3. It was resolved that the offer be accepted, and the instru- ments be handed over to the maker for the necessary re- pairs. It was stated that the whole of the eight cases of typhoid fever in the workhouse were from Whiston, and comprised a whole family. - -------
COMMITTEE MEFTING3. The minutes of the following Committees were read and

passed : GENERAL PURPOSES COMMITTEE. A meeting of this Committee was held on the 28th April, at which Mr. Paris was appointed chairman for the ensuing. year.—The Clerk submitted Dr. hail's report on the overcrowding in the workhouse, but the consideration of the sime was further postponed.—The Committee examined the applications for the office of nurse, and the following were selected to ap- pear before the next meeting of the Board :—Louisa Apple- yard, 34 years of age, Prestwich Union; Agnes Johnstone, 41, Boundary-street, Liverpool; Madeline Pritchard, 30, Macclesfield Union; Emily Sheen, 38, Tarporley, Cheshire; Mary Turner, 28, Manchester Workhouse Infirmary. BUILDING COVMITTNE.—At a meeting of this Commit- tee, held on the 28th ult., Mr. T. Eatock was appointed chairman.—The letter from Messrs. Weeks and Hughes, dated 18th April, referred frem the Board,was recommended to be laid on the table.—The contractor, ly,r. Lyon, attended before the Committee respecting the balanee of his account. the subject was referred to Messrs. Fisher, Sadler, Buckley, nd the Chairman. VISITING COMIAITTEE.—A meeting of this com- mittee Was also held on the 28th ult. The clerk was directed to draw the attention of the
contractor to the inferior quality of the butter supplied to workhouse and the master was directed to return the same. Recommended, that the boiler in the cellar under the cook- . _ _

ing kitchen be removed to the new piggeries; that carbolic soap be used in the house; that the new imbecile wards be whitewashed by pauper labour, and that tenders be obtained for the painting, dm., of the outside of the imbecile ward

buildings.— The special committee appointed to consider whether or not the balance of 1.39 18s. should be paid to Mr. Lyon for "pointing" the boundary walls of the workhouse, in conse- quence of the mortar having given way through the frost, met that (Thursday) morning, and after giving the subject due consideration, they recommended the board to pay the balance to Mr. Lyon.—Mr. Meadows objected to the money being paid. He thought Mr. Lyon should "repoint" the wall without extra pay; it was a custom in the trade.—Rev. T. Chambers thought that after the special committee had recommended the money to be paid it would be an un- gracious act not to pay it.—After further discussion, Mr. Paris moved that the money be paid.—The motion was seconded, and, on being put to the meeting, was carried. THE SERVICESrOF MR: HARTLEY.
A letter was read from the. Local Government Board,
, dated 3rd May, sanctioning the payment of LSO to Mn Hartley for his services of clerk to the School Attendance Committee of the Prescot Union during the past year.

THE APPOINTMENT OE NI7ESE. All the applicants, with one exception, for the office of nurse, rendered vacant by the resignation of Miss Latham, summoned to appear before the board, attended. On a vote being taken 14 guardians were in favour of the appointment of Louisa Appleyard, of the Prestwich Union; seven in favour of Madeline Pritchard, of Macclesfield Union; and one in favour of Agnes Johnstone' of Boundary-street, Liverpool.—The Chairman declared Mrs. Appleyard as duly elected, and she was called into the room and informed of the result. Mrs. Appleyard thanked the guardians, and hoped she would be able to give satisfaction. She would endeavour to get to the workhouse and commence her duties as soon as she possibly could. THE CENSUS AND TIIETRATEIBLE VALUE OPITIII UNION. The CLERK read the census returns of the whole of the townships in the Union, a report of which will be found in another column. The, total _population of the Union was

117,938 as compared with 92,569 in 1871, being an increase during the ten years of 25,439. The rateable value of the Union was £561,398; the rateable value in 1871 was £405,675; being an increase of £155, 723. The clerk observed that these figures proved that the Union was increasing. _ _
Mr. FIDLER : And how has pauperism increased? ;Laughter.)
Tl.l-0 CLERK: You have had that before. TFIE NEW CHAPEL:

The Rev. Mr. Crt',smarts said he was hoping that by an early post Mr. Hartley would receive the sanction of the Local Government Board for the building of the chapel. He therefore begged to propose, for the sake of expedition of business, that when Mr. Hartley received the letter be advertise for tenders for the building of the chapel, ard also that he communicate with the architect. He (Mr. Chambers) did this because of the weather; they all knew the value of good weather for building. If the chapel had been com- menced in April it would have been erected by October. If what he had proposed was adopted then Mr. Hartley could have the tenders for their inspection and approval by the next Board day. Mr. DOBELL seconded, and the motion was agreed to. THE OUT-DOOR RELIEF SYSTEM.—APPOINTMENT OS • COMMITTEE.

Mr. TYREE drew the attention of the Board to the large amount of money given in out-door relief in the St. Helens No. 2 district, which he observed was nearly three times as much as that given in the Widnes district. He could not understand why there was such a difference in the cheques drawn for No. 1 and No. 2 districts, and did not think there was a greater. number of paupers in the St. Helens No. 2 district, in proportion to the population, than there was in other districts. He considered that a committee should be appointe4 to look into the matter. Mr. MEADOWS agreed with the previous speaker, as the amount given in out-door relief in this special district had been increasing for the last two years. He thought there were many cases which might be struck off the books. Mr. TYRER remarked that that would necessitate a revi- sion again. There was a revision regstlarly, but it did not seem to affect it. At the revision last year some cases were struck off, but it did not seem to affect the permanent in- crease in that district, and he would like to know the reason for it. Mr. MEADOWS characterised the revision next to useless. Cases were struck off, but in the course of a short tisne they were put on again. Mr. HALL understood that when cases were knocked off they could not be put on again without previously coming before the Board. That was the case a few years ago. Several members were of a similar opinion. Mr. FIDLER observed that the inference to be drawn from What bad been said by a previous speaker, was that the com- mittee which considered the relief cases in Wenley's (No. 2) district, was far more liberal than the other committees. He could say for himself and on behalf of the other members of the committee that each case was taken on its own merits. and it was inquired into thoroughly. The committee was not more liberal than the other committees. They must not forbt the fact that they had Greenbank, and some of the worst portions of the town in Wenley's district. Mr. TYRER said the union would stand very badly as compared with other unions, and he was afraid they would fare badly in Mr. Caine's returns. Mr. HALL observed that the amount given in relief in the two St. Helens districts during the last fortnight was about ,e 330 which together with the relief given in kind would snake a total expenditure of £430. The CHAIRMAN remarked that perhaps it would be tetter fer the Widnes relief committee to take the relief Cases for the No. 1, St. Helens district, and the relief committee for the latter district to take the relief cases from Widnes. After some further discussion it was resolved that a com- mittee. consisting of the Revs. T. Chambers, and J. Barnacle, and Messrs. Tyrer, Meadows, Fidler, Hall, Leatherbarrow, Paris, Matthews, and Birchall should be appointed to con- sider the system of administering out-door relief in the , whole of the union, and report to the Board.

div.head: MAY DAY AT ST. HELENS.
div.p: MAY DAY AT ST. HELENS.

The first of May falling on Sunday the usual procession of horses took place on the day following. There was a good turn-out and this year the Corporation horses joined in the procession. The principal streets in the town were visited, among them being Corporation, Church, Duke, and Peter-streets, and Liverpool-rd. The following owners allowed their drivers to join in the procession :—Messrs. the Greengate Colliery; James Farrell, Corporation-street ; William Chia- nail, hay and straw dealer; George Burrows and Sons, Pro- vidence Works; G-reenbank Alkali Company, wagons carry- ing cylinders and tiles; R. Varley, ironfounder, large iron wheel ; John Varley and Co.; C. Harris and Son, builders, timber; E. Lyon, Fccleston Hill; Pilkington Brothers, a load of hay; the Railway Company, several wagons; J. Heaton, pavionr, paving setts; William Berry and Son; Wilcock and Son, brewers ; Greenall, Whitley, and Co. ; Charles Blanborn ; James Howarth, Buxton lime burner ; James croodban, carter, Sutton ; T. Walker, Mertonbank Alkali Works ; T. Roberts, builder ; J. Lawrenson, builder. Prizes were awarded as follows, and distributed at the Eagle and Child Inn, by the Mayor :—For the neatest and cleanest pair of cart horses: let, Messrs. Greenall, Whitley, and Co., J. Balshaw carter; 2nd,-Greenall, Whitley, and Co., driver J. Critchley : 3rd, J. Varley and Co.; extra prize, Gvenall, Whitley, and Co., J. Vose driver. For the neatest and cleanest single horse, cart, and harness: Ist, J. Harris and Son, driver Peter Glover; 2nd, London and North-Western Rail way Co ,driver C. Lil ley ; extra 2n3, J. Varley and Co., driver Platt; 3rd, The Corporation of St. Helens' driver Peter Finnigan ; extra third prize. Corporation of St. Helens, driver J. Bolton ; also another prize awarded to J. Harris and Son, driver R. Ashcroft. For the best, neatest, and cleanest tradesmen's cobs, in harness: let, T. Hatton; 2nd, John flatton • 3rd, James Hatton; extra prize, Mr. Rose, Sutton Mills. 'For the best, neatest, and cleanest entire horse, Mr. James Penketh was awarded the prize for his horse "Lord Lyon," leader John Large. The MANOR congratulated all the prize winners, and hoped that all would be stimulated to further exertion. He was a ;mat admirer of horse-flesh, and he could say that this was ,me of the pleasantest events that he had been invited to oarticipate in during his mayoralty. He suggested that nezt year a prize should be given to that person who treated qis horse the kindest.

Poon•RATE POll PRESCOT. —On the application of Mr. Henry Makin, assistant-overseer, at the L'reseot Petty iesgions, on Tuesday, a poor-rate of ls. 6.1. in the pound was granted for the township of Freseot. Thu arrears Wel t stated to be £l3 h. 3d.

div.head: PRESCOT HIGHWAY BOARD.
div.p: PRESCOT HIGHWAY BOARD.

The first monthly meeting of the Present Highway Board for the ensuing year was held at the Clerk's Offices, on Tuesday. There were *sent Messrs. W. L. Evans, J.P., M. Lowe (Roinhill), H. Fogg (Whiston), ad B. Tyrer (Knowsley) ; with Mr. Cross (clerk), and Mr. Goldsworth (surveyor).

APPOINTMENT OF CHAIRMAN AND VICE-CHAIRMAN. Mr. LOWE moved that Mr. Evans be re-elected chairman for the ensuing year. Mr. TYNER, in seconding the motion, hoped Mr. Evans would be long spared to conduct the business of the Board:
be motion was unanimously carried, and Mr. Evans, on taking the chair, returned thanks. On the motion of Mr. nuEn, seconded by Mr. FOG, Mr. Lowo was elected vice-chairman for the ensuing year.

div.head: FOOTPATHS AT RAINHILL.
div.p: THE FOOTPATHS AT RAINHILL.

Mr. GOLDSWORTH, in answer to the chairman, said he was informed that some of the owners of property at Rainhill wek> wilting to contribute one-third of the cost of putting the footpaths in the village into a thorough state of repair. He had ordered some materials, so that they could commence operations on those footpaths opposite the respective proper- ties of those gentlemen who had consented to contribute a portion of the cost. He had no doubt that when the work was commenced the dissentients would agree to con- tribute.
Mr. Lowz said he understood there was only one owner who was rather backward in contributing his portion, and that was Mr. Lawton of the Post-office.

The matter then dropped. SURVEYOR'S EXPENDITURE. The SURVEYOR submitted his statement of expenditure for the month ending April 28th, 1881, which was as follows: --Bold, £ll 14& 3d.; Knowsley, £lO 115. Rainhill, £lO ss. 6d.; Whiston, £9 lie. 3d.; team labour,, £l7 138. 11d.; new materials, £49 9s. 7-0.; incidental ex- penses, £1 is. 111 d. ; total, £llO 7s. 6d. Deduct £lOO, advanced March 25th, leaving a balance of £lO 78. 6cl.

div.head: FINANCE.
div.p: FINANCE.

In answer to Mr. Tyrer, it was stated that no arrears were owing on the old call 9 by any of the townships. Of the new calls made in April, Bold had paid £lOO. None of the other townships had paid anything. The amount now due from all the townships was £1,085. There was a balance of £348 14s. 9d. in the bank against the Board. MISCELLANEOUS..

The CLERK stated that he had received the precepts of the election of members• of the townships comprising the Bond's district. In answer to Mr. Tyrer, the SunvEvort said he had not yet had any applications for the 'carting of slag. Mr. TIMER said it was a busy time with the farmers at present. The SURVEYOR produced estimates of materials required in the various townships of tho Board for the ensuing year, together with the prices. The estimates we!..3 accepted.
‘ . ....- _ The SURVEYOR also produced and handed to each war warden a statement of the &uncial position of his town- ship at the present time and the probable position at the end of the year.
