div.p: RUNCORN INIPROVEMENT COMMIS- SIONERS. This Board held their monthly meeting on Monday, Mr. George Marshall presided, and there were also present— Messrs. Williams, P. Speakman, Shaw, Handley, Frith Collier, Meadowcroft, McDougall, Hazlehurst, J. J. Spe man. Dobson, Lyon, Linaker (law clerk), Brookes (secre- tary), Barker (surveyor), and Mouritz (medical officer). MEDICAL OFFICER'S REPORT. This report, which was presented by Dr. Mouritz, stated that the number of deaths registered in Runcorn during the month amounted to 36. Of these 11 were due to whooping cough, 6 pulmonary affections, 6 nervous affections, 5 ab- dominal aft actions, 2 phthisis, and 2 senile decay. Cancer, measles, dropsy, and diarrlicea accounted for one each, re- presenting a death-rate of 28 per 1,000 per annum. Nine- teea deaths occurred amongst children from five years of age and under; and 12 one year and under. Four inquests were held, making the total year 40..1The births numbered 54, making an average of 43 per 1,000 per annum. TIER CHAIRMAN ON THE CENSUS. The Csaficumr congratulated the Board on the fact that the census which had just been taken of the town showed that the population was over 15,000. He expressed a hope that the prosperity of the town would keep pace with its aumerical increase in point of population, and that at the eat Of the next decade Runcorn would even show a greater

Increase. ENCLOSING LAND BELONGING TO FREEHOLDERS. Mr. FRITH wished to know whether the instructions had been carried out as to enquiries being made as to why a piece of land on the Weston-road, belonging to the freeholders of Ike town, had been enclosed by some one—he believed by Mr. John Frodsham ? Mr. BA.RKER said he had made the necessary communica- tions on the matter, but had received no reply. Mr. FPITH considered the question one which ought to be bade public, as land belonging to freeholders was being taken in by property owners and devoted to their own use. In answer to Mr. P. Speakman, the Clerk said the Coro- nun" 'loners, being themselves freeholders, had a right to take Vas initiative in the matter. Mr. FRITH thought that if they did not take some steps in tbs matter, it would look as if they were conniving at what was almost robbery as affecting the interests of the rate- pagers Mr. Snaw said he should be willing to support a proposal fa the removal of the fence if the people concerned would not give an undertaking to pay rent, or make some acknow- .

letigement. Mr. BARKER said he bad seen Mr. Frodsham who said he should not reply to the letter of the Board. The Law CLERIC remarked that before they passed a resolution to remove the fences they should first ascertain whether it was common land or not. Mr. Handley said the town's books conclusively showed that the land was the property of the freeholders. Before the present Board was formed the old surveyors of the high- ways met on purpose to define what were the freeholders' rights, and that very piece of land was then used as a garden known as Cox's Croft. The walls were knocked down by the surveyors, and the piece of land had lain waste since. The books also showed that the land had been periodi- cally ridden over. Mr. Donson objected to the freeholders' land being en- closed by priVate individuals, and said if they did not take action they might expect other enclosures to be made. Mr. LYON thought the matter ought to be looked into thoroughly. Committees had on two different occasions been appointed to look after the public footpaths and the rights of the public, but little had been done. He thought the proper course now would be for the question to be intro- clac( d at the close of the meeting. Mr. FRITH adopted Mr. Lyon's suggestion and at the close of the proceedings the matter again came up, and it was resolved, on the motion of Mr. FRITH, seconded by Mr. HaNntmY, that the following members be a commit- toe to consider the rights of,the freeholders and the present encroachments made on their property :—Messrs. Norman, Williams, Handley, Shaw, and McDougall. DE. AICDOUCIALL AND TIIR SURVEYOR.. ANOTHBIZ LITTLE SCENR. The minutes of the Highway and Sanitary Committee referred to a letter from the Bridgewater Navigation Com- pany objecting to a flagged footway being constructed on the north side of Percival-lane. The committee recom- mended that the footpath should be paved with Stafford- shire bricks, and the previous minute as to flagging re- scinded. The surveyor reported that he had ascertained from Messrs. Guest and Son that the extraordinary traffic helm Runcorn Hill to Top Locks would cease immediately ori.tompletion of the tunnel they were making. The sur- veyor had been instructed to see Mr. Statham with a view to getting him to submit plans for the erection of property in a line with Leinster garden. Resolved that the offer of Messrs. Simpson, Davies and Son to deliver 6,700 tons of Nevin broken stone at Top Locks, at 7s. 6d. per ton, should not be entertained. It was recommended that tenders be obtained for a supply of 500 tons of Peninaenmawr stone. The amended plans of Mr. P.Speakman's property in Bridge street had been considered and disapproved of in consequence of the cellar kitchen being more than the prescribed depth. At a further meeting the Surveyor reported that Mr. Statham had promised to submit plans for the erection of property in a line with Lein3ter Gardens. The commit- tee also recommended that with reference to the Big Pool nuisance, and counsel's opinion thereon, the Clerk re-state the case ; that the horse, gears, rugs, drc., water cart, stand- pipe, and hose, sweeping machine, and iron cart, be sold to Mr. Cliff for the sum of £6O; that the Surveyor obtain ten- dare for the remaining plant for which he has no use; and that the men to be discharged be allowed to take the coats provided by the Commissioners. Dr. MCDOUGALL proposed, and Mr. J. J. SPHAKMAN seconded, the confirmation of the minutes. The SCRTEYOR, in reply to Mr. Dobson, stated that the whole of the men, except five, employed by the Board, had been discharged. Mr. HANDLEY suggested that the Board should advertise for tenders for stone, leaving out the word " Penmaenmawr," an I that they should ask for tenders for unbroken as well as for broken stone. They might then find employment for the men they had had to discharge. Dr. McDorGALL declined to embody the suggestion in his

motion. Mr. HANDLEY then moved as an amendment that the minute should read, "That tenders be obtained for a supply of stone for the current year, both broken and un- broken." Mr. SHAW seconded the amendment, believing it was not business-like to tie the Board to obtain the stone from one market. If the resolution was passed it would be left in the hands of those persons tendering—and there would, per- I haps, not be more than one or two—to arrange their own prices. Then, as a matter of charity to the old men, there should be as many openings as possible for them to gain a livelihood. Mr. Donsort sympathised with the remarks made by Mr. Shaw as regarded finding employment for the discharged

men. Mr. Bangnit said stone-breaking was a trade by itself, and could not be done by the old men. Mr. MEAnowcnotv agreed with the Surveyor, and said if the Board received the atones at Runcorn unbroken, they would have to consider what facilities they had to break them, and whether the expense would be less or greater than purchasing the stones already broken. Dr. McDolacteLL did not think the surveyor was compe- tent to judge of the qualities of the various kinds of stones nroposed IQ be tendered for as be, like the members of the oard, only gained his knowledge from practical experi- ence. Mr. SHAW said they were not discussing the abilities of the surveyor. Mr. Shaw was proceeding, when he was in- terrupted by Dr. McDoromx, who said: Mr. Chairman, I object to you being made a cat's-paw for Mr. Shaw to air his elo- quence and interrupt me. The CHAIRMAN: Do go on, doctor; though I think you are speaking wide of the mark. Dr. McDouGar.S. : I wish to explain. The CHAIRMAN : Yes, 4ce know you do: but pray go on. Dr. MeDountal.: I will go further, and say that I d. not think Mr. Barker is a geologist. (Laughter.) The CHAIRMAN : That is not a question for us to con- .

Dr. MCDOTGALL : He simply gains his knowledge from practical experience, as we all do. Mr. Suaw protested against the remarks of Dr. McDougall as did also several other members. Dr. McDoV6itr. observed that he must really ask the Chairman to request those individuals who had interrupted him to conduct themselves like gentlemen. It appeared to him that any person who came to that Board to express his opinions could not do so, as there was a persistent attempt to sneer him down. The CHAIRWAN: Will you please go on, doctor? Dr. McDornatc: I am offering an explanation on the conduct of some of the members. • The CEAIRMAN: Oh, yes; we know that. You are always offering explanations. (Laughter.) Speak to the minutes, and not about me being made a cat's-paw. That is not the truth. Go OR, sir, if you please. Dr. McDornatt said he was sorry he had used such a dignified term as cat's-paw in describing the course which had been taken. He considered the motives of the gentle- men who had adopted it very evident. r Mr. SHAW protested against the motives of members being brought into the discussion. After some further remarks, Dr. McDoromm said he im- puted nothing to anybody. The CRAIRMAri: Go on, sir ; go on, sir. Dr. MCDOUGALL did not see what benefit would be derived from adopting the amendment. The amendment was then put, and was supported by Messrs. Handley, Shaw, Collier, Meadowcroft, P. Speakman, Williams, Lyon, and Dobson. Messrs. McDougall and =peakman voted against it. The amendment was then car- ed aa the substantive motion, and the minutes approved. Taus DRAINAGE OF Tug INTENDED NEW 1102PITAL. The minutes of the Canal Boats and Hospital Committee state d that a letter had been received from the solicitors to the st, amais of Cholmondeley to the effect that the Commis- sioners. .1 could purchase for the trustees the land they required for the l_logeirtart. its full value or they could make a free area, not exceeding an acre, grant fo, teoeer ;ieusnesrveodt toanhias and the committee under the ied that the Law Clerk be to reply that recomtnen, -sioners would take a free grant of one acre.—A the Comm t ion had been placed before the Committee commun teat icoin, Weston, and Halton Water Works Corn- from the Rut the Board to pay particular attention to the I) toy. asking • intended hospital at Runcorn Hill, which drainage of the l should be most effectually done, so as to they considers'

prevent the the slightest contamination of the water intheir well. The site of the hospital was not far distant as the crow flevr, and the dip of the strata was exactly in that direction. It would be a fearful thing for any of the sewage to find its way to the water supply of the inhabitants of three townships and must be prevented at any coat. Mr. P. SPEAKMAN moved, and Mr. LYON seconded a motion 1 approving of the minutes. Mr. Siam said that in -Runcorn there were 15,000 people, but it seemed very singular that the sewage from so many houses was not taken into consideration it all by the Water- works' Company. hither it was possible to prevent the drain- age from the houses now erected from contaminating the water or it was not. If it was not, then the water company must admit that the water was contaminated already,in some respect, frown every dwelling in the town. FINANCE' The minutes of this committee recommended that the surveyor and secretary be empowered to visit several neigh- bouring local board offices for the purpose of obtaining information as to the working of the new order of accounts. It was decided that 40s. should be allowed as

expenses. The minutes were passed on the motion of Mr. Lvow, seconded by Mr. HANDLES. AN EXCESSIVE CHARGE ET THE REGISTIZAE, SEE. COLEBERN. THE AEDIT. The SECENTAIIT reported that at the audit of the accounts the auditor objected to the payment of 305. per annum to Mr. Coleburn, registrar of births and deaths for supplying a monthly return of the births, as being extravagant and . .

unnecessary . It was resolved, after a short discussion, on the motion of Mr. Strew, seconded by Mr. J. J. SPEAKMAN, that the practice be discontinued. The Sncrtrrartir ales said the auditor had drawn attention to the printing of the abstract of the committees' minutes. It was resolved, "That in the opinion of the Board the business could not be so efficiently or conveniently con- ducted if the members did not receive the printed agenda prior to the meetings." THE REVISED EYE-LAWS.

The committee appointed to revise the bye-laws reported that they had completed their work. It was decided that the revised building bye-laws be submitted to the Highway and Sanitary Committee for consideration ; and that the latter part of the recommendation be referred to the Hospital Committee.

THE CENSURE ON THE BOARD BY DARESBURY MAGISTRATES. The SECRETARY stated that he had received a reply from the clerk to the Daresbury magistrates, stating that the newspaper report of the remarks reflecting on the Commis- sioners as to the non-registration of a boat, was correct. It was decided that, as nothing further had been done, to report the alleged carelessness to the Local Government Board, the matter bc allowed to drop. CANON BARCLAY AND THE BOARD. Mr. Minot; wished to know whether there had beeu any further communication between Canon Barclay and the Board with reference to the recoat case against him. The CHAIRMAN said there bad not. Mr. SHAW: Does Mr. Dobson want to know whether the money has been paid? Mr. Donsow : I want to know how we stand with Canon Barclay at the present time. Mr. Strew: We stand this way; that we are bound to have the money. The LAW CLERK said that he gave notice for a special case, and that day he intended to ask for two of the mem- bers to enter into recognizances on behalf of the Commis- sioners, assuming that they intended to carry the case into the Court of Queen's Bench. It was decided that as the auditor had not yet completed his report, the Board should adjourn until it was finished, which it was expected would be done in a day or two. It was agreed that the next ordinary Board meeting should be held on Friday, the 3rd June.

div.head: RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIAN.
div.p: RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIAN.

The monthly meeting of this Board was held at Dutton Workhouse on Tutsday. The Rev. Canon Barclay presided, and there were also present the Rev. J. W. N. Tanner, and Messrs. John Ashton (vice-chairman), W. Handley, Thomas Norman, W. Whittaker, W. Fisher, J. Midwood, H. Broady, H. Lowe, J. Knowles, Charles Rigby, Thomas Lewis, J. Campkin, T. Andrews, J. Challoner, Thomas Wright, G. Whitlow, W. Jackson, J. DArbyshire, R. Ashton, W. Picker- ing,J. W. Baguley, John Weir, H. Neild, and W. H. Linaker (deputy clerk).

MASTER'S REPORT. The Miasma reported that there were 163 inmates in the house against 161 in the corresponding week of last year. There were 21 boys and 31 girls at the Workhouse school, and 12 boys and 21 girls receiving industrial training. Out- door relief had been given to 604 persons at a cost of £6l 6s. 10d., against 679 persons at a coat of £7O lls. in the cor- responding week of last year. MR. LOWE AND THE MASTER. Mr. Lowe, in accordance with previous notice, rose to speak in favour of a re-arrangement being made of the basis on which the family of Mr. Jones, the Workhouse master, were maintained. The system on which the master was at present charged had been in existence a number of years, and sadly needed altering. It had been said in favour of the comparatively low rate which Mr. Jones was paving, that his sons, who were out learning businesses, were only getting small remuneration; but ratepayers who put their children out to business had to meet the very same diffi- culty. He did not see why the master should reeeive excep- tional treatment because of this. Mr. HANDLEY, whilst of opinien that Mr. Lowe was quite justified in drawing attention to the matter, thought it would be a wiser coarse to refer it to the Visiting Com- mittee, so that they might investigate it, rather than to move any definite resolution that day. Mr. Jones was at present paying something like £3O per year for the Main- tenance of his children, and during the last 12 months' he had offered to make a new arrangement, but-the committee considered that the better coarse would be to leave it until the close of the official year, which had only just terminated. Mr. LOWE desired to know why the pocket of Mr. Jones should not be touched as well as those of the ratepayers. They must not forget that the gentleman in question was a man of independent means, as well as rooster of that house. As far as he (the speaker) less, concerned, he did not care about referring so many subjects to committees, for in such case a number of gentlemen might be elected, who might take a one-sided view of the subject under consideration. Mr. NORMAN agreed with the course adopted by Mr. Lowe in bringing the subject forward, but at the same time, he considered it would be well for the Visiting Committee to carefully consider the details of the question, and then bring it before the Board. Mr. Jotces, the master, was called into the room, and, in reply to questions by the Chairman, said that it wa& ten or eleven years since the last arrangement was made a. -to the maintenance of his children, at which time they ntmbered 11. It was decided that £5 should be deducted for each of them, with the exception of one. making £5O a year. Ile had now served the Board for 23-years, and he thought it was scarcely fair that they should try to reduce his income after such long service. Mr. LOWE said he did not believe in taking 2,1. or 3d. a week off a poor pauper, or Od. frcm some old woman—in whose case he should rather prefer to be a little extravagant —and letting the case of the master remain uninvestigated. He proposed that the two sons of nr. Jones (who were about 15 and 19 years of age), should pay 10s. per week.each for their maintenance. Mr. ANDREWS seconded the motion. Mr. HANDLEY moved an amendment, which wanaeconded by Mr. NIELD, in favour of referring the question to the Visiting Committee for consultation. Sixteen members voted for the amendment, and only four o which was declared lost. The eonrtigwinasal aratifteorwoan;ds put as the substantive motion, for al declared carried. The other business before the Board was not of public interest.

div.head: WIDNES POLICE COURT.
div.p: WIDNES POLICE COURT.

MONDLl.—Before Mr. F. H. Gossage (chairnaan), and Mr. Holbrooke Gaskell, junr. AN ALLEGED WHOLESALE SHOP ROBBER CAUGHT. George Redford, a middle aged man, was chaged with steal- ing a clock, value Bs., the property of Edward Loins, on the 31st of July, last year. Prisoner had deen apprehended on the previous Saturday, as he was leaving Walton gaol, where he had been imprisoned for felony. Some time ago the prisoner was apprehended at Wigan for shoprobbing, and on his house at Widnes being searched, it was found to contain an immense amount of stolen property. Prosecutor stated that he was a furniture dealer, carrying on business at Widnes- road. On the 31st July, 1880, he hung the clock produced outside the shop. He saw it safe at a quarter to nine in the evening, and a few minutes past nine, he found it had been stolen. He did net see it again until the 24th August last, when he had occasion to go to the prisoner's house in Mus- pratt-street. lie there saw the clock, which he identified as his property. P. C. Clarkson proved receiving the prisoner into custody as he was leaving gaol. Prisoner said he bought the clock on the Market-ground at St. Helens, for 6s. 9d. Prisoner was next charged with stealing two shirts, the pro- perty of John Noon, on the 23rd. August last. Prosecutor is a draper carrying on business in Anne-street, West; and on the date mentioned, about elevenjn the morning four woollen shirts were hung outside his shop. Th:y were seen at four o'clock, and missed shortly afterwards, when informationwas given to the police. Sergeant Eastham said that on the date named he searched the prisoner's house, and found. the shirts amongst a large number of other goods. They were shown to the prosecutor, who identified them as his property. Pe.soner made a somewhat similar defence to that in the last charge, alleging that the shirts were bought by him with some other articles, from a man who was hawking in the dis- trict. Prisoner was also charged with stealing two boxes of Caper tea, valued. at £2 16s. 10d., the property of Messrs. Ellewood & Co., tea dealers, Widnes. Mr. Joseph Smith. one of the partners in the firm, said that on the 23rd November, 1879, they received a consignment of four boxes of Caper tea at the Widnes-road shop. The boxes were delivered about three o'clock in the afternoon, but were allowed to stand out- I side the shop until room was made to take them inside. At dusk witness found that two boxes had been stolen. Sergeant Eastham said that on the 31st of last August, when searching the prisoner's house, he found the boxes now produced under a counter in the shop. One was broken into and the other was not. Prisoner was committed to the Liverpool Quarter Sessions for trial on each charge. STEALING SCRAP IRON. Thomas Quinn, Thomas Tansey, Peter Rawlinson. and John McDonnell, four youths, were charged with stealing scrap iron from the brickfield of Messrs. W. H. Kershaw and Co.—An engine driver, em- ployed by the prosecutor, stated tkat on the previous Fri- day morning, about half-past eleven, he saw the four prisoners picking up iron in a smithy on the brickfield, and they carried it into an adjoining field. They afterwards re- turned, but on seeing witness they dropped some iron and ran away. Witness followed them, and caught Quinn, whom he gave into custody.—McDonnell, who is only about eight years of age, was discharged with a caution. The other prisoners were ordered to receive six strokes with the birch rod. UNWARRANTABLE Assermr 051 & YOUTH.— Michael COD. my was charged. in custody, with unlawfully assaulting a youth named Michael Fowler. Complainant and the pri- soner were both engaged at Messrs. Hutchinson's works. It was part of Fowler's duty to ferry the man across the canal from one part of the works to another. On Wednesday, the prisoner went up to the complainant and charged him with wetting a besom belonging to him. Prisoner hit complainant several times in the face with the besom, and then struck him two or three times in the eye with his fist.—A witness was called who gave corroborative evidence.—The Inspector of Police said that the proceedings in the case had been in- stituted by Messrs. Hutchinson, who had discharged the prisoner, as they considered the assault a very unprovoked and aggravated one. Prisoner admitted that he assaulted the complainant, but said that if he (complainant) bad been looking after his own work, the affair would not have hap- pened.—The magistrtaes fined the prisoner 20s. and 9s. 6d. costs, and, in default of payment, ordered him to be corn- nutted to gaol one month. ioHisiorEo T alil, jDunrsrT. SCHOOL.— RILL WEDNESDAY.—Before Mr. Geo. Pilkington (chairman), and lir. COMMITTED Holbrook GO mi ske N Two Lens c Wm. Redford, James Liptrot, and Harriet Holland were each fined 6d. and 4s. 6d. costs for not sending their children to school.—Mr.Danby, clerk to the Widnes School Board, pro- secuted. The same gentleman also asked the Bench to send two lads named Thomas Burns and John Burns, who were constantly in bad company, and had proved entirely un- manageable by their parents, to an industrial school. The father was called in corroboration of Mr. Danby's statement, and he also expressed his willingness to contribute 3s. per week to the support of his children, whom the Bench com- mitted to Beacon-lane Industrial School until they are 16 years of age. KEEPERS OF DOGS WITHOUT LICENSES.—Peter Matthews, William Smith, and Thomas Hunt were each fined ss. and 12s. costs for keeping dogs without licenses.—The cases were proved by P.C. s Pitt and Clarkson. A YOUNG WOMAN STABBING WITH A TABLE KNIFE.- Catherine Cannon, aged about 19, was charged with assault- ing Catherine Macnamara. a married woman, with a table knife.—Complainant said that on the 30th ult., as she was sitting on her door step in High-street, the defendant seized her and stabbed her in the arm with a table knife.—Defen- dant denied the charge, and called her father, who said his daughter only endea enured to separate complainant and her mother who were having a struggle in the street. He was certain defendant did not use a knife ;—in fact they had only one knife in the house, and that had no handle to it.— The Chairman said the Bench considered the case proved, and such practices must be put a stop to, as far as possible, in that district. Defendant would haveto pay a fine of 20s. and costs, or be committed to prison one zionth.—She said she could not find the money. CATTLE DEALERS WITHOUT NECESSAWS CERTIFICAT James Burns, a Widnes butcher, was summoned for allowing a cow to be driven along the highway, at Ditton, without a certificate, and contrary to the provisions of the Contagious Diseases' (Animals) Act.—.% young man in his employ named Thomas Foyles was also summoned for driving the animal. P.C. Pechlar proved the case. The toaster pleaded that he was Merely taking the cow to be killed, and the man that he was acting under his employer's instructions. Burns was fined ss. and costs, and the police withdrew the summons against Foyles.—Joho Flewitt, a Ditton cow- keeper, was proved to have committed a similar offence at Ditton, on the 20th ult., when be was met by P.C. Peddar. Defendant was fined ss. and 12s. fici. costs.: STRIKING A WORSAN.—A married man named Joseph II Cook, was summoned for assaulting his sister, Vary Bratley. Complainant said she was at Ditton, on Sunday evening, when the defendant struck her in the eye with his fist, and causedit to be discoloured. Cook's defence was that com- plainant had threatened to hit him. •The Chairman said defendant's conduct was most disgraceful, and be would he fined 10s. and Is. 61 cos%. ANOTHER CASE OF SCRAP IRON STEALING.—John Dillon, and James Dillon, aged' 12 and 13 years respectively, were charged with stealing scrap iron from the the works of Messrs. Muspratt and Sons, chemical manufacturers. The boys were seen to take the iron by Mr. George Junor. a clerk employed' by the firm, who followed them to Simcock's marine store, in Appleton-street. The dealer was seen to weigh the iron, for which he agreed to give the lads six- pence. Tile elder boy was ordered to he given n:ne strokes with the birch rod, and the younger four. A DisuotrusT Worntstata—A fireman named Alfred Dear. den, employed at Messrs. Hutchinson's chemical works, was ch aged with stealing four pieces of timber, a joiner's chisel, and some leather belting, the property of the firm. Prisoner was on the night turn during the night of the 4th inat, and at about twenty minutes to one, was seen by P. C. Evans, who was on duty in Mersey-road, carrying the timber. He followed hien into Back James-street, and asked,Dearden where he had got the wood. He replied that it had been given him by the captain of a fiat. He afterward& searched the prisoner's house and found the belting. The chisel and timber were identified as being the property of the prosecu- tors, by a joiner named Thomas Barton, and the belting by a young man named Joseph Latchford. Ptisoner pleaded guilty, and was committed to gaol one month, with hard labour. A Licirsism APPLICATIOW..—A Runcorn sailmaker named Dutton, applied that a license of the Sportsman's Arms, Widnes, now held by a man named Wright, might be tem- porarily transferred to him. Superintendent Brindle said that the Runcorn superintendent of police (Mr. Williamson, did not consider the applicant a fit man to hold the license and he had. to oppose thee granting of it The Bench ad- journed the hearing of the ease for one week.

THE CHARGE OF THEFT AGAINST A BUTCHER.—HaITY Harrison a butcher's assistant, was charged on remand, with stealing Sibs. of suet, 3lbs. of beef, four iron weights, one saw, 24 beef hooks, and 100 skewers the property of his master, Mr. George Booth, of Regent-street. Most of the evidence was similar to that reported in the last issue of the Examiner.—Walter Albert Wynne, who occasionally works for the prosecutor, said that on the previous Wednesday afternoon he told the prisoner about the suet being in the slaughter-house, when Harrison said he wished he had let him know before, as he would have put it in his pocket. In the evening he met the prisoner at the Barleymow public- house, and it was arranged that Harrison should fetch the suet on the following morning. He afterwards told the prosecutor, and on Thursday morning, he (witness) saw Harrison take it out of the slaughter-house.—Mr. Beasley defeuded,and said he considered the evidence of the last witness strongly in favour of his client, and he should advise him to plead not guilty, and let the case go to the Sessions. Prisoner adopted the advice of his solicitor, pleaded not guilty, and was committed to the Knutsford Quarter Sessions for trial. A DANGEROUS PRACTICE.—John Ford, a carter, was fined 20s. and costs 9s. 6d., for being found asleep in his cart on the 19th ult., at noon, in Hatton-read, by Sergeant Walley. A GOOD FRIDAY'S VISIT TO HALTON CASTLE INN.— Henry Earlam and Francis Branmon, were each fined 2s. 6d., and costs 10s. 6d., for having been found in the Halton Castle Hotel, occupied by Mr. Berthold Rehberg, on Good Friday last, during prohibited hours.—Mrs. Rehberg explained that the men got into the house without permission and contrary to her husband's wish.—P.C. Lowndes gave evidence in the ease. NEGLECTING TO MAINTAIN A STEF-SON.—George Water- worth, the step-father of Wm. By. Dunbavin, had an order made upon him to contribute towards the maintenance of the lad at the rate of Is. per week during his stay in the Bleasdale Reformatory, to which he has been committed until he is 16 years of age. TRANSFER DAY.—The following transfers were made:— Public-houses: Dock Hotel, Weston Point, from Eliza Okell to John Roughsedge ; Mariners' Hotel, Percival-lane, from Thomas Hodgkinson to John Walker; Devonshire Hotel, Ashridge-street, from Wm. Roger Wass to George Shone. Beer-houses: Volunteer Inn, Granville-street, from William Bushell to Wm. Green; Angel Inn, Wellington-street, from Murdock Campbell Nicholson to Thomas Hodgkinson; Nag's Head, Regent-street, from John Healey to James Payne. CLAIM FOR SEAMEN'S WAGES.—Mr. William RabillSOß Smith, solicitor, Mr. John Edward Evans accountant, and Mr. Samuel James Goldsworthy, grocer, Al cf Swansea, and owners, or part owners, or part owners, of the brigantine "Topaz," were summoned by seamen formerly employed upon that vessel, for the following amounts due for wages: —James Stroyan, £l4 10s. id. ; Thomas E. Davies, £l4 13s. lid.; Oliver Bristow, £l4 Ss. lid.; Jacob Williams, £l4 13s. 7d.; and Alfred Browitt, £l6 13s. 3d. Mr. Burton appeared for the complainants, and Mr. Lake (Messrs. Day and Lake) for the defence. The amounts sued for included 4s. 7d. per day for each able seaman since the date of their discharge. The vessel had been seized under an order from the Court of Admiralty. The various complainants signed articles at Swansea, for a voyage to Spain, at the rate of £2 12s. 6d. per month; and they were discharged at Run- corn on the 16th March. Since that date the men had been waiting for a settlement, but, owing to the ',easel being in the hands of the officers of the Court of Admiralty, it could not be seized for the wages.—Mr. Burton said he thought it only fair that the seamen should be allowed the legal ex- penses to which they had been put owing to their wages not being paid.—Mr. Ashton (magistrates' clerk) said the Mer- chant Shipping Act did not permit the Bench to grant such costs.—After some remarks from Mr. Lake, the magistrates said they would allow the amount usually granted in that court for the advocate's fee (10s. 6d.) in each case.— Evidence was then given in support of the claims by the eeanien whose names are mentioned above; and the magis- trates made an order for the various sums claimed. I WEDNESDAY.—Before Mr. John Brundrit and Mr. S. B. Chadwick. ASSAULTING A PARAMOUR.—Jonathan Thomas, brought up under a warrant, was charged with having, on the let lost, assaulted Martha Worthington.--Complainant stated that she had formed an improper connection with the prisoner, who was a sailor, and had lived with him five years. He returned to Runcorn on Sunday, and, as she happened to be out of the house, he went to. a neighbour's to enquire about her. Here he was told a number of tales, which she alleged to be untrue, about' her, and when he afterwards found his way home, he struck her on the face, knocked her down, and kicked her several times. She asked the magis- trates to deal leniently with the man, as she took out the warrant whilst angry.—The Bench said they would accede to her request, and only fine the prisoner 10s. and 12s. 100. costs; er in default of payment, 14 days' imprisonment.

WESLEYAN BAZAAA AT WARRINGTON. Tb. 4 Warringten Pu'.lic Hall has not for a long time had the charming appearance it possessed on Tuesday last, the day upos which the Wesleyan bazaar was opened. In con- nection wide Warrington Wesleyan Methodism, several bazaars, dic., have been held, the first of which took place in 1840 and was a great success, and the last, which was held about six years ago, was also a most gratifying success. In holding the present bazaar the Wesleyans have several objects in view. Of late years the cht:pel in Bold-street has worn a very sombre aspect, and it was thought the time had come when the edifice should be renovaZed and beautified, a process which the chapel has only onco undergone since it was opened. The exterior of the Wesley cOapel in Bewsey- roadand the ministers' houses, which are situate in Palmyra- square, and Bewsey-road, also require to be.' dealt with in a similar manner. A further object is the I,woposal to build class rooms adjoining Wesley Hall, Silver-sweet. In this ball the Sunday school connected with Bevraey-road chapel is conducted, and on week days the hall is usa.l as a day school, which is under Government inspection. :1.1,0 attendance of the scholars, however, is so large that th e managers are required, owing to the reports of Her Majesty's Inspectors, to provide at once more room for the younger children. The final object of the promoters of the bazaar is to provide funds to liquidate a number of small debts, that have been incurred in connec- 'ion with the circuit work, the most notable of which

The MA.YOR' in reply, said as mayor of the borough he thought it his duty to be present—(hear, hear),—and on all occasions to assist those who were doing their best to pro- mote the good of the town. .Finis coronat opus. He hoped that the work would be done, and that at the end of the bazaar they would have plenty of funds in hand to carry out what they so much wished for. (Applause.) The sale of articles was then proceeded with. There was very little in the way of exhibitions and enter- tainments for the instruction and amusement of visitors, but what was lacking in quantity was certainly compensated for by the excellency of those provided. Mr. Rigby gave exhi- bitions of the art of glass engraving, and executed several in- teresting desians in the presence of a large number of spec- tators. Mr. Rigby also exhibited a number of tumblers and goblets which had been most artistically engraved, and on one of the goblets was a faithful representation of the War. rington Town Hall, and a view of the pond in Bank Park. The amusements consisted solely of an unique exhibition described as a "living waxwork.'; Following the custom of proprietors of waxwork exhibitions, the collection had been divided into chambers, of which there were three—the cham- ber of horrors, the kingly, and domestic chambers. In the first-named chamber were several villainous looking charac- ters who would have done credit to a genuine chamber of horrors. The kingly chamber contained only one exalted w.,,ersonage.—" Old King Cole," who reminded the audience that he "was a jolly old soul," by complacently smoking a chutshwarden on undergoing the process of "winding up." The mt:st mirth-prodaking model in the domestic chamber wal "Mrs. 41,7n510w," who showed the efficaciousness of her "soothing ecrup" by administering the contents of a bottle of that mixture to the child upon her knees. The exhibition would have been incomplete without a prodigy of some kind, but there were two models of this description a "Chinese giant," and the "Siamese twins." The general "get ap" of the figures was iNcl in ra b e, and the "models" are to be com- mended for their clever imitations of automata, fortitude with which they endured the ordeal of exhibition, being the sourse of much wonderment. The entertainment concluded with the exhibition of a live "Zulu," whose grotesque war dances excited the risibilitiec of the audience. The show waslargely patronised and proved a fruitful sourceof revenue but we ought to state that much of its success was due to the untiring energy of the showman, Mr. A. Woods, (whose des- cription of the disasters experianced by his figures reminded owe of the "outrage" on Artemus Ward's famous collection), and his assistants, Messrs. J. Butterworth, J. Dutton, E. Boyle, and F. Booth, the latter acting as pianist. The proceeds of the bazaar during the three days was as follows :—No. 1 stall, £92 17s. 11d.; No. 2 stall, £214 ss. 4d.; No. 3 stall, £l6l 4e. 4d. ' • No. 4 stall, £l5l 2. ed.; No. 5 stall, £95 78.0 d. ' • The Misses Coleman and Smith, £6 7s. id; Flower stall, £l5 15s. Od. ; Refreshment stall, £4l ; 607 pennies collected by Mrs. Harvey, £2 10s. 7d.; Waxwork exhibition, £l7 ; Entrance Money, £5l 15s. Od ; Proceeds of sewing meetings, £lB 12s. id.; total, £867 16s. 10d.

, is a debt contracted by the re-pewing and im- provement of the chapel in Martinscroft. About nine months ago the funds of the circuit were found to be in a very discouraging condition, and when the matter came under the notice of the quarterly meeting, at which all financial arrangements are discussed, it was suggested that a bazaar should be held as the best means of putting the finances on a proper footing. The suggestion met with cordial approval, and was immediately acted upon. A meeting of the ladies of the denomination was called, and the eta te of affairs having been explained to them, they at once concurred in the idea of a bazaar, and entered into the project with much spirit. Numerous sewing meetings were held, at which the ladies worked with praiseworthy perseverance to convert yards of calico and other material into articles of wearing apparel, drc., and the result of their labours was seen on Tuesday in the magnificent and valuable array of goods which were so temptingly displayed on the several stalls. The stalls, which were five in number, were erected under the gallery, and had been neatly and attractively decorated. The foot of each was prettily ornamented with a sort of trellis work formed of muslin and blue baize while from the top arose a canopy of crimson baize, bordered with muslin. On the peak of the canopy there stood with outstretched wings a small white eagle, from whose feet hung a large ring containing a gas globe, which was utilised at night for illu- mination purposes. The spaces between the several cano- pies were relieved by shields and flags in various designs, and the general effect of the decorations was greatly heightened by the judicious disposition of flags and banners, and several arches of evergreens which spanned the body of the ball. The pleasing appearance of the hall reflected much credit upon Menssrs. S. E. and R. Johnson, who had charge of the decorations, and much praise is due te Mr. Henry Collin for the active part he took in setting out and superintending the erection of the stalls and the various decorative arrangements. On No. 1 stall, which was presided over by Mrs. W. J. Horton, Mrs. Isaac Hayward, and Miss Hayward, the most noticeable objects comprised a doll elegantly attired in satin, a gipsy table, several pairs of beautifully worked gentlemen's slipppers, which, before the bazaar commenced, were marked " sold; " a pair of brackets neatly worked in leather and a pair in needlework, beaded breakfast tray and footstools, a number of lady's embroidered aprons, and beau- tiful antimacassars, tea cosies, toilet tidies, music stool covers, three cages containing canaries, whose vocal per- formances attracted considerable attention, a large stock of infantile clothing, and an assortment of toys, etc. An interesting collection of china, vases, terracotta figures, plaques, epergnes, plain and also beautifully-painted china flower pots, glass, epergnes and flower steeds was exhibited on No. 2 stall. The other articles which arrested the attention of the visitor included two neat gipsv tables, banneretts, photo frame; work boxes, brackets, Japanese umbrellas, ottomans' albums, Japanese antimacassars, tea cosies, a group of dolls variously attired, and a host of other articles useful aid ornamental. This stall was in charge of Mrs. W. rs. E. J. Guest, Mrs. Jones, Mrs. Richar- dson, and Miss Dutton,&Hos. At the stall under the superintendence of Mrs. W. Benson, Mrs. W. P. Chorley, Mrs. R. W. Collin, and Mrs. James Muir, there was a large variety of goods, which were attractively displayed. Amongst the more conspicuous were several dollssbeds and swing cradle, banneretts, pair of horns, flower fern stand, a number of pictures, leather work baskets, fancy baskets, fancy cushon under glass shade, drawing cabinet, trinkets, a nice assortment of earthenware, and a large array of anti- maccassars and juvenile wearing apparel. Mrs. J. Bennett and Mrs. R. Cook presided over No. 4 stall,. on which were a really handsome drawing chair worked in crewels and satin, a beaded breakfast tray, a variety of fancy cosies and cushions, a gipsy table hand- somely worked in crewel; several brackets worked in the same materials, beautifully-worked footstools, elegant pairs of slippers, garden and glass vases, flower stands, a quantity of toilet and other mats, and a number of dolls and doll perambulators. There were also two basket chairs, a sewing machine, a large assortment of ladies' underclothing, together with a quantity of household linen and a host of I other articles of a miscellaneous character. The most striking objects on the fifth and last stall, devoted to the sale of "useful and ornamental" articles comprised two oil paintings, by Frantz Huard, handeemely framed; a splendid drawing room chair, footstools, break- fast tray, screens and brackets, wall basket, vases, china and glassware, card baskets and gipsy tables, toilet soaps and ecents, pretty pincussions, and several copies of " St. Paul's Epistle to the Romans" by the Rev. J. A. Beet; the other articles on the stall consisting of the indispensable collec- tion of antimacassars, infantile clothing, toys, dec. The ladies in charge of the stall were Mrs. E. 0. Coleman, Mrs. J. A. Beet, Mrs. W. Barlow, and Mrs. T. Starkey Smith. At the foot of the platform was located a flower stall, under the superintendence of Miss Garnett and the Misses Dutton, and upon it had been effectively placed numerous flowers, which emitted a most fragrant odour. On the platform was an appropriate background to the flower °MI' in the shape of an arch of white calico, and decorated wit evergreens and flags, a large mirror being placed beneath. DETERMINED ATTACK UPON THE LIFE OF A ST. HELENS POLICENIAN. On Monday, at the St. Helens Police Court, before Messrs. W., and W. W. Pilkington, in a full court, James Donoghue, a young man, was charged with assaulting P.C. John Groarke, to which charge the prisoner pleaded guilty.— Superintendent Johnston said this was a most unprovoked assault on the police. The body of a man who had been for some time missing, had been taken from the canal and de- posited at the nearest public-house, kept by Mr. Elliott. P.C. Groake on Sunday afternoon went to the public-house to learn the particulars of the case, and whilst there the prisoner tried to get in through the back yard, as he ex- pressed it, to see the body. He was told that he could not see the body, as it was being laid out, but the prisoner per- sisting in his attempts to get in, the police officer went out to him and told him to go away. He refuse 1, and de- liberately struck the officer in the face. By this time they had got in the middle of the street, where twenty or thirty people had assembled, and a struggle ensued between the officer and the prisoner. The crowd increasing, jostled the two about until they got to the canal. They then shouted, "Drown him," and prisoner tried to throw the officer into the canal, but fortunately the rails did good service until another officer came on the scene.—P.C. Groarke, on being sworn, gave evidence to the above effect, adding that if no one had come to his assistance, he believed he would have gone into the canal. When at the rails he got his staff out to defend himself, and he dealt a blow upon the prisoner, who seized the staff and threw it into the canal. The canal had been dragged, but the staff could not be found. He was black and blue all over, and was very sore.—Superintendent Johnston exhibited one of prisoner's clogs.—Prisoner said , the officer was drunk.—Mr. Elliott, keeper of the Phoenix , public-house, corroborated the statement of the officer so far as it related to what occurred up to the time of the struggle in-the street.—P.C. Hossack said a woman told him that a policeman had been thrown into the canal, and he went with all haste to the spot. He found the officer and the prisoner on the ground together. On their way to the Town Hall, the prisoner kicked P.C. Groarke very violently. Prisoner had some drink in him.—The magistrates said they did not believe the statement that the officer was drunk.—A long list of convictions against the prisoner for assaults on the police, &c, was shown to the Bench, but there were no con- victions from 1876 to 1880, during which time he had been in the army. In December last he was sent to prison for two months for an assault on the police. The Superinten- dent said he had been told that the prisoner, while serving in the armv, spmt nearly the whole of his time in gaol.— The magistrates said it was a very fortunate thing for the prisoner that the policeman was not put into the canal, as there was but little chance for a man with his clothes on to get out. Considering his previous bad character and the very serious attempt made upon the life of the officer, they would give him the full penalty, and send him to prison for nine months, with hard labour.—Annie Smith, half-sister to the last prisoner, about 15 years of age, was also charged with assaulting P.C. Groarke, on Sunday. While the officer had the last prisoner in cnstody, she kicked him, pulled his hair, and threw stones at him. Several stones hit him on • the back.—The magistrates said they did not like to send her to prison being so young, but she would be kept in the lockups for a day; and the offence would be written down • against her, so that if she was brought up again she would get into trouble. .

div.head: CENSUS. PRESCOT UNION.
div.p: THE CENSUS. PRESCOT UNION.

Thu- census returns for the Frescot Union, which com- prises. 20 townships, were completed on Wednesday, and show the total population of the entire union to be 117,938, as against 92,509 in 1871, being an increase during the decade of 25,429. In the townships comprising St. Helens (including the rural portion of Eccleston), the increase during the IC years has been 12,453, and in Widnes 10,587. A rather extraordinary feature revealed by. the census is, that there is in St. Helens, a predominance of males over the females to the number of 2410, while in Widnes there are 1,946' more males than females. In Preseot, although the population has decreased every census, this year's returns show an increase, in spite of the bad state of trade in the town, of 469. In 1871 the census showed that the populatbre of the union had decreased in only two townships —Prescot and Knowsley—but the returns just taken, show a decrease in Bold, Hale, Knowsley, RANI!, Tarbock, Much Woolton, and Speke. In the latter township there has been a decrease of 432, and in Much Wootton a decrease of 107. The reterns are as follow :- 1881. 1871. HOW TO BE SUCCESSFUL Deal fairly with everybody, give good Svalue, and never disappoint your cus- ptomers by not having an ordereompleted at the promised time. Be polite and lEcivil with every one, and attend strictly' Rto the various requirements of your , patrons. In the Tailoring trade it is necessary, above all things to employ good cotters, use the very best materials only, and employ the most skilful workmen to make up every garment. Besides this it is essential that the work. men employed should be close at hand so as to be under the supervision of the A Hcutters, otherwise—as is the case at some establishments—the garment is often spoiled.
